#3415. These Are the Best Early Black Friday Deals on Cordless Power Tools

Becca Lewis is home maintenance writer who aims to foster confidence in and inspire DIY enthusiasts at all skill levels.

Becca attended Southern Connecticut State University, where she studied technical theater and design. She has a background in carpentry and fabrication and has worked in specialty shops, using a wide variety of tools and materials, for more than 20 years.

If you have a DIY enthusiast on your list—or if you just want some new tools for your own projects—Black Friday sales are a good time to snag low prices on quality tools. Lots of big box stores are looking to thin out their inventory and make room for next year’s upgrades, so in addition to encouraging a holiday rush, retailers are motivated to price things to move. If you know what to look for, you can get up to 65% off on trusted brands. Here are a few of the best deals out there right now.

If you’re building a new cordless tool set, or updating your battery system, getting a cordless tool set can save you some money because these combos usually include batteries and a charger, which can be the most expensive part of your tool set. Here are a few of the best early Black Friday deals on cordless tool sets.

The Ryobi 6-tool 18-volt combo set is on sale for $199, 33% off its regular price at Home Depot. The set comes with a drill, an impact driver, a circular saw, a sawzall, an oscillating multi-tool, a work light, a 1.5-amp-hour battery, a 4-amp-hour battery, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a good deal on a trusted home tool brand.

The Ryobi 18-volt drill and driver set is on sale for $99, 34% off its usual price at Home Depot. The set comes with a drill, an impact driver, two 1.5-amp-hour batteries, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a great starter set because it has the first two tools you need for a cordless kit and it comes with batteries so you can expand your set for cheaper as you develop your skills.

The Ryobi 4-tool, 4-volt project set is on sale for $99, 61% off its typical price at Home Depot. This set comes with a rotary tool, a project light, a glue pen, a mini drill, two rechargeable batteries, a charging cable, a set of starter rotary bits, and three glue sticks. This set is handy for DIY projects that require fine detail, like wood carving, craft projects, or framing pictures.

The DeWalt drill and driver combo set is on sale for $129, 46% off its regular price on Amazon. This set includes a drill, an impact driver, 2 1.5-amp-hour batteries, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a good deal on a trusted brand for drills and drivers, and a good start for a cordless DIY tool set.

If you have a cordless tool set already and you want to expand your kit, or if you have a DIYer in your life who already has a particular brand of battery and you want to get them something they can use, a single tool deal can be just the thing.

The DeWalt 20-volt compact drill/driver is on sale at Home Depot for $99, 45% off its usual price. This tool comes with a 20-volt, 2-amp-hour battery and a charger, so it’s ready to use out of the box. It’s a good first tool for a set.

The Milwaukee 18-volt impact wrench is on sale at Home Depot for $199, 68% off its typical price. This tool comes with two 5-amp-hour batteries and a charger, so it’s ready to use out of the box. This is a good tool for driving bolts through tough materials and for automotive projects.

The DeWalt 20-volt oscillating multi-tool is on sale at Home Depot for $99, 50% off its regular price. This tool comes with a 2-amp-hour battery and a charger, so it's ready to use out of the box. This is one of the most versatile cordless tools, allowing you to cut a wide range of materials and use a sanding attachment to do finishing work as well.

The Milwaukee 18-volt tire inflator kit is on sale at Home Depot for $199, 65% off its usual price. This tool comes with two 5-amp-hour batteries and a charger, so it’s ready to go right out of the box. This is an excellent addition to your emergency roadside tool set because you can use it to inflate a car tire with the charged 18-volt batteries.

The DeWalt 12-volt cordless powered ratchet is on sale at Lowe’s for $99, 50% off its typical price. This is a tool-only deal, so you’ll need a DeWalt 12-volt battery and charger to use it. This is a good tool for working on cars or for home appliance maintenance because it can fit into tight spaces.

The Makita 18-volt cordless electric 2-inch brad nailer is on sale on Amazon for $336.19, 36% off its regular price. This is a tool only deal, so you’ll need a Makita 18-volt battery and charger to use it. This is a good tool for attaching trim or paneling.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday, November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

#3413. Jesse Eisenberg and Julianne Moore on ‘The Debut,’ Testing AI to ‘Make Sure It’s Bad’ and Hoping ‘Now You See Me 4’ Gets Made

Awards Circuit Podcast: The roundtable discusses the “Blue Tsunami” on Election Day, and the movies still to come.

Jesse Eisenberg has a confession about the biggest moment in “The Debut.”

When the crowd at the Telluride world premiere broke into mid-film applause after a showdown between Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti, also known as “the rent is due” scene, his first thought wasn’t relief.

“Oh no! Can they go on the ride?” he recalls to Variety. That’s because the next scene is dramatic. “If you’re a paranoid and worried person, all signs lead to panic.” Related Stories 'Baywatch' Reboot Sets January Premiere Date on Fox

That’s the man who wrote, directed, produced, scored and stars in the A24 musical comedy, which has taken awards season by storm. He also built the entire film around his muse, Oscar winner Julianne Moore, who plays Mona Friedman, a shy housewife who picks up a flyer and auditions for a community theater musical for the first time in her life. Eisenberg wrote the role for her.

On this episode of the Variety Awards Circuit podcast, we sit down with the two collaborators to discuss their latest film, their anxieties about the future of the industry and Eisenberg’s hopes for another “Now You See Me” sequel. Listen below!

Moore has been nominated for five Academy Awards — supporting actress for “Boogie Nights” (1997) and “The Hours” (2002) and lead actress for “The End of the Affair” (1999), “Far From Heaven” (2002) and “Still Alice” (2014), winning for the latter. Eisenberg was nominated for best actor for his portrayal of Mark Zuckerberg in David Fincher’s “The Social Network” (2010) and for best original screenplay for “A Real Pain” (2024), which won supporting actor for Kieran Culkin.

A24’s “The Debut,” Eisenberg’s third feature as a director, had its world premiere at the Telluride Film Festival to rave reviews. It has since played the Toronto, New York and Middleburg Film Festivals, the latter of which is where this podcast episode was recorded.

Moore has spent decades as Todd Haynes’ muse. Now she belongs to Eisenberg, too. When I ask whether he’s warned Haynes off, he says jokingly, “He gets it.” Eisenberg’s explanation for why directors keep coming back to her is one of the best cases for her career I’ve heard in a while. He gets “pissed off” reading reviews of “May December” that praise its depth and darkness without recognizing what he sees: “an unbelievably brilliant comic creation.” She has, he says, “a funny bone within drama that is so unusual,” the kind drama school trains out of you.

A24 opens “The Debut” in theaters on Dec. 11

The conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Eisenberg: Oh my God, of course. You hope there’s some sentient reaction from the audience. But there’s another weird thing that’s less expected. When you’re working on a movie, you’re working on it for two or three years and everybody you’re working with is an ally. No one’s criticizing it or poking holes in it, except in good-natured ways. It’s, “Can we try this? Can we try that?” So you forget that it’s going to be critiqued, and you forget that it could be a disaster because you’ve spent three years with people who all love it. At that point, this little moment of panic creeps in because you realize this whole thing could have been for naught. So the fact that there was a great reaction to it, an audible reaction, is a kind of relief.

Eisenberg: I have such paranoia that my first thought after it gets huge applause and laughter is, “Oh no! Can they go on the ride?” Because the next scene is dramatic. If you’re a paranoid and worried person, all signs lead to panic.

Moore: She was completely original, and so original on the page. It’s an extraordinary feat of writing and character development that Jesse just handed me. I’m so lucky to embody someone right on the brink of change. She’s relatable because she’s all of us who’ve been in a place where we know we want something different, but we don’t know what it is and we’re willing to take a chance. What leads her to that place? Why does she pick up that flyer and audition for the first time in her life? She’s following a desire without knowing where it will lead her. She doesn’t know anything. She’s so literal in her understanding, and she goes on a complete voyage of character development, finding community, meaning and purpose. Mona, in a sense, is any of us who’ve tried something new.

Eisenberg: That’s such a nice and perceptive question. I didn’t think I wanted the audience to be off balance. All I wanted to do was create a subjective story. Because the movie is about the world of musical theater, it gave me permission to make a heightened movie, because we’re living in that theme and tone. So whatever Julianne is feeling in a particular scene is heightened 20% in that direction. If she’s feeling scared, she’s walking past people warming their hands over a garbage can fire in this fantastical-looking, terrifying 1920s version of a city. If she’s feeling welcomed, then it’s Halle Bailey, the world’s sweetest person and loveliest actress, coming to tell her, “I know we’ve just met, but I can tell we’re going to be sisters.” I wanted everything to be filtered through this woman, who’s a baby and has experienced such invisibility. That’s why it sometimes feels fantastical in a positive way, with Halle, who’s wonderful in the movie and sometimes overly terrifying, like the scenes with Paul Giamatti, who’s a genius. It’s all about what she’s feeling, not objective reality.

Eisenberg: When we were looking for titles for this movie, my friend suggested “Rent” because it’s a musical and it’s all about her getting the rent.

Eisenberg: I think we looked into it. No, it would be too comic.

Moore: First of all, oh my God, thank you. It’s unbelievably flattering to be called someone’s muse. It’s unbelievably rewarding to spark someone’s imagination and to think you’ve been part of their creative process in any way. That’s the most magnificent thing as an actor: having a real collaboration. That’s what we’re all about. Jesse wrote a movie about a creative journey and where it happens, and it happens in community. It happens with another person. We don’t do what we do alone. We can’t. It’s even reflected in the relationship with Paul’s character. People talk about him being an antagonist, an adversary. He’s not at all. He’s her creative partner. He grows with her, and at a certain point, he has to say, “Now you’re on your own. Now you perform. I’ve taught you as much as I can teach you, and now you go.” It’s everything I’ve ever wanted in my career: to have people who want to work with me and to somehow add to their work as well.

I’m always saying I got one shot at this, and if we do it again, then OK, now I know I can do it.

Moore: I was jealous, though, because he said, “I’m doing this movie.” He had already written “A Real Pain” and was on his way to make it when we finished “When You Finish Saving the World.” I’m like, “There’s not a part for me in it?”

Eisenberg: It’s funny that you brought up her being a muse for people because, while you were asking, I was trying to think about what that means. It’s something quite specific. It’s not just that this person is phenomenal and famous, and it certainly has nothing to do with “Oh, she can help me get my movie financed.”

Eisenberg: It’s purely creative. There’s something so unbelievably funny about her that I find gets overlooked when I read notices about her movies, because she’s also this glamorous, phenomenal dramatic actress. I always get pissed off when I read responses to “May December.” Everybody’s like, “This wonderful performance, so rich in depth and darkness.” It is all those things. But I watch it as an unbelievably brilliant comic creation. “Far From Heaven,” again, another dramatic thing, but there’s such humor in the repression she’s experiencing. Maybe that’s why people love her so much. She has a funny bone within drama that’s so unusual, because you go to drama school and they don’t encourage you to be funny.

Eisenberg: Exactly, and don’t you dare compromise the stakes by having a funny bone. She’s so naturally funny without ever being a comic, and it’s so rare. I think for people like Todd Haynes, who I don’t know that well but know is funny, that’s a real joy.

Moore: Jesse’s wonderful about putting stakes in real life. So often, I read screenplays and the only way they’re able to create stakes is through a murder, a missing child or an asteroid that’s going to hit the Earth. Yes, obviously there are stakes involved in that, but there are stakes in everyday life. Is somebody going to call you? Is the meeting going to go well? Are you going to burn dinner? There are stakes, and they matter to us. The fact that Jesse can invest his films with those kinds of emotional stakes is really interesting to me, because I think that’s how we live. That’s who we are.

Eisenberg: Also, with the asteroid stuff, anybody would react the same way, which is panic. Whereas, if you have a real character, they’re putting life-and-death stakes on something the rest of us might not agree with. She wants to be in this play. I think 90% of people, if Paul Giamatti yelled at you on the first day of rehearsal, would just quit the show. But because this person is coming into this world with so little, she ends up imbuing this silly thing with life-and-death stakes and then we can relate.

Moore: I loved it. I thought it was so funny as written, and I was also worried it would be distracting. So how do you imbue this action with enough meaning that it’s equally funny but not distracting when you’re trying to do something emotional? Oddly, it’s her first engagement in an imaginary circumstance, which is what they teach you in acting. How do you make something real when it’s not real? How do you make an audience believe it’s really happening? If you make the audience believe it, they won’t laugh. You can laugh at it from out there, but when you see her doing it and making it real, it won’t distract from the emotional content. It’s something you do when you’re first starting out: stir a pot, open a door, button a shirt. You’re pretending, but it has to be exact and you have to believe it, too. I did say to Jesse when he was putting it together, “Is it distracting? Is the smoking weird?” He was like, “Nope. It’s perfect.”

Eisenberg: It’s also a woman discovering her sensuality — not sexuality, but sensuality — where she’s starting to feel things in her body. She’s drinking. It’s what happens to an actor. You try to open yourself up to sensuality.

Moore: I think we all tend to look forward, not back. When you’re living your life, you’re just like, “What’s next? What’s in front of me? What am I working on? What am I eating next? When’s breakfast?” You don’t reflect on what you’ve done, and sometimes, as people mention it, you’re like, “Oh, yeah, that movie.” Something odd happens. You construct something, and then you forget it in performance as well, because there’s an unconscious aspect to performing. You want to be prepared enough that when you’re actually doing it, you lose consciousness of your actions and that in itself leads to forgetting. Sometimes, if I see things I’ve done, I’m like, “I don’t remember doing that with my head or walking that way or making that vocal choice.” You do it, and then it’s behind you. I never think about it. I’m just grateful that I have something to do, because that’s what propels me. What am I doing? What am I engaged in?

Eisenberg: It’s funny to hear Julianne Moore, and I’m using your full name on purpose, talk about just looking forward, because her career has touched so many people and contributed so much to culture. I feel the same way, and I see it as fear. What will I be doing next? What will I work on? Part of the reason I’m doing so many different things isn’t just because I have this amazing, creative, expansive mind. It’s because I’m kind of terrified that none of them will work out. Doing five jobs on this movie is how I protect myself for the future. I can be a writer if you want that, or I can go direct a deodorant ad or something and, worst case, I can promise you I can do it because I did “The Debut.” I have that feeling about everything. We’re in an unstable industry, and I don’t do well with instability in general.

I’ve been thrust into this job, which I’m very lucky to have, but it’s not a good job for my personality and wiring. My counter to that is to try to do as many things as possible. And I am unpretentious. The next movie I want to do more than anything is “Now You See Me 4,” and I’m praying that they write it, because I love that more than anything. I don’t have this feeling that, now that I’m directing these more independent, serious movies, I don’t want to be in something a little more Hollywood-ish. I like working. I feel so lucky to have done what I do, and I feel so hopeful that I get to do it more.

Moore: I was thinking about this just this morning. Creatives keep appearing. I was thinking about talking to young people because I’m going to do a master class at SCAD when I’m down there. A friend I worked with a long time ago runs the department. What do you say to students? What I always say is, “These are your peers. Look around. You’re going to be working with these people. Your creative life starts now.” People keep emerging, and we always act surprised. “Oh my God, look at this filmmaker.” But they were there. Here they come. You don’t know that the 22-year-old you spoke to at SCAD will be the next big filmmaker in 10 years. People talk about the business, but it’s really about the stories people are telling. What are they writing? What are they directing? Where are these actors coming from? They keep being born.

Moore: Absolutely not. This charming, wonderful young actor emerged in “Roger Dodger” and people were like, “Look at this kid.” You were what, 17?

Moore: So his acting career started then, but no one would have said, “Oh, he’s going to be a really important filmmaker.” And yet, there he was.

Eisenberg: I have a paranoid answer for this. I’m totally paranoid. I sometimes experiment with AI to see whether it’s good at writing. And it’s still not. I’m paranoid, so I check and it still isn’t. Thank God. I say, “Write a scene like this.” I’m just testing it to make sure it’s bad, and it’s still bad. So I’m relieved, but, like, how far away is it from being good? How far are we from a kid putting on a pair of goggles and saying, “I want to watch a movie about me where I rob a bank and then kiss the girl I’m in love with at school. Here are pictures of her, here are pictures of me” and then they press play? I’m paranoid about that.

The saving grace is two things. One is what Julianne said: Creative spirit will find ways to entertain and delight us and speak about things in a way that maybe computers won’t. The other thing I think about all the time, and she’s about to go to a play in New York, is that I do these Greek plays, which were written 2,500 years ago and we perform them the same way they were performed 2,500 years ago. If they’ve lasted that long, they’ll still be there. People want to be in the same room as other people, watching and listening to stories. It’s as old as cave people sitting by the campfire telling stories, and there will always be room for that. What I do worry about is whether we’ll still be able to make a living from it. I’m not 100% sure about that.

10 QUESTIONS WITH JULIANNE MOORE & JESSE EISENBERG

Eisenberg: This is not ironic: “Wild Thing,” because I was a really rambunctious basketball player. I’m not joking. If you meet somebody who knows me, they’ll know.

Moore: Witchcraft. I just loved witchcraft. I used to buy books on the occult and cast spells and stuff.

Moore: I’ve never done karaoke in my life. In the shower, stuff from “Dear Evan Hansen.”

Eisenberg: My karaoke song was “Hold On Loosely” by .38 Special, and in the shower, it would be “Rose’s Turn” from “Gypsy.” Somewhere in the middle is where I live.

Eisenberg: We just talked about that. “Rent.”

Moore: Or “No One Cares.” That was the original title. That’s what we filmed it under.

Eisenberg: I do more voice work than people expect. My kid and I do really great impressions. I don’t think those will make it into a multiplex, but I do some pretty funny voice work.

Moore: Vanilla. Soft-serve vanilla. It’s not a brand. But now it gives me a stomachache, so I’ve really got to watch it as we get older. Can I also say that this is my second favorite, and everyone thinks it’s disgusting? Rum raisin.

Eisenberg: For me, it’s pistachio, only because I am a paranoid person and eating ice cream makes me feel like I’m doing something bad for my body. If I have the illusion that it’s derived from nuts, it makes me feel calm. I’ve had rum raisin once, and it’s delicious.

Eisenberg: Maybe “Seinfeld.” But who would I be? I’d be the boy.

Moore: You can be an extra. You don’t have to be one of the main ones.

Eisenberg: Could I start with a cop-out? Mona Friedman. I watch that, and I’m like, “That’s me.” Everything is me in her.

Moore: Countess Olenska, because she’s so self-sacrificing. I admire her, but I don’t know that I could do it.

Eisenberg: Bob Odenkirk screamed at me for writing commercial romantic comedies when I was 21 and said, “You’re a thoughtful young person. Be an artist. Write something personal.” It changed my whole life.

#3412. IEEE Offers More Services to Cities That Want to Be Smarter

They include webinars, educational resources, and conferences

Georges Zissis is an IEEE Fellow and chair of the IEEE Smart Cities Technical Community.

Satish Sani is an IEEE senior member and chair of the IEEE Smart Grid Technical Track.

More and more city governments are using advanced technologies to improve livability for their residents. Municipalities use data from smartphones and sensors for traffic enforcement, traffic control, and waste management. They also have implemented artificial intelligence and deep learning programs.

Dubai, Paris, and Coral Gables, Fla., are among the cities that have invested heavily in programs to become smarter.

Although many initiatives have delivered real innovations, not all have been successful. Inefficient global coordination has hindered projects with unclear standards, socioeconomic differences, and a lack of worldwide governance, leading to a disconnect between the technologies and the ability to adapt to them.

Smart city projects are complex and expensive endeavors that involve politicians, citizens, technocrats, and engineers. Successful projects require citizens to be fully engaged and to have strong collaborations with the participants, especially engineers, as engineering is the cornerstone.

Collaboration with universities, research institutions, and technology experts can bridge knowledge gaps on the behavior of complex socio-technical systems. What’s missing, though, is a global platform where those involved can discuss their experiences.

To help solve those and other challenges, the IEEE Smart Cities Technical Community (formerly the IEEE Smart Cities Initiative) was launched in 2013 by IEEE Future Directions, which incubates emerging technologies and new applications of current ones. The technical community provides city leaders and others with credible, unbiased information and educational content developed by IEEE experts.

Since then, IEEE Smart Cities has launched services including its flagship International Smart Cities Conference, a media center with educational and technical resources, and a contest to recognize the best smart project completed by city officials. The platforms bring together practicing engineers, academic researchers, policymakers, and city leaders to collaborate and exchange ideas and experiences about moving toward a smart-city model.

In 2021 the IEEE Power & Energy Society began managing the Smart Cities program, which is supported by the IEEE Communications, Industry Applications, and Intelligent Transportation Systems societies and other IEEE entities.

Thanks to volunteers’ dedication and determination, IEEE Smart Cities launched several services. But the initiative’s structure limited the development of long-term projects and the creation of new activities.

To address the situation, the IEEE Technical Activities Board (TAB) created the second-generation technical community ad hoc committee, also in 2021. It was a pilot program whereby IEEE Smart Cities formed a board of governors to oversee the community’s operations and leadership, and created a policies and procedures manual.

In November 2025 IEEE Smart Cities became a TAB technical community.

Today more than 7,000 volunteers collaborate on various aspects of the community within at least one of the following technical tracks:

New webinar series, workshops, conferences, educational resources, and other offerings are being created.

Two events were launched recently: the IEEE European Technology and Engineering Management Summit, held in May 2025 in Belgium, with the next one planned for 2027; and the IEEE Sustainable Smart Lighting World Conference, scheduled for 2 to 6 December in Athens.

The Smart Cities Ambassadors program aims to raise the technical community’s visibility outside IEEE by holding roundtables and other events at non-IEEE functions.

IEEE Smart Cities volunteers are working on launching journals. In addition, standards are being developed in collaboration with the IEEE Standards Association, societies, and councils.

The program is collaborating with the Open and Agile Smart Cities and Communities network, the Instituto de Competitividad e Innovación para el Desarrollo y Transferencia de Tecnología, and the International Project Management Association.

All of those actions have the ultimate objective of boosting IEEE Smart Cities’ growth and sustainability, as well as strengthening the leadership and educational offerings to technical community volunteers.

#3411. Windows Laptops Just Closed a Major Gap With the MacBook Neo

To say the MacBook Neo disrupted the laptop market would be an understatement. When the Neo dropped, former Apple CEO Tim Cook said Apple had its best-ever launch week for first-time Mac customers, and the company is reportedly planning on doubling the MacBook's sales for 2027. It's not hard to see why the MacBook Neo is such a hit: Apple is offering the essential Mac experience at a fantastic price point. You no longer need to spend $1,000 or more for a MacBook, so long as you're okay making some sacrifices to get there—which, it seems, many customers are.

While the MacBook Neo has been a boon for Apple and Apple fans alike, I can only imagine the stress it brought to PC manufacturers—especially those with budget or midrange machines. Windows PCs have long won the price war against Apple. While MacBooks have their passionate customers, buyers looking for the best value have had to weigh expensive Apple laptops against many far cheaper options from companies like Dell, HP, ASUS, and Lenovo. But with the Neo, suddenly a MacBook was competing in this space, and well.

Part of the issue for PC manufacturers was Apple's control over its own ecosystem. Unlike most PC makers, which only produce the hardware for each machine, Apple makes both the hardware and the software for its MacBook lineup. As such, the company has the advantage of optimizing that hardware. It can design macOS to run more efficiently on weaker hardware, in a way that companies like Dell or ASUS can't. You might be comparing the MacBook Neo against a Windows laptop with similar specs, or even better specs, but because Microsoft makes Windows, not the laptop manufacturer, it's possible the Neo ends up with the better overall experience. While that might still be the case, Microsoft may have just closed that gap in a meaningful way.

This week, Microsoft announced key upgrades to memory-management efficiency, particularly for machines with 8GB of RAM. This is the amount of memory the MacBook Neo has, as well as many budget and midrange Windows laptops. That's not much memory for 2026, regardless of platform, but Apple seems to have squeezed a lot out of it for the Neo. Now, Microsoft may have just done the same for PCs, as Windows is reportedly 20% more responsive, with 40% faster multitasking.

In its blog post, Microsoft highlighted improvements that users with 8 GB of RAM can expect from Windows going forward. First, Microsoft says it focused on better utilizing the RAM your machine already has. The company compares its memory management to a desk: Anything on the "desk" is stored in RAM; anything in your "drawer" is stored in your drive. As you use your PC, Windows used to move more of your apps and tabs to your drawer to free up more RAM for other things, meaning you'd need to reload those items whenever you returned to them. Going forward, the company says that Windows can keep up to 2GB more of your active data in RAM instead of moving it to slower storage elsewhere. That means apps and tabs should refresh less frequently when you leave and return to them.

Microsoft also says that small actions should be faster across the board. When you open the Start menu, search across your PC, right-click, open Settings, launch the Snipping Tool, and open File Explorer, those actions may be up to 20% faster than they were in January. Microsoft Edge may open up to 33% faster, while Teams can enable Efficiency Mode by default on 8 GB machines, which means it can launch up to 20% faster too. Microsoft put together an interesting stress test to compare multitasking performance between today and January. It opened 20 tabs in Edge, a 4K video, large Word, PowerPoint, and Excel files, then Outlook and File Explorer, all without closing any windows. That experience was 40% faster following this latest update.

Microsoft says it also improved the memory efficiency in its apps: The company claims it reduced committed-memory growth by up to 900 MB, and saved up to 360 MB in RAM across Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and Outlook. That extends to third-party apps as well: Microsoft says that WhatsApp has double-digit memory improvement now. Widgets also only load when you open the app, which saves 200 MB of RAM when the app is closed, while Edge tabs go inactive after 15 minutes instead of two hours.

Microsoft isn't making these upgrades in a vacuum. Hardware costs, particularly for RAM, have skyrocketed in the age of AI. Microsoft knows that people are likely going to hold onto existing hardware for longer than they usually do, or that they'll opt for less-expensive configurations, including, perhaps, machines with 8 GB of RAM.

PCMag's Chris Hoffman was adamant before this latest Windows update that buyers should steer clear of PCs with 8 GB of RAM. Now, he's pulling back a bit. In his testing, Hoffman noticed improvements when multitasking on an 8 GB PC when compared to similar tests from months ago. He could run multiple Chrome tabs, a Microsoft Word window, and Spotify without bogging down the computer much. Hoffman isn't a lightweight user, so he still wouldn't personally choose an 8 GB machine, but he admits, "If I were an average PC buyer looking for a reasonable desktop experience and could save hundreds of dollars by opting for 8GB of RAM, I might be happy with the performance."

To that point, I think this new Windows update makes 8 GB PCs competitive, especially against the MacBook Neo. We'll still need direct comparisons to know how well this new Windows experience holds up across the board, but these updates are promising. Users with 8 GB machines just got a free, valuable update overnight; new customers can opt for a more affordable PC without feeling like performance will take a nosedive just because they opened one too many Edge tabs.

As Hoffman says, 8 GB of RAM is not ideal for any user looking for serious multitasking or professional workflows, regardless of whether they choose a Mac or PC. But for the average computer customer looking for a solid machine without breaking the bank, I no longer see the Neo as necessarily the default choice. After all, Apple has slowly raised its price, too, from $599 to $699. If you're platform-agnostic, or even prefer Windows to macOS, these updates from Microsoft are quite promising. If you're in the market, check out PCMag's excellent list of budget laptop recommendations.

#3410. I tested the Philips Café Aromis 8000 Series — and this superautomatic espresso machine is my biggest $2,000-shaped disappointment of 2026

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Philips Café Aromis 8000 looks beautiful, with a bright, full-color screen and a gorgeous wooden embellishment on the group head. However, it’s outrageously expensive in the U.S. and makes a mid-tasting brew. I would personally skip this one, unless you value appearance over taste.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

I have yet to find a fully automatic espresso machine good enough to earn a permanent place in my kitchen. I’ve tested upwards of twenty now, and they all leave a little to be desired. But nothing’s been quite as disappointing as the Philips Café Aromis 8000 Series… let me explain.

The 8000 Series looks beautiful. It’s easily one of the prettiest superautomatic coffee machines I’ve ever tested. There’s a wood-veneer group head, a cup warmer, and two silver rails on top — just like a commercial espresso machine. My hopes were sky high.

However, I’m not convinced it’s one of the best espresso machines. It’s outrageously expensive in the U.S. ($2k!), makes mid-tasting coffee, and can only make one type of milk texture. I’ll go through all the information in this Philips Café Aromis 8000 Series review.

The Philips Café Aromis 8000 Series is a high-end automatic espresso machine. It’ll set you back $1,999 at Amazon U.S. and £895 at Curry’s U.K.

This is a premium price for a premium machine. Similar options would be the KitchenAid KF8 ($1,999) and the De’Longhi PrimaDonna Aromatic ($2,499).

If $2k is a little too much for you, don’t worry. De’Longhi also makes the $1,499 Rivelia, my favorite superautomatic coffee machine to date. For the money-savvy, there’s also the $795 Terra Kafe Demi, which can’t froth milk, and the Smeg BCC13, which is even cheaper at $749 but doesn’t have a full-color LED screen.

Philips also makes the $394 2200 Series. What’s actually different between the two? Honestly, not as much as you might think. The 2200 Series still has a built-in milk frother, unlike the $795 Terra Kafe Demi, and has a bright screen, unlike the $749 Smeg BCC13. Sure, the 2200 only makes “espresso”, “coffee”, and “hot water”, but that’s the foundation of any coffee drink. While the 8000 Series is much easier thanks to its one-touch recipes, I’m not sure this justifies a whole $1,600 extra. Personally, I would get the $394 2200 Series, or a standalone milk frother, like the $139 Subminimal Nanofoamer Pro Gen 2 for more finesse.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Oh, the Philips Café Aromis 8000 Series is a sight to behold. It’s gorgeous. I’d go so far as to say it’s the most beautiful automatic coffee machine I’ve ever seen. Of course, it’s essentially a big plastic-and-metal box — it’s still an automatic coffee machine, after all — but there’s a sense of finesse missing from other machines (yes, even $2,000 ones).

There’s a cup warmer on top of the machine, complete with two stainless steel rails on either side, and a low-profile grinder. The grinder holds a whole 250g bag of beans at once, even though it’s only rated for 200g.

But my favorite part is the wood finish on the portafilter. Rather than plastic or metal — boring! — the 8000 Series has a gorgeous, glossy wood veneer, making the machine look more like an automatic version of the Lelit MaraX3 than something like the Casabrews Ultra Pro.

You might be sensing a theme here, but it only gets better. Even though the water tank looks pretty small, it’s actually 64 fluid ounces (just under 2 liters). And it’s a slide-out tank, so you don’t need counter space with overhead clearance, unlike the KitchenAid KF3 ($999).

At 15.3 x 9.9 17.8 inches, the 8000 isn’t the slimmest automatic coffee machine I’ve ever tested — that would go to the aforementioned KitchenAid KF3 — but it doesn’t look as bulky as its dimensions might suggest. I had this out in the office for a week (making around ten drinks a day) and it looked right at home.

If you value a good-looking automatic coffee machine, the 8000 is surely for you. I really have nothing bad to say about its appearance.

However, the 8000 Series has “app functionality”. Here’s a screenshot of said “app functionality”.

All you can really do is set user profiles and scroll through recipe ideas — most of which require extra ingredients, like custard or chocolate sauce. While I like that you can customize and save up to 8 drinks for each user profile, I do wish there was more purpose to the app. Sure, you can remote control brewing, but I wish there was something more. Or there’s not much point even having an app.

I also have a bone to pick with the language in said app. As you can see from the screenshots above, the app describes a latte as having “slightly light body, slightly bitter taste”. Coffee shouldn’t actually taste bitter. The central flavor note in a latte should not be bitterness. It should have a little bitterness to balance it out, but the prevailing taste should be fruitiness, chocolate, or nuttiness (depending on your beans). Maybe this is why the coffee tastes mediocre — because the machine is trying to make it bitter.

The standout feature on the 8000 Series is its ease of use. One touch makes 40+ recipes. Some of the recipes I’d never heard of, like Melange and Galão. Of course, there are also a range of cold drinks, but these are extracted hot, so in theory you could pull a normal espresso and top it up with cold milk to achieve the same results.

Here’s a photo of a straightforward espresso.

As you can see, it has a nice layer of crema, but the shot itself is a little pale. This espresso tasted rich and smooth, but with a little too much bitterness at the back of the palate for my personal taste.

You can easily customize the espresso settings for every drink (and then save your customized drinks to profiles). You can adjust the strength from 1-7, temperature, and use ground coffee if you please.

The grinder is also manually adjustable, but the machine calibrated itself based on my beans. Pressing the bean button brings up a built-in AI, which asks questions about roast and species of bean. After I provided this information, it adjusted the grind size to suit.

I found most drinks were way too bitter by default. I like the taste of coffee — I drink straight espresso to taste-test every single coffee machine. However, the 8000 Series brought out an unpleasant bitter note in my usual Ethiopian, medium-roasted testing beans, so I had to increase milk volume for every drink recipe.

The oat flat white (pictured in the “Milk” section below) was almost black. This is incredibly weird. I would recommend adjusting the default recipe for each drink to ensure it’s not overly strong.

I appreciate the 8000 Series comes with both a hot and cold milk frother — more versatile than the De’Longhi Rivelia, which makes you spend extra for the cold milk system. However, you can’t customize the milk texture at all. You can adjust milk volume, but not texture. Iced latte, hot cappuccino, flat white, macchiato… all the same milk texture.

I’m sure the drinks are intended to be different milk textures, but they’re not. Everything is a little too aerated. There’s also no non-dairy/dairy milk setting, so oat milk is treated the same as cow milk, which is disappointing to see on such a pricey machine.

Here are three photos: one is an oat flat white, one is a cow milk latte, and one is an oat layered latte.

As you can see, the milk texture is relatively similar, and describable in one word: bubbly. For a $2,000 machine, it’s just not good enough. De’Longhi’s high-end milk systems allow for a three-prong customizer: you can choose low, medium, or high foam.

So, while I value the inclusion of a cold milk frother, the said milk frother isn’t as effective as De’Longhi’s “LatteCrema” systems.

At 10 inches wide, 18 inches deep, and 15 inches tall, this is no small machine. However, it doesn’t require any overhead clearance thanks to the flush grinder hopper and side-accessible water tank, so you could theoretically get it even if your counters only have 16 inches of space.

The 8000 Series comes with a water filter, which I’d recommend installing regardless of water hardness. If you live in a particularly hard water area, you will need to descale more often than the machine recommends. Don’t worry if you don’t know your water hardness — the machine comes with a test strip.

Philips makes a descaler: $16 for two packs at Amazon. This should last you around six months depending on your water hardness.

Cleaning is also easy: the milk frothers and drip tray are dishwasher safe (but they take up a lot of space in said dishwasher), and the machine will alert you when you need to rinse internal brewing elements. Be warned that coffee grounds go moldy quickly, so empty this at least every day.

Finally, warranty. Philips offers a 2-year standard warranty, which is the same as KitchenAid, De’Longhi, Ninja, and Breville. I’d like to see coffee companies start to move towards a 5-year warranty, especially when these machines cost so much.

I really don’t think the Philips Café Aromis 8000 Series is worth $2,000. It tastes like coffee you can get on the $394 2200 Series. If you really, really want to spend two grand, I’d recommend the KitchenAid KF8 instead. If you want to save money but get an automatic machine, I’d go for the $1,400 De’Longhi Rivelia or $895 Smeg BCC13.

While the Café Aromis 8000 Series looks gorgeous and is incredibly easy to use, I cannot find anything to justify that price. Sure, it can make 40+ recipes, but are you really going to make a Melange or Galão on a fully automatic coffee machine? Not really. Just make it manually — it’ll taste better. As the machine can’t actually make different milk textures, it’s not a true Melange or Galão anyway.

I would personally skip this one. It’s much too expensive in the U.S. and doesn’t make nice-tasting coffee — but if you value appearance and ease of use over anything else, you might not be disappointed.

#3409. How to get access to Sonos AI features, as company aims to avoid another app disaster

When Sonos tried a major app update two years ago, things did not go well. Much-loved features disappeared, older speakers experienced connection problems, and accessibility features were broken. That debacle saw the company’s CEO fired.

The company is taking a much more cautious approach as it moves into the AI era with a Sonos 27voice update, enabling natural-language voice control via Hey Sonos requests …

The whole mess started when Sonos launched the company’s first headphones, the Ace, intended to compete with AirPods Max. The app needed to be updated to support these, and the company decided to use it as an opportunity for a ground-up rebuild, launching a completely new app just ahead of the launch.

Customers responded angrily to the loss of key functionality, compatibility issues with older speakers, and accessibility problems. Sonos initially downplayed the complaints, but CEO Patrick Spence subsequently emailed customers to apologize, and provide a timeline for fixes, subsequently making seven promises. However, customers weren’t impressed, and called for Spence to be fired – later getting their wish.

This time around, Sonos started out with a modest update in the form of the Sonos 27 app, leaving the more substantial changes to a subsequent Sonos 27voice version. This will replace the more limited voice control available today, much like the update from old Siri to Siri AI.

Rather than pushing it out to all customers, Sonos is adopting a very cautious approach. First, you’ll have to request early access to the beta and be approved. Second, the company is testing the feature with a relatively small group of users. Third, it’s seeking detailed feedback from beta testers before a planned launch next year.

The new features work in much the same way as Siri on HomePods.

You can use Sonos 27voice at any time by saying the wake word, “Hey Sonos.” While Sonos is listening, the white status light on your Sonos product will glow brighter and the volume will lower if any audio is playing. A confirmation tone will play after Sonos understands your request.

#3408. Walmart Will Have Three Major Shopping Events This Holiday Season

If you're thinking of picking up any big-ticket items soon—whether for yourself or as a gift for someone on your list— I would advise you to wait until you see what retailers have in store for the holiday sales season, which will kick off in earnest in mid-November. Walmart is the first major retailer to announce its Black Friday and Cyber Monday plan for 2026, and they actually involve three major shopping events between now and the December holidays.

As it did in 2025, Walmart will hold three sales between Nov. 12 and Dec. 2, as outlined in a recent press release. The sales will be both online and in-store, and will target a mix of Walmart+ members and general shoppers.

The events will take place on three different dates:

Walmart's Black Friday Deals Event 1: Nov. 12–15

Available online and in stores starting at 6 a.m. local time

Walmart+ members get six hours of early access beginning online at 12:01 a.m. ET on November 12

Walmart's Black Friday Deals Event 2: Nov. 23–29

Online only: Nov. 23 starting at 12:01 a.m. ET

Online and in stores: Nov. 27 starting at 6 a.m. local time

Walmart+ members get six hours of early access online beginning Nov. 23 at 12:01 a.m. ET

Walmart's Cyber Monday Deals Event: Nov. 30-Dec. 2

Walmart says that you can expect discounts on electronics, toys, fashion, beauty, home goods, gifts, and everyday essentials. Although the company doesn't provide much in the way of specifics in its press release, last year's sales included discounts on TCL TVs, Dyson vacuums, Dreo appliances, and toys from LEGO.

Walmart already has plenty of good deals out early. You don't need to wait for the official sale to start to find some products going for their lowest prices ever. Here are some of the best ones I've found so far:

The holiday season will see major sales from the same list of retailers that compete for your dollars throughout the year—namely, Best Buy, Target, and Amazon. Each will have its own version of Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales. So far, only Walmart has revealed its plans.

In short, yes. Though they aren't quite as impactful as they once were, Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales offer discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. Whether it's a major purchase you've been saving up for or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts, especially on items like appliances and electronics. Last year's sales included categories such as tech, home improvement, and fitness.

Black Friday used to be when major retailers offered their best deals on expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Now, however, the distinction is almost meaningless: Every major retailer offers sales on both days, which means the smart move is to know what you want, use price trackers to monitor the deals, and refer to our Black Friday coverage, where we do all the searching, curating, and price tracking for you.

#3407. This Hidden Device Could Free Up Gigawatts of Grid Power

Variable frequency drives can slash motors’ power use

Zurich-based ABB is one of several manufacturers of variable frequency drives (VFDs), such as this ACH580. VFDs could help make the millions of electric motors running in industrial facilities more energy efficient.

This article was originally published by Canary Media.

America’s energy supply crunch is driving a surge of federal and private investment in new electricity generation—from polluting gas turbines to cleaner developments like solar farms and geothermal plants. But gigawatts of power are already available for the taking across the U.S. economy in the form of wasted energy from an unexpected source: motors.

Some 50 million electric motors drive the fans, pumps, and compressors found in virtually every factory and building. Together, they gobble enough electricity to equal nearly a third of total U.S. power demand. Often, the motors use far more energy than they actually need to keep America’s machines humming.

Companies can install devices known as variable frequency drives, or VFDs, to make motors run super efficiently. Yet adoption remains relatively low, in part because of the perceived hassle of retrofitting equipment and because they’re typically not required. On average, only 16 percent of motor systems at industrial facilities and 4 percent of commercial-sector motors use VFDs, according to a 2021 market report by Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

However, there are now more reasons than ever to equip the nation’s motors with power-saving devices, energy experts and device manufacturers say. They’re urging federal agencies, utilities, and deep-pocketed tech giants to spur a wider rollout of VFDs through financial incentives and efficiency standards.

For one, slashing motors’ power use would free up grid capacity for large electricity users like data centers and electric vehicles, they argue. It would help curb costs for factories that are switching from fossil-fueled heating systems to electrified, motor-based solutions like heat pumps—all at a time when industrial power prices are climbing fast. Plus, VFD technology has become far more sophisticated and less expensive to install than earlier iterations.

“This is low-hanging fruit that gives a lot [of energy] back and is reasonably simple,” Nik Sawe, a senior policy analyst at the nonpartisan think tank Energy Innovation, says of the technology.

Energy-wise, the main problem with electric motors is that they’re always running at full capacity. Consider an office building, which empties out in the evening. The heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning system can wind down in those hours, with dampers and valves restricting the flow of cold or hot air. But the motors and fans that drive the whole setup are still working in the background, wasting energy.

VFD technology, such as the Danfoss iC7 series, has gained some momentum in recent years among factories and buildings trying to combat rising electricity costs. Danfoss Drives

VFDs are electronic controllers with temperature sensors that continually adjust the speed of motors, automatically ramping up or down to match demand. The technology, which is also called adjustable speed drives, has the potential to curb a motor’s energy use by around 40 to 60 percent, says Neal Elliott, director emeritus of the American Council for an Energy-Efficient Economy.

All those energy reductions add up. Toyota, for example, installed VFDs on over 200 motors inside the HVAC system at its auto manufacturing plant in Georgetown, Kentucky, as part of a US $1.25 million pilot project in 2015. The automaker saved more than $700,000 in annual electricity costs thanks to the VFDs, and it continues to use the technology at other manufacturing facilities across the U.S., the company said by email.

“We’ve known for many, many years that there’s a huge opportunity for energy savings by varying the speed of the motor,” says Elliott, who noted that he literally wrote the book on energy-efficient motor systems in 2002.

Certain aspects of the technology have historically held the drives back since they debuted in the late 1960s. Measuring the flow of water, air, refrigerant—whatever is moving through the system that the motors are driving—was for decades an expensive engineering process. Accurately controlling motors to deliver the right amount of juice, at just the right time, faced similar issues.

But recent advances in sensors and machine-learning algorithms have significantly slashed the cost and complexity of using drives, Elliott says. Modern VFDs have also benefited from the increased production of advanced power chips that are used in high-voltage applications such as electric vehicles and solar power inverters.

Another long-standing challenge has been that commercial and industrial building developers often prioritize reducing upfront costs over netting long-term energy savings, and so they don’t always build to the highest efficiency levels, says Zack Valdez, senior director of regulatory and industry affairs at the National Electrical Manufacturers Association, whose members include drive and motor makers.

“If the facility that you’re putting it into doesn’t require it, then oftentimes people will overlook [VFDs], because they’re just trying to build to a minimum set of energy requirements,” he says. And if companies don’t install drives from the start, they’re likely less inclined to take time to retrofit an operating system.

The trade association recently launched a pilot program with manufacturers, utilities, and energy-efficiency groups to collect real-world data about how VFDs reduce motors’ electricity use and lower utility bills. The goal is to demonstrate how the technology can benefit not only individual facilities but also the wider grid—giving utilities a concrete reason to provide rebates for industrial customers.

Proponents say they hope the results will help the U.S. Department of Energy shape future efficiency measures and incentives that encourage adoption of the drives, including in federally owned buildings. Despite the Trump administration’s open hostility toward home appliance and equipment mandates, agency staff have apparently been receptive to discussing solutions that could meet the soaring power needs of data centers.

“If you added a drive to all the motors that are out there, you could provide [power for] up to five years of data center growth without having to build any new generation,” says Kirk Anderson, director of government relations and public affairs for ABB. The global manufacturing giant makes VFDs domestically near Milwaukee.

Anderson floated the idea of having tech companies help pay for factory owners to install VFDs to free up room on the grid. After all, hyperscalers are already spending many billions of dollars to revive shuttered nuclear plants, support next-generation geothermal projects, deploy fleets of grid-scale batteries, and supercharge the build-out of gas turbines and power plants.

“Instead of ‘bring your own power,’ it should be ‘offset your own power,’” he says, referring to a growing effort by states to get data centers to secure their own power resources and prevent rising costs for regular customers.

Michael Reckamp, the director of enterprise strategy for Danfoss Drives, North America, another VFD manufacturer, said that despite the traditionally low adoption rates, the technology has gained some momentum in recent years among factories and buildings as rising electricity costs and other grid-wide challenges make it harder to justify wasting energy.

Still, “it hasn’t permeated enough to get everyone utilizing it,” he says. “In the current situation, where we’re having so many issues with grids, brownouts, and now data centers wanting to take the load, I think there should be a renewed focus on putting drives out there to really reduce the stress on the grid and improve energy savings.”

Maria Gallucci is a clean-energy reporter with Canary Media.

Thank you for pointing out this accessible opportunity. I wonder why the industrial and non-residential building sectors still haven’t implemented this technology on a broad scale. The variable frequency drive (VFD) technology is very mature, widely available, and not new. It’s such a low-hanging fruit to implement wherever there are rotating machines and actuators to save energy, money, and also make the whole integrated energy system potentially more flexible and efficient.

#3406. Apple still charging 300% of costs on iPhone storage upgrades, says WSJ

Opting for more RAM or storage when buying Apple devices has always been an expensive business, with the company famously charging huge markups.

Apple said in its most recent earnings report that even after the price increases, its margins are being squeezed by higher component costs. But an analysis suggests that the company is still charging three times its own costs for higher storage tiers on the iPhone 18 Pro …

To be fair to Apple, some of the criticism about the premiums charged on configuring a device with more memory or flash storage hasn’t been comparing, well, apples with apples. The SSDs used in Macs, for example, are very much faster than the lower-spec third-party storage cards people typically cite as evidence for the company’s greed.

why are people defending Apple? They are bending everybody over double to keep their profit margins. They buy a billion memory chips or SSD's at a time so they are getting them much lower in price even if the price has gone up.

All the same, there’s no denying that the iPhone maker has always applied extremely high markups to its own direct costs. With the iPhone 17 Pro, for example, upgrading from 256GB to 1TB cost a buyer $400. A Wall Street Journal analysis cited by Macworld says that Apple’s cost at the time was $42, almost a 1,000% markup.

Apple this week warned that memory costs will reduce its holiday quarter profit margins.

When you remove the tariff refunds from both the June and September quarters, both company and product gross margin would be down about one point sequentially, primarily driven by higher memory costs. Parekh added that the pressure on Apple’s margins isn’t expected to ease anytime soon.

However, the WSJ’s number-crunching suggests that we probably don’t need to get out the violins just yet. The paper compared the same upgrade on the iPhone 18 Pro, where Apple has increased the price difference to $600. Although the Cupertino company is paying dramatically more, with an estimated direct cost of $192, that still amounts to customers being charged more than three times the price paid by Apple.

Market fundamentals remain tight. Middle East exports have recovered from lows reached in the Spring, However, the recovery has been uneven.

While Strategic Petroleum Reserve Releases And Coordinated Refinery Measures Across The G7 are providing some relief at the margin, they are not a substitute for consistent and reliable supply from the region. The security of these flows remains a key variable in shaping near term market conditions. While we expect oil prices to remain volatile, we continue to be constructive on oil market fundamentals for several reasons. First, oil demand has demonstrated considerable resilience. Despite elevated product prices, consumption has held firm and as supply has returned to the market, demand has recovered alongside it. This reinforces our view that demand observed early in the conflict was temporary in nature rather than a structural shift.

Second, although the pace of inventory draws is beginning to moderate, global inventories remain well below their 5 year average. We expect the process of rebuilding stocks to those historic levels will take considerable time. Third, the supply recovery remains fragile. As recent events have shown, the restoration of flows from the Middle East is subject to ongoing disruption risk. Taken together, we expect oil prices to remain above mid cycle price levels in both the near and medium term, and we see the balance of risks supporting upside price volatility. Turning to the natural gas outlook, we continue to see the North American market evolve from a seasonal commodity story into a strategic energy resource.

While storage levels will continue to fluctuate year to year, underlying demand remains robust with LNG exports, electricity demand industrial growth and grid reliability increasingly competing for domestic supply. Our medium to long term outlook remains constructive and our deliberate investment in building a low cost natural gas position with access to premium markets and as a complement to our core oil business, provides ample opportunity to capitalize on this demand growth. Looking to 2027, we are well positioned with tremendous flexibility. Earlier this year, we redirected capital to oil assets, raising liquids production setting a strong foundation for growth in 2027. If current oil supply demand fundamentals persist, we believe the market needs more oil supply next year.

Of course, when you are looking at the CapEx, we do have the strategic infrastructure that we have talked about, the Janus expansion that would need to be contemplated on top of that.

And then a little bit of increased growth, but it is really more on the margin than adding anything significant to capture that low single digit As we talked about before, we really took this year to kind of position ourselves to not only grow liquids production in 2026, but actually to position ourselves to be able to grow into 2027 as well. With regards to the 3 year scenario and where we are at here towards the end of year 1, obviously, the first year, there is been a significant increase in the commodity price from what we had forecasted before.

Think what we have is illustrated on a $60 to $80 range over that 3 year period, and year 1 is obviously coming in at current strip somewhere right around $87 for the year 1. So that would lead us to know that ROCE is on the high side, free cash flow generation is on the high side. As far as maybe capital expenditures that were contemplated or not contemplated in 3 year scenario, really the only 1 would be that Janus. Would be on top of it. That was not originally into the 3 year scenario.

And again, that is a strategic option for us that at the top of the cycle, feels like a great time to layer that in. And for 2027, it is essentially a $200 million capital investment that we are planning for.

Phillip Jungwirth: Okay. that is great to hear. And then this might also be contributing, but you noted in the script, Permian well performance outperforming your expectations of steady year on year. We have probably all noticed this in the public data. But 1 thing that stood out to me was really across all your plays, the well performance looks better or at least consistent with last year. Just wondering if you could speak to some of the bigger drivers here on the productivity side, just whether it is some of the high intensity completions targeting or other items that you have that you have pursued operationally in 2026?

Keith Trasko: Yes. Good morning. This is Keith. I will start with the Delaware. Yes, we are very pleased with how our Delaware Basin developments progressing. We have not really made any changes to our development plan relative to what we communicated earlier this year. Well productivity has been a little better than our expectations. The results are flat to slightly up versus 2025. And the important thing is that we expect similar consistency and productivity going forward. 2026 plan reflects the changes that we made last year to our development strategy. So, we continue to take advantage of the operational improvements to maximize, the value of the asset.

And that is really driven by our ability to drive down costs, allowing us to add new target zones that meet the strict return hurdles, better maximize the value capture across the assets. So we are really happy with the Delaware. We expect consistent returns and cash flow for the next 10 years.

Ezra Y. Yacob: And yes, a lot of it is on the completion side. Like said, our high intensity fracs adding horsepower and doing smart tests just on various things on the completion side. And that had its genesis in the Eagle Ford in the early and we applied it to the Permian, we applied it to the Utica very early on. We are seeing improvements in Dorado associated with that. And as we take those learnings and iterate them, we have been able to apply that back to our Eagle Ford oil as kind of a revision 2 and 3 and 4. We have seen improvement there as well. So very happy with our well performance across the board.

Operator: The next question comes from Scott Hanold with RBC Capital Markets. Please go ahead.

Scott Hanold: Yes, thanks. If we could go back to where the Q and A started and that is on gas sales agreement. it is kind of a 2 part question with that. Number 1, you know, the commercial turns, I understand there are lot of confidentiality around it. But like in this market that we have seen for the past 9 months, how are you all able to get a contract like that done at this point? And do you see the economics a little bit different from the original ones? And as you look going forward, how much exposure to these international markets do you want?

Should we expect you guys continuing to layer on new types of contracts like these? Or is there a certain threshold you want to limit yourself to?

Jeffrey R. Leitzell: Sure, Scott. it is Jeffrey Hibbert. Maybe I will take that 1. So US LNG projects continue to reach FID and operators are still seeking commitments to get additional capacity built. As, the LNG market has expanded, both physically and financially over time, it is created really new and different opportunities to seek international price exposure for us. So, look, we remain engaged with several potential partners and look for attractive win-win opportunities as they present themselves. So I would expect us to continue to look at those types of deals. We really have a number of advantages.

Again, that make us an attractive counterparty for folks. it is our low-cost multi-basin portfolio, it is our extremely strong balance sheet, and it is our track record. With these types of deals. So, yeah, I think you can continue to see us, always looking at those, going forward.

Scott Hanold: Appreciate that. If I could pivot to shareholder returns, you know, appreciate your, again, commitment to the. annual 70% return. Based on, I guess, your $9.7 billion forecast and buybacks today, including what you have done based on the 10 Q looks like there is probably another, what, $1.5 to maybe $1.6 billion that needs to get done through the balance of the year. That seems like a lot. And given the volatility in commodity prices, how do you manage hitting that annual threshold when we are coming up on the end of the year?

Jeffrey R. Leitzell: Yeah. Look. I mean, it is Jeffrey again. I would say, cash returns remain a priority for us. You heard Ezra mention it early on in the script, and we remain confident in our ability to meet our threshold commitment of 70% of our annual free cash flow.

You hit the numbers on the head at $88 WTI and $3.40 Henry Hub, we expect to return $6.8 billion of cash this year and when you back off our dividend commitment, which is that $2.2 billion I think your numbers are accurate I think given the volume that we have, you know, in our stock, we feel very comfortable being able to achieve, those amounts and look, we continue to see a lot of value in our stock. So consequently, we favor buybacks for additional cash return. I think we will be able to get there.

Leo Mariani: Hey, good morning. Just wanted to touch base on your initial comments for 2027. You talked about low single digit oil growth. That certainly seems to be reasonable in this price environment. Just wanted to kind of get a sense do you see a contribution from the UAE there to get to those numbers for next year?

Jeffrey R. Leitzell: Yeah. Leo, this is Jeffrey. You can actually see in our guidance, we did guide towards a little bit of volumes, but it is fairly minimal. As far as that. We are still in the exploration phase even though we are seeing outstanding strong results over there. You know, before we really see meaningful amount of volumes and we start getting closer to a DOC, I would not expect them to be a huge part of the overall 2026 volumes. So, ultimately, you know, we feel great about it. I think we are getting to a place where we are getting closer and closer to DOC with the results that we are seeing, and we are excited about.

So you will just kind of see that in our guidance as we move forward and we will keep you updated on the results.

Leo Mariani: Okay. Appreciate that. And then just want to also just ask, obviously, you announced a new gas sales agreement today. Clearly, you made a commitment to expanding the Janus plant. Just can you provide a little bit more color just on your thoughts around gas. Is EOG making a larger pivot towards gas as we get later in the decade? Do you see great opportunities for returns on the gas side in several years?

Ezra Y. Yacob: Hey, Leo. This is Ezra. Yeah. I want to say that EOG is making a big pivot to gas or a big call on gas. I mean, what-- this all starts with our organic exploration effort. And the fact that we captured Dorado. We do continue to believe that Dorado is the lowest cost gas in North America And then we are advantaged in the geographic position of it being close to multiple demand centers. What that is really allowed us to do is basically invest at the right pace, capitally disciplined, to grow what we think is essentially a premium gas company underneath the umbrella of our premium oil company here at EOG.

We continue to invest in gas as we develop and capture markets, We are not just growing or investing in gas to move a whole bunch of gas to the Gulf Coast and hope that at prices. On gas, because the margins oftentimes are so skinny and volatile, you have got to be very, very diligent and disciplined looking at the entire value chain. It starts with low well costs, continues with low operating costs including transportation, And then, the last part of it is making sure that you are delivering molecules to a demand center and getting yourself exposed to premium pricing.

And then the second thing on that, which has really been a big mover here as of recent is our exports. And so, yes, you end up-- it is really to be negotiated if we wanted to turn less of the concession over into production or the entire 900 thousand-acre. Today, where we are at, we are seeing very, very strong results in those initial 2 wells as highlighted previously.

They responded very, very well to the artificial lift and then we brought a couple additional wells on We do not have 30-day rates. it is a little bit soon for that, but the wells look good.

And quite frankly, with the efforts that we have seen the conversations we have had with oilfield service partners and their level of engagement to enter the country At this point, I would say we are I would reiterate what Keith said before is that we are well on our way to targeting kind of a DOC probably long before the expiration of the exploration agreement. that is been probably in that field development plan, that is where you would finally sort of walk down sort of CapEx, how many rigs you are gonna run, what the production forecast would be.

In a conventional field, that would be pretty well constrained, but with unconventionals, you can dial up, dial down, and grow. I guess there would be flexibility in what your field development plan would look like? Yes, Bob. I think what you have hit on is something we have highlighted whenever we talk about going to whether it is conventional or in this case unconventional. it is the importance of aligning yourself with the right partners. Folks that understand what it takes to make these plays work, what it takes to make unconventionals work.

It really comes back to where we have spent a lot of time talking today. About our marketing strategy and making sure that we have got the flexibility and diversification even at an asset level to be able to make sure that we put gas into a premium market.

#3404. Sony Wants to Give You Up to $400 for Your PS5

Companies usually want you to buy something from them. They might cut prices to make their products more enticing, or introduce perks and upgrades to make stagnant prices (or even price hikes) more appealing. But rarely do I see companies encourage customers to sell their products.

Such is the case with Sony and its PlayStation console. This week, the company began reaching out to some customers with an odd prompt: Rather than buy a new PS5 or PS5 Pro, you can sell your existing PS5 console for up to $400. There are stipulations there, of course: Your console needs to be in good working order, and, apparently, come with two controllers—even though Sony only includes one in the box. The price could also fluctuate depending on your console model, storage capacity, and included accessories. But, still, the company says it'll help you net up to $400 for your existing PS5.

It's a bizarre deal, especially when you consider who you're trading your console to. Sony isn't necessarily accepting trade-ins itself. Instead, it's partnering with BackMarket. The thing is, you can trade in your PS5 directly through BackMarket and get a better value than Sony is offering through its direct link. When I try to trade in my standard PS5 with one controller, BackMarket offers $435, $35 more than Sony's highest offer. If I add a second controller to that deal, BackMarket bumps up the total to $455.

You might also be wondering why Sony would do this. Not only is it weird for a company to encourage you to sell one of its products, but the PS5 is about to have a big moment. Grand Theft Auto VI is finally about to launch, and it'll likely be one of the biggest video game launches, if not the biggest video game launch, of all time. Why, then, would Sony encourage users to jump ship?

While Sony doesn't say, the answer likely has to do with how expensive it is to pick up a PS5 right now. Even though the console launched back in 2020, units are few and far between, jacking the price up to unreasonable levels. Sony raised international prices due to tariffs last year, but the current shortage is more probably tied to the ongoing memory crisis that's putting a strain on all tech, including game consoles. A new PS5 on Amazon will easily cost you over $800. If you want to find a PS5 Pro, don't be surprised to find it well over $1,000. Sony likely wants players who aren't using their consoles to sell them, so that active players (who will also buy games like GTA VI) will pick them up. It's not just Sony, either: Microsoft has been offering similar deals to inactive Xbox gamers this year.

If Sony reached out to you directly, you can take advantage of the deal without issue—just click the link in the email. But if you never received such an offer, you still have options. For one, that BackMarket deal is live for anyone. That links takes you to the deal for the standard PS5, but you can also head to this link to enter the info for your specific PS5 model. GameStop, of course, will happily take your PS5 off your hands, but it doesn't seem as generous as BackMarket. Right now, it seems you can get up to $275 in store credit, or $192.50 in cash for a standard PS5.
