#3401. With iOS 27.3, Apple will start checking iCloud public links for ‘harmful content’

iOS 27.3 adds lots of new iPhone features, and it also makes a change to how public iCloud links work with the aim of preventing harmful content from being shared. Here are the details.

This week Apple released the first iOS 27.3 beta, which adds Siri AI improvements, new Safari features, the all-new Apple Health app, and more.

Per a newly published support document on Apple’s website, iOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and more also include a key change to how iCloud public links work.

Apple currently provides two main options when sharing photos, files, and more via iCloud. You can share with ‘People you choose’ or create a public link that works for ‘Anyone with the link.’

Starting with iOS 27.3 and companion updates, the ‘Anyone with the link’ option will start being checked by Apple for harmful content.

When you share content that’s stored in iCloud, such as a photo in iCloud Photos or a file in iCloud Drive, you can choose to Share a Link or Send a Copy of the item. If you choose Share a Link, you can either share the item with “People you choose” — only people you invite or approve — or with “Anyone with the link,” which makes it accessible to anyone who has the link, including Apple. Starting in version 27.3 or later of iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS, items shared using Anyone with the Link will be checked by Apple for harmful content.

If Apple flags the content you’re sharing as harmful, the support doc says it “reserves the right to move, refuse, modify, remove, or delete the content at any time.”

I’m okay with Apple doing this. HOWEVER, they should publish at least rough guidelines on what they will consider “harmful”.

Saying nothing more than “harmful” leaves way too much open to arbitrary interpretation.

For anyone trying to upload harmful content, the company may “take action against your Apple Account, including blocking or disabling your Apple Account, blocking the ability to create a new Apple Account with the associated email address or phone number, or if necessary, involving law enforcement.”

As outlined above, choosing the ‘Anyone with the link’ option has always made it accessible to “anyone who has the link, including Apple.” That’s because it’s a public link.

What’s changing now, though, is that Apple says it will begin checking those public links for harmful content.

Do you use iCloud public links? What’s your take on this change? Let us know in the comments.

#3400. No, We Aren’t All Eating 'Too Much' Protein

If you’ll permit me a rant—I promise to make it fact-filled and interesting—I am sick of the articles that seem to pop up every few months claiming that we are all eating “too much” protein. They convey an inaccurate picture of how the body uses protein, and they demonize perfectly healthy meals that happen to be high in protein. It’s time to set the record straight.

It is true that most of us eat more than the RDA (recommended daily allowance) of protein, but that's a good thing—the RDA is meant as a minimum. It's true that protein-boosted foods are trendy, and that they're not necessarily great dietary choices in the big picture. It's also true that you can eat a healthy diet with little to no meat, but meat is not synonymous with protein. Let's look at what we actually know about the role of protein in a healthy diet, and how to tell if you're eating too much or too little.

As a refresher, protein is one of the three calorie-containing macronutrients (fats, carbs, protein) that make up most of the food we eat. Proteins are made of amino acids, and these amino acids are required for the growth, repair, and functioning of our bodies.

We can get protein from a variety of sources. Meats are particularly protein-dense; a chicken breast contains about 35 grams of protein. Other animal products, like milk and eggs, are also rich in protein. Plant-based foods tend to have less protein than animal products, but it’s not hard to meet or exceed protein requirements even on a vegan diet. Beans, grains, and soy products like tofu contain significant amounts of protein, for example.

If you’d like a cheat sheet on how much protein you’re supposed to eat based on your activity level, you can find one here. And that’s a good place to start dissecting this “too much protein” myth, because before we can declare an amount of protein to be “too much,” we need to understand how much is “enough.”

The government communicates targets for different nutrients to encourage us all to eat a healthy, balanced diet. These targets are the basis for the “% daily value” labels on the back of packaged foods, and for the nutrient makeup of school lunches. The RDA, or recommended daily allowance, is defined as “the average daily dietary intake level that is sufficient to meet the nutrient requirement of nearly all (97 to 98 percent) healthy individuals in a group.”

In other words, if 100% of us were to eat the RDA of protein, at least 97% of us would be getting enough protein—we'd be meeting the minimum to be healthy. That's right, this number is a minimum to avoid malnutrition, not a maximum, and not a recommendation for optimal health.

By the way, if you're wondering how that number is determined? For protein, it is based on nitrogen balance. Humans break down proteins, as part of our body’s daily function, and we excrete nitrogen as a result. If you eat enough protein (which contains nitrogen), the amount of nitrogen you excrete will be the same as, or more than, the amount you eat. In other words, if you aren’t breaking your own body proteins down (in excess of what you eat), then whatever you’re eating must be, in some sense, enough.

In this way of thinking, the RDA is the minimum to stay healthy. More is fine; less would mean that you may not be getting enough. For some nutrients, there is also an UL, or upper limit, telling you that more than a certain amount is too much. Upper limits are calculated for vitamins and minerals; there is no upper limit defined for protein.

Therefore, there is no official definition for “too much” protein. If somebody eats more than the RDA, they’re not eating too much; they’re just eating more than the minimum. You’re supposed to eat more than the minimum.

The RDA for protein is set at 46 grams per day for a 125-pound woman, and at 56 grams per day for a 154-pound man. (The USDA chose those as their examples.) That’s based on an RDA of 0.8 grams of protein per kilogram bodyweight, which works out to 0.36 grams per pound. So a 200-pound person would need 72 grams of protein per day.

This USDA report found that most adult men average roughly 90 to 100 grams of protein per day, although men aged 70 and up only get about 80 grams of protein per day. Women tend to average around 70 grams per day, with those aged 70 and up averaging 62 grams.

Above the RDA? Yes. Too much? I don’t see any way of arguing that. And before you say that we’re getting almost double the recommendation, let's check the math. Those RDA numbers are for 125- and 154-pound people. On the other hand, the averages for what we eat are based on actual people, not ideals. The average American man is 200 pounds, and the average American woman is 171 pounds. So, to compare the numbers:

The average woman is 171 pounds, so her RDA would be 62 grams per day. (Women, on average, eat 70 grams of protein per day.)

The average man is 200 pounds, so his RDA would be 72 grams per day. (Men, on average, eat 90 to 100 grams of protein per day.)

Again, there’s no need to stick to the minimum; going 8 grams over, or even 28 grams over, is fine. It’s probably better to go over than to just scrape by, and many of us arguably don’t get enough. Let me explain.

Let’s start with older adults. Not only does protein intake tend to decrease with age, older adults are vulnerable to issues that stem from a loss of muscle mass. People tend to lose 3-5% of their muscle mass per decade starting at age 30, but strength training and protein intake can support maintaining our muscle, and thus likely prevent or reduce that decline.

The Dietary Guidelines include a note that “About 50 percent of women and 30 percent of men 71 and older fall short of protein foods recommendations.” Meanwhile, a study found that older adults who don’t meet the recommendations are “more likely to be limited when stooping, crouching, or kneeling, standing or sitting for long periods, walking up 10 steps, preparing meals, and walking for a quarter mile.”

So even if it’s true that the average adult gets more protein than recommended, there are clearly a lot of elderly folks who don’t. These are the same people who have more issues functioning in everyday life. This may be a chicken-and-egg situation—was the functional decline a cause or an effect of the change in their diet?—but this sure does not seem to be a group of people who should be eating less protein.

There’s another large group of people who benefit from more, not less, protein: people who are pregnant or lactating. Instead of 0.36 grams of protein per pound of body weight (62 grams for a 171-pound person), the RDA for people who are pregnant or lactating is 0.5 grams/pound (so, 86 grams of protein per day).

When you’re pregnant, you also have higher caloric needs, so the increased total amount of food makes it easier to get the higher protein amount. Still, it makes more sense to spend your energy on making sure you’re getting enough protein, rather than worrying about getting too much.

You knew we were heading in this direction (I say between reps of barbell squats, wiping protein shake off my lips): People who exercise should get more protein than just the RDA.

While the fear-mongering “too much protein” articles sometimes mention that bodybuilders or elite athletes need their protein, they tend to hand-wave this away as a special concern that doesn’t apply to normal people. But I think it’s worth a closer look—and honestly, this situation applies to a lot more people than just a few athletes.

Officially, there isn’t an RDA for athletes; people who exercise can stave off malnutrition with the same 0.36 grams per pound as everyone else. But that doesn’t mean that the RDA is the best target to aim for.

The International Association of Athletics Federations, which governs track and field competitions, recommends that most athletes who are maintaining or gaining weight eat 0.59 to 0.77 grams of protein per pound of bodyweight per day. That’s 101 to 131 grams for the average 171-pound woman, and 118 to 154 grams for a 200-pound man.

A group of organizations, including the American College of Sports Medicine, largely agrees, recommending a range from 0.54 to 0.9 grams per pound for all athletes whose weight is stable or gaining. That includes people who do endurance training like distance running, as well as strength athletes whose exercise involves mainly lifting weights. Those ranges would go as high as 153 grams for our 171-pound woman, and 180 grams for our 200-pound man.

You don’t need to be an Olympian to consider yourself an “athlete” in this sense. If you’re training for a half marathon, you’re doing plenty of distance running, and should fuel accordingly. And if you’re “just” lifting weights in the gym, but taking it seriously enough that you’re training regularly and working hard, you should consider eating in these ranges as well.

Dieting to lose weight is not only a popular American pastime, it’s also arguably good for at least some people's health. If you’ve been on a diet recently, or if you’re planning to go on one, you aren’t a person who should settle for the RDA either.

Research shows that protein intake (and strength training—they go together!) is important to maintain muscle mass when we’re losing weight. After all, you’re aiming for fat loss, not trying to get your muscles to waste away. Muscle loss is especially a concern with weight-loss drugs like Ozempic, but any dieter should be aware of this issue.

For example, this study found that diets ranging from 0.48 to 0.72 grams of protein per kg of body weight (that’s 82 to 123 grams for our 171-pound woman, 96 to 144 for our 200-pound man) resulted in less weight regain after the diet, and helped people to maintain muscle mass and feel more full while they were dieting.

And if you’re losing weight and exercising? The IAAF recommends that athletes who are “undertaking high-quality weight loss” need at least 0.72 grams per pound of bodyweight, and possibly as much as 1.09 grams per pound. That would be 186 grams for a 171-pound athlete, or 218 grams for a 200-pound athlete. Most people won’t need to go that high, and it’s unclear whether athletes need to go that high. But I’m including these numbers so you see how high the ranges actually go.

Ultimately, weight loss is widely understood to be more effective and have healthier results with higher protein intakes rather than lower ones. When people focus on just eating less, without thinking about what their diet actually consists of, it’s easy to forget about protein. But the evidence suggests that you should increase protein when you’re decreasing overall calories.

The idea that protein causes weight gain is a common talking point in those articles about “too much” protein, and it’s sort of true—but it also doesn’t mean what you think it means.

When you eat more food than your body needs, your body can store it as fat. That’s true no matter what the excess is made of—protein, carbs, fat, or even alcohol. The protein you eat gets used for many different things in your body. You can build it into muscle tissue, use it for growth and repair of different kinds of cells, and so on. You can also use it for energy—basically, burning it for the calories.

So if you were eating a perfectly balanced diet, and then decided to add an extra 100 grams of protein per day, then sure, a lot of that protein would be used for energy, and since we’d have excess energy, it would get stored as fat.

But if you ate more protein, but that protein replaced other foods in your diet, then there would be no excess calories to store. Nobody is saying you should chug a couple of protein shakes on top of your regular diet. They’re saying (I’m saying) that you should plan your meals and snacks to include more protein.

For example, if your regular lunch is a turkey-and-cheese sandwich with a side of chips, you could improve the protein content of your diet by adding more turkey to the sandwich and replacing the chips with an apple. Same total calories, but more protein. As long as your total calories for the day aren’t in excess of your needs, the “extra” protein won’t get stored as fat.

In general, high protein diets don’t have any serious health consequences. There’s a major exception, though: in some medical conditions, you may be told to limit your protein intake to protect your health.

For example, people with chronic kidney disease are often advised to use the RDA (0.36 grams per pound of body weight) as a maximum rather than a minimum. Your kidneys play a role in processing protein for excretion, so a lowered protein intake reduces the amount of work that a damaged kidney has to do. That said, once a person with chronic kidney disease begins dialysis, they may be advised to increase their protein intake for better health now that their body has help to handle the higher levels.

People with certain other disorders, like phenylketonuria and homocystinuria, may also be advised to eat a low-protein diet. Obviously, if you have one of these conditions, you should be getting your dietary advice from your medical team (ask for a referral to a dietitian!) rather than from general articles on the internet.

Besides those known medical issues, the occasional findings about eating “too much” protein tend to fit into the “X is good for you/X is bad for you” ricochet news cycle. They’re not holistic assessments of protein in general on health in general, but rather specific research questions that are still being figured out.

For example, this 2017 study found that a high-protein (and high-fiber) diet seemed to slightly worsen one measure of insulin resistance, but it also improved metabolic health and body composition. The researchers concluded that the subjects’ body chemistry was probably just responding appropriately to the changed nutrient content of their diet. A few years later, a study of high-BMI women with insulin resistance saw improvements to their insulin resistance on a high-protein diet.

Or to take another example, a study in 2024 found a link between high-protein diets and atherosclerosis. But if you look at what the researchers were actually studying, they were looking at how leucine (one amino acid found in protein) affects the mTOR biochemical pathway in certain types of white blood cells. By the way, that mTOR pathway is involved in a lot more body processes than atherosclerosis, and does a lot of good things too.

So are these results interesting, and worth further study? Definitely. Worth changing protein recommendations? Only if this effect turns out (1) to actually lead to worse health outcomes, and (2) to outweigh the known benefits of higher protein. The body of evidence doesn’t yet support lowering protein recommendations, nor adding an upper limit.

So if protein is good for us, and most of us can’t really get “too much,” why are so many people arguing that we’re overdoing it? I think part of the reason is just misunderstanding (the writers don’t tend to have a background in nutrition and especially not in sports nutrition), but more often, I think they’re talking about a different issue entirely.

Often the “too much protein” stuff is just a way of talking about the environmental effects of meat consumption or dairy farming. People making this argument are trying to pry the double cheeseburgers out of our hands and reassure us that we’ll be okay. I don’t think an attack on protein is an appropriate way to make that point, since plant-based proteins exist and are a fine alternative. But I understand where they’re coming from.

Ultimately, if you’re trying to make the argument that we’re eating “too much” protein for our health, you really can’t do that without some evidence that we’re eating so much protein that it’s harming our health on a widespread level. And that evidence just doesn’t exist.

#3398. MacBook Neo 2 is coming, and Apple reportedly expects a massive hit

Apple has a MacBook Neo 2 planned for early 2027, per Mark Gurman, and a new report from Digitimes indicates the company is expecting it to be a massive hit.

When the MacBook Neo debuted earlier this year, it became an instant hit.

Driven primarily by MacBook Neo, Apple set a new record for its best ever sales week among first-time Mac buyers.

But as popular as the first MacBook Neo has proven, it sounds like Apple is planning for its successor to be an even bigger hit.

Apple has given suppliers a shipment forecast of 16 million MacBook Neo units for 2027, about double the nearly 8 million units expected in 2026, according to supply-chain sources.

16 million units for 2027 is a huge increase from MacBook Neo’s 2026 numbers.

A small portion of that increase can be attributed to the MacBook Neo being on sale for longer in 2027. The original Neo arrived in March 2026, so 2027 will have the advantage of January and February sales.

But those two extra months can’t come anywhere close to accounting for the doubling of units. Especially since they’re slower periods for consumer electronics sales.

With reporting pointing to a MacBook Neo 2 launching in early 2027, it sounds like Apple is confident the Neo will prove even more popular in the year ahead.

#3397. 3 Stocks Down More Than 30% From Their Record Highs to Buy in November

Three consumer stocks that just reported earnings are down from their highs, and each spent the fall doing something a stock chart cannot see.

Earnings season is the one time of year a company has to say, in plain numbers, what it has been doing. For most of the market, that meant another round of data center budgets. For the three consumer companies below, it meant something smaller and more human: a new drink on the shelf, a shipment that went out ahead of schedule, and a running shoe that keeps selling in countries where it did not exist five years ago.

All three reported in the last two weeks, all three trade around 30% to 85% below their record highs, and all three spent the fall doing work a stock chart cannot see.

Deckers Brands (DECK -1.17%), the parent of HOKA and UGG, trades near $80, about 55% below the record it set in January 2025. The stock fell again after the company reported on Oct. 22, which says more about expectations than the quarter. Sales rose 3.5% to a record $1.48 billion, HOKA grew 6.8%, and international sales climbed 9% while the U.S. business was flat. Management raised its full-year earnings guidance to $7.80 to $7.95 per share, which puts the stock at about 10 times this year's profit.

The part that matters for November is what Deckers is doing with its cash. The company bought back $299 million of stock in the quarter at an average price of $93.65, and its guidance assumes $1 billion of repurchases for the full year. It still has $1.2 billion in cash and no debt. That is a company telling you it thinks its own shares are the best thing it can buy.

The risk here is that CEO Stefano Caroti called the consumer environment "challenging," and direct-to-consumer comparable sales fell 6.4%, the channel where a brand's heat shows up first. According to Retail Dive, UGG also depends on a cold winter. If December is warm, the fourth quarter will be too.

Columbia Sportswear (COLM +1.90%) sits about 32% below its April 2021 high. But the stock is on a tear over the past month. It reported on Oct. 29, and the headline was that delayed fall wholesale orders shipped sooner than the company expected, which pushed third-quarter sales up 2% to $962.6 million and earnings to $1.66 per share. Columbia raised the low end of its full-year sales and earnings guidance and said U.S. e-commerce, the channel it calls "the pinnacle expression of our brand," is gaining ground.

What the company has been doing this fall is rebuilding its leadership one brand at a time. It named Joe Vernachio president of SOREL in June and Peter Rauch president of Mountain Hardwear in September, the two smaller brands that took a $29 million write-down a year ago. The ACCELERATE strategy, Columbia's plan to win younger and more active customers, is in its second year, and CEO Tim Boyle said it is gaining traction. The company repurchased $200 million of stock through nine months and has no borrowings.

Boston Beer (SAM -1.93%) is the hardest case here. The stock trades near $215, about 85% below its 2021 peak, when hard seltzer looked like the future. It was not. The company reported on Oct. 22 that revenue fell 3.2%, with Twisted Tea, Truly, and Samuel Adams all shrinking.

Two things keep it on this list. First, gross margin reached 51.7%, the highest quarterly rate since 2017, because the company has spent three years closing the gap between what it brews and what it sells. Second, Sun Cruiser, a vodka-iced tea launched in 2024, grew again and is now the brand that founder Jim Koch talks about first. According to Brewbound, Sun Cruiser is on track to double this year.

This fall Boston Beer hired Allison Stransky away from Samsung Electronics America as chief marketing officer, put Twisted Tea in Realtree camo cans for hunting season, and brought back a non-alcoholic Octoberfest. None of that fixes a shrinking beer category, but the company is buying back stock, carries no debt, and trades at 19 times next year's expected earnings for a business that makes more money per case each year.

None of these companies is asking you to believe in a turnaround that has not started. Deckers is profitable and buying itself. Columbia is shipping. Boston Beer is more efficient than it has been in nine years. To me, the right move in November is a small position in each, sized so that a warm winter or a weak beer season is an annoyance rather than a problem, and the patience to let the buybacks do their work.

Micah Zimmerman has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Deckers Outdoor. The Motley Fool recommends Boston Beer. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3396. Five Race-Day Smartwatch Hacks Every Marathon Runner Should Know

I love my Garmin Forerunner 970, but the fact is, most runners don't need all the features it has to offer. In fact, for most road races, you can get by with whatever smartwatch you already own—as long as you know how to use it. If you've got a marathon or half-marathon coming up, these five tricks will only take a few minutes to set up, and they can save you from one of many of the small-but-avoidable disasters that can derail a good race.

Nothing spikes pre-race anxiety like standing in a corral of hundreds of people watching your watch fail to latch onto a signal. Tall buildings, crowded starts, and a sea of other devices make the first minute of GPS unreliable, which can leave your opening mileage pace wildly off.

The fix is simple: start the GPS search early. Step outside, into the open, as soon as you've dropped your bag, and select your run activity at least 10 to 15 minutes before the starting gun. If your watch supports multi-band or dual-frequency GPS, turn it on in the activity settings, since it's noticeably better in dense downtown starts. Then, don't press start until the gun goes off (or you cross the line, if you want chip-accurate pacing).

Bonus tip: If you're in a start corral with a long wait, you can lock the signal and then pause the activity screen. Just remember to hit start when you actually take off.

Multiple data screens are great for training, but overwhelming during a race. Too many numbers invite overthinking, and seeing the "wrong" number at mile two can lead you into a very stressful mile ten.

My recommendation is to build a dedicated race screen with three to four fields at most:

Lap pace or average lap pace (not instant pace, which jumps around constantly with GPS)

Distance or lap distance, so you know where you are relative to the mile markers

Heart rate, especially in the early miles when adrenaline tempts you to go out too fast

Elapsed time, for splits against your goal

Keep it clean and stripped down, and avoid the temptation to add cadence, power, vertical oscillation, and everything else. You can always review those stats during your cool-down.

A text from your boss at mile 14 is nobody's idea of a good time. Before race day, switch your watch to Do Not Disturb or Airplane mode, or turn on a dedicated activity mode that blocks notifications. This also saves battery, which matters if your marathon is going to take you four-plus hours.

After blocking the outside world, you can set race-specific alerts, like a high heart-rate alert to keep you honest in the first half. I also know runners who set a recurring time or distance alert for fueling—say, every 30 to 40 minutes, or every 5 miles—so remembering to down a gel or a sports drink doesn't depend on your fading brain.

Here's one thing I learn the hard way, every time: Your watch will almost always say you've run farther than the race course says you have. Race courses are measured along the shortest possible route, but along the way, you'll weave around people, take wide turns, and generally add extra distance. I've run marathons where my watch reads closer to 26.6 miles (nearly an extra half mile), so my "on pace" watch is actually behind my chip time.

The hack: Ignore the watch's auto-lap and press the lap button manually at each mile marker (or at every kilometer marker, if that's what the course uses). This gives you pace data aligned to the official course, not the satellite's best guess. It also gives you a quick mental check against your plan. If you've set up your watch for it, display average lap pace, then glance at it a few hundred meters after each marker to see how you're tracking. And don't panic if your watch beeps for a mile before you pass the marker—trust the course and your lap presses, and do your best to ignore the mismatched distance adding up.

Rain, sweat, high-fives, and a hasty cup grab at an aid station can all trigger accidental taps on a touchscreen watch. Few things are worse than discovering at mile 18 that you accidentally paused, ended, or switched screens on your activity. So before the race, turn on your watch's screen lock, so a stray touch doesn't do anything.

If your watch has a configurable wake gesture, consider turning it off to save battery, and set the backlight to a short timeout. While we're talking watch-wearing protocol, remember to wear it snugly, one finger-width above your wrist bone, for a better heart-rate reading as you sweat. Finally, if your watch has one, use the post-race auto-save reminder. (Otherwise, do your best to hit stop after you cross the finish line.)

Again, you don't need the most premium running-specific watch ahead of race day. If you have time, test these hacks on a long run, so that you're not wasting any precious mental energy during the big day.

#3395. Security Bite: The record $6.3B Binance heist started with a fake Homebrew install on Mac

9to5Mac Security Bite is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Making Apple devices work-ready and enterprise-safe is all we do. Our unique integrated approach to management and security combines state-of-the-art Apple-specific security solutions for fully automated Hardening & Compliance, Next Generation EDR, AI-powered Zero Trust, and exclusive Privilege Management with the most powerful and modern Apple MDM on the market. The result is a totally automated Apple Unified Platform currently trusted by over 45,000 organizations to make millions of Apple devices work-ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

Last week, news broke that hackers had stolen $6.3 billion from wallets on Binance, the most popular cryptocurrency exchange in the world. The company was able to freeze about nearly $3 billion of it, but the attack quickly made headlines, and rightfully so, as the largest financial heist in human history.

At the time, I suspected, along with security researcher Christopher Lopez and plenty of others, that this could have very well started on a Mac. As Lopez pointed out, the $1.5 billion Bybit heist last year also began on a developer’s Mac. On top of that, Macs are hugely popular among DevOps engineers and crypto folks, and they’ve been on the receiving end of a steady stream of malware and social engineering campaigns over the past few years.

I can now say any suspicions that this heist originated on Mac were right. I’m still in a state of shock. Dazed not by the amount stolen, but how the said hackers did so using the same ol’ social engineering tricks they’ve been using for years. No sophisticated multi-milllion dollar underground zero-day here.

Yesterday, Binance published a more detailed breakdown of the attack. The company never actually says “Mac,” but the malware it published targeted /opt/homebrew, which is where Homebrew lives on Apple silicon Macs. In other words, this was almost certainly an M-series MacBook.

The attack basically transpired in two steps.

According to Binance, in June this year, a DevOps engineer working on Wallet searched for an AI coding tool and downloaded a malicious clone of the Homebrew installer in Google Search. Binance claims it caught it early and stopped any damage. However, what it didn’t know was that it allowed the attackers to learn which employees worked on its wallets. This was phase 1.

Fast forward a few months to September, a different engineer who, you guessed it, worked on wallets for Binance, was lured into a fake job interview. As these sort of social engineering attacks normally go, they told to run a coding “assignment” on their work computer. This was not caught by Binance security, and on October 29, the world learned that hackers (now widely speculated as North Korean hackers) walked off with billions.

Of course, most of what we know so far comes directly from Binance, so if you’re looking for more details on exactly how this happened, you’ll likely be left empty-handed.

It’s important to note here though, none of these two attack vectors are new. Back in early 2025, I wrote about fake Homebrew ads at the top of Google Search pushing Atomic Stealer to Mac users. Binance only says the engineer found his installer through “a search engine.” Of course, I can’t confirm it was a sponsored ad, but if history tells us anything…

This is a rather uncomfortable situation for Apple to be in. The largest financial heist in history happen on Mac last week, though to be fair, there’s no security feature that can stop a developer from running a script he wants to run.

Sure, the Terminal paste warnings introduced in macOS 26.4 could have helped here. But realistically, if someone’s convinced they’re doing a coding test for a job they really want, a warning pop-up probably isn’t going to stop them.

I’m having Christopher Lopez (@L0Psec) a professional macOS reverse engineer back on the Security Bite Podcast this week to talk about the Binance situation with me. Follow the show so you don’t miss that.

#3394. iOS 27.3 upgrades Apple Music in two ways, here’s what’s new

Apple Music is getting two upgrades in iOS 27.3, which just debuted in beta this week. Here’s what’s new.

The most noteworthy upgrade is a new ‘Selfie Sing’ feature for creating karaoke videos. It was discovered by Aaron Perris in iOS 27.3 beta 1, and beta users can try it by searching for Apple’s ‘Selfie Sing’ playlist.

Here’s a walkthrough of what it looks like via Digital Trends on X:

Apple Music has a new selfie karaoke mode now, and it's so much fun. It just landed with iOS 27.3 developer beta update. pic.twitter.com/O6AcDOSppu

Essentially, Apple is leveraging the existing Apple Music Sing features into a standalone selfie video tool. You’ll be able to create your own selfie karaoke videos for sharing on platforms like TikTok, Instagram, and more.

Another iOS 27.3 upgrade for Music is found when using the lyrics view in landscape mode.

Apple needs to find a way to recover lost or grayed out songs. I have hundreds of songs like that. The sync method doesn’t work and I have to search for a duplicate song one at a time. I pay for Apple Music and they need to fix this.

Similar to what’s available on iPhone Duo, the animated artwork for what’s playing now bleeds further into the lyrics view. It’s a great look that’s now coming to all iPhone models.

Here’s are some examples posted by Beta Profiles on X:

New in iOS 27.3 Beta: Animated artwork blends into the Apple Music player in landscape mode, and it looks so good. pic.twitter.com/k8rgSEALGo

What do you think of the new Apple Music changes in iOS 27.3? Let us know in the comments.

Apple Music is available for $11.99/month, or you can get it as part of the Apple One bundle.

#3392. Meet the 20 first-place apps from RevenueCat’s Shipaton 2026

A cozy habit tracker, a smarter snippet library, and a rooster that wants you out of bed: this year’s Shipaton winners offer plenty of new apps to explore.

RevenueCat’s annual app-building competition drew 3,985 project submissions in 2026, according to its winner announcement. Across the 20 first-place categories, developers tackled everyday frustrations, built inventive games, and found new ways to connect people.

You can get a look at every first place winner below, and read RevenueCat’s full winner announcement for every more.

Keeping a routine is easier when there’s something to look forward to. Mio pairs self-care and habit tracking with a pixel companion that grows as you make progress. Check off habits, earn coins, and unlock new companions and collectibles, with friends and groups adding a social reason to keep going.

Mio took Shipaton’s Grand Prize, with RevenueCat highlighting its revenue and growth in a crowded habit-tracking market.

That dog you met on your morning walk can become part of your collection. Boop identifies cats and dogs and turns their photos into stickers for a digital book, giving pet lovers a playful reason to pay attention to the animals around them.

Creator Taiwo Omisore’s “100 Boops” challenge took the app into the real world, where printed pet portraits and conversations with owners helped shape the product. That hands-on approach earned Boop first place in #BuildInPublic.

If you have fond memories of futuristic arcade racers, Nitelore has a familiar appeal: hovering vehicles, neon tracks, and plenty of speed. Chase your own ghost in time trials, take on combat races, or compete online.

Free tracks offer a starting point, while paid unlocks and daily and weekly challenges give players more to explore. RevenueCat’s Best Game judges singled out the art direction, effects, and haptics.

Explaining how you see color can be surprisingly difficult. See as Me: Colorblind makes that conversation visual, using a split-screen camera to compare different types and degrees of color blindness. A shareable link lets someone else see the comparison without installing the app.

Developer Javier Jiménez drew on his own experience with protanopia. That personal perspective helped the app earn the RevenueCat Peace Prize.

Clucky’s rooster is determined to get you out of bed. Turning off an alarm can require solving a problem, moving around, or finding an object, bringing a little friction to the temptation to snooze.

Its personality runs through the entire interface, including a time picker that uses the rooster’s scrolling eyes and yellow beak. That consistent character, animation, and attention to detail earned Clucky the RevenueCat Design Award.

Adversary starts with a familiar challenge: flip cards and find matching pairs. The catch is a hidden Danger card with no matching partner. Reveal it, and an ad becomes part of the board you’re trying to remember.

That idea earned Niv Ben-porath’s game the Catvertising Award. Players can continue with ads after an initial ad-free period, or choose a permanent unlock that removes ads and adds difficulty options.

Put a few phones on the table, and Bubble Games turns their screens into a shared game board. Objects move between devices as friends compete in minigames, including a virtual hot potato.

Built by four software engineering students at Université Laval, the Next Gen Award winner uses the phones people already have to create a shared activity. Its Shipaton submission includes ten minigames. The winner announcement links to the Android release on Google Play.

1st place • HAMM Award (Help Apps Make Money)

GRIDLOCK takes a game everyone knows and adds up to four players, online rooms, and eleven special moves. The result offers more ways to disrupt an opponent’s plans than the familiar three-by-three board.

Its HAMM Award win recognizes how the business model fits the game: a shared Credits currency connects rewarded ads, optional packs, and a subscription, while core modes remain free. Players can choose the option that fits how often they play.

1st place • Influencer Award – Nutrition & Healthy Eating: Abbey’s Kitchen

Just Add begins with a craving. Type what you feel like eating, describe it aloud, or take a photo, and the app suggests three meals built around it, adding protein, fiber, and healthy fats to round out the plate.

Shopping support, hands-free cooking, and remembered preferences help carry the idea through to dinner. The winner of Abbey’s Kitchen’s nutrition challenge also impressed judges with a dinner-host feature that accounts for other people’s preferences.

1st place • Influencer Award – Productivity: Christopher Lawley

The reply you send every week, the PDF you keep hunting for, and the image you paste repeatedly can all live in SnipStash. It organizes reusable text, images, and files across iPhone, iPad, and Mac, with a keyboard, Mac quick palette, hotkeys, and Shortcuts bringing them within reach.

Private iCloud sync connects the library across devices. Its speed and native interface helped it win Christopher Lawley’s productivity challenge.

1st place • Influencer Award – Career Coaching: Leadership Heather

Knowing what you want to say and saying it aloud are different things. Rehearse – Hard Conversations gives you an AI counterpart to practice with before a difficult workplace discussion.

Choose from 33 prepared scenarios or bring your own situation, then review feedback on clarity, empathy, assertiveness, and structure. A prep card helps you take the useful points into the real conversation. The app won Leadership Heather’s career-coaching challenge for its focused, straightforward approach.

1st place • Influencer Award – Gaming: Mr Lewis Blogs Gaming

You see a game in a short video, mean to look it up later, and forget its name. Game Magnet lets you share the clip to identify the games and save them to your backlog.

Processing happens in the background, with a notification when the result is ready. Shelves, ratings, and ranked lists help organize what comes next. The app won Mr Lewis Blogs Gaming’s challenge by making discovery and keeping track of games easier.

1st place • Influencer Award – Yoga & Fitness: Simone Sharice

FeelGood: Movement Menu starts with a short check-in about your energy, available time, and how you want to feel. It then offers a small menu of movement, with an appetizer, main, and optional sides.

The options span yoga, Pilates, strength, walking, stretching, and breathing. Rest is part of the experience, too. Yusra Salam and Ameena Malik’s app won Simone Sharice’s yoga and fitness challenge, with judges praising its calm, inviting design.

BoatBrawl brings arcade boat battles to a group of up to eight players. Steer, fire, and scramble through interactive arenas, with bots and shared-screen play offering more ways to join in.

Rehaan Cubes and Ashwin K M used Kotlin Multiplatform and Compose Multiplatform to bring the game across phones and computers, including iOS, Android, Mac, Windows, and the web. Its smooth browser play helped it take JetBrains’ Ship Kotlin Everywhere award.

Trazo: Golf Ball Tracer adds a ball-flight line to your own golf videos. Select the ball twice to start, and the processing runs on the phone.

Julian Praest’s app won Most Viral App for the way its team introduced the product through organic content. Golf humor and practical advice set up the tracer reveal, making the finished video part of the pitch. For golfers, the appeal is simple: make the shot easier to follow when you share it.

One Piece Card Game collectors know that similar-looking cards can be very different finds. Grandfolio helps identify artwork variants, manage duplicates, and track collection prices and progress.

The Best App for Galaxy winner impressed judges with layouts that adapt to folded, tabletop, and open-screen use. There’s an App Store release for Apple users, too, making this a relevant discovery even if your collection starts on an iPhone.

Let’s Get Support by 3Dadz is designed for partners, parents, and friends affected by someone else’s addiction. Check-ins, journaling, boundary-setting tools, and local resources give those supporters a place to focus on their own needs.

Joshua Burgess and Aaryn B. built the app from community conversations in British Columbia, using Replit to turn the idea into a live product. It won Replit’s Idea to Income award. The announcement links to its Android release.

PoquitoTalk: Bocas del Toro turns English into local Spanish voice notes for WhatsApp and helps translate the replies. The recipient doesn’t need to install the app, keeping the conversation in a tool people already use.

Creator Dorien Van den Abbeele drew on years of life in Bocas del Toro. Its Growth Loop Award recognizes extensive growth experiments and an honest account of what the measurements could show. The announcement links to Google Play.

Parky! combines wait times, dining availability, and memories from Disney and Universal visits. Built by former Disney Cast Member Chase Van Derrick, it aims to offer useful help throughout a park day.

Dining alerts can become conversations on the Lock Screen, where you can ask about another time or restaurant. Alongside queue Live Activities and recap messages, those interactive notifications helped Parky! win the Keep Them Coming Back Award.

In Your Own Words offers short, real-world speaking scenarios and feedback on pace, hesitation, and filler words. Speech analysis takes place on the phone, giving users a way to practice the words before they need them.

Natasha Wilson’s app won the Funnel Vision Award for connecting a web quiz, a relevant practice deck, and a web purchase that unlocks access in the app. The introduction to the product begins before the download.

Friendpire turns the idea of a board-game night with friends into a shared hex-tile world. Gather resources, build farms and docks, and grow an empire together. RevenueCat employee Erik MacInnis built the game to make it easier to stay connected with friends who rarely find time to play.

Friendpire won the separate Conflict of Interest Award, which was open to RevenueCat and sponsor employees and judged by Shipaton participants. It is included here as an optional sidebar and is not part of the 20 first-place count above.

From a useful tool for the workday to a game for your next night in, Shipaton’s winners show how much can come from taking an idea all the way to a shipped app. Explore the winners above, or browse RevenueCat’s full announcement for more apps from the competition.

Explore all Shipaton 2026 winners  |  Learn more about Shipaton

#3391. Canopy Growth (CGC) Q2 2027 Earnings Call Transcript

Margins slipped as Canadian medical reimbursement fell, even as revenue climbed.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Canopy Growth Corporation (CGC -3.58%) reported significant top-line expansion driven by a triple-digit increase in international medical cannabis revenue and the integration of the MTL Cannabis acquisition. Management stated that the company is moving toward adjusted EBITDA positivity in the second half of fiscal 2027 by focusing on cultivation excellence and cost discipline. The company reported a strengthened European supply chain following new certifications, while also addressing margin headwinds in the Canadian medical market. Management indicated that the focus remains on high-quality flower production to satisfy demand in core markets across Canada, Germany, and Poland.

Operator: Good morning. My name is Joanna, and I will be your conference operator today. I would like to welcome you to Canopy's Second Quarter 27 Financial Results Conference Call. Currently, all participants are in a listen-only mode. I will now turn the call over to Jonathan, you may begin your conference call. Thank you, Joanna, and good morning, and thank you, everyone, for joining us. On our call today, we have Canopy Growth's Chief Executive Officer, Luc Mongeau, and Chief Financial Officer, Thomas Carlton Stewart. Prior to the opening of financial markets today, Canopy Growth issued a news release announcing the financial results for its second quarter ended September 30, 2026.

The news release and financial statements have been filed on EDGAR and SEDAR and will be available on the website under the Investors tab. Before we begin, I would like to remind you that our discussion during the call will include forward-looking statements that are based on management's current views and assumptions and that this discussion is qualified in its entirety by the cautionary note regarding forward-looking statements included at the end of the news release issued today. Please review today's earnings release and Canopy's reports filed with the SEC and SEDAR for various factors that could cause actual results to differ materially from projections.

In addition, reconciliations between any non GAAP measures to their closest reported GAAP measures are included in our earnings release. Please note that all financial information is provided in penny and dollars unless otherwise stated. Following the remarks by Luc and Thomas Carlton Stewart, we will conduct a question and answer session where we will take questions from analysts. And with that, I would like to turn the call over to Luc.

Luc Mongeau: Thank you, Jonathan. Good morning, everyone. And thank you for joining us today. Our second quarter of fiscal 27 results show continued momentum with another quarter of strong year-over-year top-line growth across most of the business. Consolidated net revenue increased 22% year over year to $81.4 million Cannabis revenue increased by 30% to $66.2 million reflecting our ability to produce and supply high quality flower to meet the demand of the Canadian and European markets.

The biggest driver of growth was our international business, where net revenue increased by a tremendous 141% over Q2 of last year, and by 28% sequentially from the first quarter to $12.3 million International growth was enabled by strong availability of flower and a strengthened route-to-market that increased our reach to patients in our core European markets. Canada Medical net revenue grew by 18% year over year to $25.8 million Similar to last quarter, we benefited from ongoing increases in patient counts, including through the addition of the MTL Medical business.

Our team is building from this new baseline following the VAC reimbursement cap implemented at the beginning of April continuing to add patients, and providing best in class service experience for our patients. We believe our position as the number 1 medical cannabis provider with Canadian owned and Canadian grown supply will remain an important differentiator. Canada Adult Use net revenue increased 17% to $21.8 million We are seeing the benefits of a strengthened product portfolio as well as the addition of the MTL brands, which perform well in Quebec and are building momentum in the rest of Canada.

We are confident in our ability to continue to grow in this market and recently made the decision to build out an internal sales force fully dedicated to growing our brands in Canada. Our growth in cannabis revenue has been made possible by our ability to provide a more consistent supply of the right flower to consumers. Elevating cultivation has been a core focus for Canopy. With efforts accelerating since we acquired MTL cannabis at the end of 26. We are applying the expertise of MTL's master growers to improve cultivation practices and drive increased yield and flower quality at our EU GMP facility in Kincardine. Our team has been busy implementing new growth methods and adding new strengths.

Early results are encouraging. We are taking steps to further increase yield and continue building on these results. We expect to see a noticeable increase in yield and flower quality as we exit the third quarter of fiscal 27 with the full impact being felt in the start of fiscal 28. We believe there is the potential to increase flower production at Kincardine by at least 25% to 30%. Within the same physical footprint. We expect increased yield and quality to drive both revenue growth and per unit cost improvements. Improved cultivation is a key foundation foundational element of our global supply chain.

In addition, we are also focusing our efforts on strengthening our global distribution and manufacturing network and improving our access to patients across Europe. On that subject, we recently received EU GMP certification at our Smiths Falls facility. As well as a renewal of the EU GMP certification at Kincardine. This makes Canopy only Canadian company with end to end EU GMP certification covering its entire supply chain, from cultivation to the manufacturing and primary packaging of sublingual oils, and dry cannabis flower. Our European sales have historically been limited to flour. The Smiths Falls certification creates a path to expand into additional categories of high quality patient ready products broadening our addressable market, and creating new growth opportunities.

Our team is actively working with existing and new channels to prioritize these avenues for growth and we expect to provide updates on this in future quarters. These capabilities are increasingly important to European customers and regulators. They enable us to maintain the highest quality standards with fewer third parties handling our products. It is clearly part of our promise of product integrity in action. Other steps we have taken to strengthen our international capabilities include relaunching the Tweed brand in Germany with MTL Cannabis Genetics. Strengthening our commercial and operational leadership team in Germany to accelerate growth, broadening our product offering in Australia, and entering the U.K. medical cannabis market.

We see international markets as a key driver of growth and we are very excited about our prospects. Turning to Storz & Bickel. We reported revenue of $50.1 million down 44% from the second quarter of last year. Storz & Bickel is managing through waves of variability consumer spending in the face of economic uncertainties in various markets, as well as evolving trends in this space. We continue to refine our product portfolio and go to market strategies to maintain our leadership position. Storz & Bickel is known for innovation, as demonstrated by their recent recognition by Safe Access Now for recent product advancements with the Venti Flower Vaporization Innovation Award.

Consistent with prior years, we expect a seasonally strong quarter in Q3 driven by the holiday season. Overall, our financial results are showing what a better execution across Canopy Growth can deliver. there is still a lot of work to be done, but we are still sustaining our momentum in the right direction. We continue to strengthen our foundation, our capabilities, which gives me increasing confidence in our ability to accelerate growth into profitability in the coming quarters. I will now ask Thomas Carlton Stewart to provide more details on our second quarter financial results.

Thomas Carlton Stewart: Thank you, Luke, and good morning, everyone. Canopy delivered strong second quarter performance driven by accelerated top line growth and disciplined bottom line execution. Consolidated net revenue climbed 22% year-over-year to $81.4 million, anchored by a 30% increase in our cannabis segment. Reflecting broad based momentum across every channel. While MTL continues to be an engine for our fiscal 27 performance, organic growth in international cannabis was equally important. Offsetting headwinds faced in Canada Medical. Sequentially, the business is demonstrating stronger underlying earnings, held consolidated gross margin firm at 31% for the quarter, despite not having the U.S. tariff refunds that supported Q1. At the same time, we drove meaningful reductions to SG&A and narrowed our adjusted EBITDA loss.

This strong execution reinforces our confidence as we remain on track to deliver positive adjusted EBITDA. In the second half of this fiscal year. Let me take a moment to elaborate on each of these points. A key growth driver for our business has been international cannabis. Which typically delivers favorable pricing on average relative to the domestic market in Canada. This makes continued growth in our international markets an increasingly important contributor to our overall performance and our strategy to drive improved shareholder returns. We expect the ongoing growth of the international business along with the improvements to our cultivation operations Luc described, to contribute to margin expansion going forward for the cannabis segment.

Adjusted gross margin was 31% in Q2 27 compared to 33% a year earlier. The decrease is primarily due to the reduction in the Veteran Affairs Canada reimbursement rate, which has had a major impact on our Cannabis segment gross margins compared to the prior year. The Storz & Bickel segment reported a modest increase in gross margin, from 38% in Q2 of last year to 39% this year, despite a decrease in revenue over the same time frame. This result was due to cost efficiencies realized under the new management team.

We are pleased that S&B margins in the first half of fiscal 27 have been well above the 33% we reported in that segment for the full fiscal 26 year. As previously mentioned, S&B benefited from a 1-time tariff refund in Q1, positively affecting our consolidated gross margin by approximately 2%. Turning to operating expenses. We continue to see progress. SG&A expense increased $3.4 million from Q2 26, even as we absorb the full MTL business, which typically incurred SG&A expense of approximately $6 million The combined company is operating more efficiently, reflecting not only a lower cost base and integration synergies, but also improved execution across the business.

We remain on track to reach our target run rate of $10 million of annualized synergies within 18 months of the March 2026 closing, of the MTL transaction. On a sequential basis, SG&A expense in Q2 was approximately $5 million lower than in Q1. Reflecting our ongoing financial discipline and cost saving actions taken to date. Adjusted EBITDA loss was $2.9 million in Q2 27. That represented an improvement of $400 thousand from Q1 27. Again, we achieved a sequential improvement despite the absence of the S&B tariff refund recorded in Q1. Turning to our financial position. We had $320 million of cash and short term investments as of 09/30/2026.

In addition, free cash outflow for Q2 improved by $3.7 million from Q2 26 to $15.6 million despite an increase in capital expenditures of $1.8 million to invest in our cultivation facility. Last month, we held a successful annual meeting where shareholders approved all resolutions including authorization for our Board to complete a share consolidation also known as the split. As a reminder, it continues to be our intention to only complete the consolidation if it is necessary to maintain our NASDAQ listing. In terms of our ATM program, we have not sold any shares since December 2025 given our strong cash position. We would look to the ATM selectively in support of strategic opportunities.

Including M&A, where we see a compelling path to shareholder value creation. In summary, Canopy has the liquidity, the discipline, and the strategic runway to fund both organic growth and potential M&A opportunities. With $320 million in cash and investments, we have the flexibility to pursue accretive, high impact growth opportunities in a disciplined manner. The track record we established with MTL demonstrates that we have the capability to integrate acquisitions efficiently and realize meaningful synergies. We enter the second half of fiscal 27 with strong momentum stringent cost controls and line of sight to positive adjusted EBITDA. I will now turn the call back to Luc for his closing remarks.

Luc Mongeau: Thank you very much, Tom. The results we reported today represent another important step forward in canopy's growth journey to build a profitable leading global cannabis company. Financial momentum such as that accelerating growth of our international business, is certainly a big part of that and is reflecting in our top line results. Perhaps even more importantly, our teams and our employees understand the power, the strength that we are establishing as a company. Our international business now has a unique competitive advantage through our end to end EU GMP supply chain for both flower and manufactured products. Canada Adult Use has clear sight lines to improve market rankings on the strength of our best brands.

Canada Medical is solidifying its leadership position, and becoming a much stronger business as they work to overcome significant external challenges. Cultivation yields at Kincardine are still improving, and the end result is within our grasp. Storz & Bickel continues to innovate and sharpen its focus on improved competitiveness. As I look across the business, I see that all cylinders are starting to fire in unison. This is turning our foundational discipline into sustained and compounding velocity. It is the driving force uniting the entire team around a shared strategic purpose. And it is beginning to deliver tangible results. I would like to thank our team for their continued hard work and commitment to achieving our goals.

Operator: Thank you. Ladies and gentlemen, we will now begin the question and answer session. Should you have a question, you will hear a prompt that your hand has been raised. If you wish to decline from the polling process, please press star followed by the 2. If you are using a speakerphone, please lift the headset before pressing any keys. We ask that you please limit yourself to 1 question. You may press star 1 again should you have any follow-up. First question from Aaron Grey with Alliance Global Partners. Please go ahead.

Aaron Grey: Hi. Thank you very much for the question here. Just want to dive a bit more into, path to profitability, Luc. And Thomas Carlton Stewart, obviously, we have been big focus since you guys came into your respective seats. So firstly, you talked about it being within reach. We have got some seasonally strong quarters coming in. Some of those cost savings, you know, are starting to flow through as well. So just more color in terms of the timing of EBITDA profitability and then maybe bigger picture. You know, what type of profitability or margin profile we could start looking at, you know, come FY 2028 and beyond? Thank you.

Thomas Carlton Stewart: Thanks, Aaron. Good morning. So for our profit. Our path to profitability, a lot of that, as you are saying, we do expect to have a stronger back half of the year, some of that driven by seasonality in the S&B business, which does carry favorable margins relative to our Canadian or our cannabis segment. I would say for us, a lot of the cultivation enhancements that we are talking about on the call that we have mentioned, we have yet to see those kind of benefit the P&L. The changes are being made. Like, we are seeing positive kind of indications early on.

But it likely will not materialize in the P&L until the as we are exiting FY 2027. So I think, you know, we still see a pathway to get to positive adjusted EBITDA in the back half of the year. But a lot of the cost savings, synergies, and whatnot, that work is ongoing in the cultivation aspect. You would not see yet in the P&L. I do not know, Luc, anything? Yeah.

Luc Mongeau: For me, listen, we have been attacking the PNL since we started. And so we started with addressing the SG&A. We over-delivered on our targets there. Second, we, you know, we said we would address cultivation. We did the acquisition of MTL. We did the integration as swiftly as possible. Brought in the MTL master growers. We are proceeding with the transformation of our main cultivation facility, Kincardine. Think about it. We have got 24 rooms there. We transition 1 room at a time to new cultivation practices. And new strains. We are 10 rooms in of 24. We do 1 a week.

So by the end of, you know, middle of Q4, we will probably be fully transitioned, takes 12 weeks to harvest a new, a new batch of flowers. So these things take time, and, you know, you will start seeing the full impact at the beginning of fiscal 2020 as well. And we did not really talk a lot about this on the call, we are starting as well the streamlining of our manufacturing and distribution efforts squarely around our Smiths Falls facility. We just kicked off the project. We have line of sights.

We have a series of initiatives that are going to be implemented in the back half of fiscal 27, and these will reap benefits on the margin lines, and we will start seeing these happening in the later part of this fiscal with full benefits in fiscal 28. So there is quite a bit of fuel in the tank. here ahead of us. And we have line of sights on all these initiatives, and they are well managed, and, you know, we are building confidence.

Operator: Thank you. Next question from William Joseph Kirk with Roth Capital Partners. Please go ahead.

William Kirk: Good morning, everybody. Luke, I was hoping you could keep going on some of the new products, the new markets commentary of what you can do out of Smiths Falls. And in particular, maybe, like, what types of products you know, which. In which market, and what the timing is for some of that.

Luc Mongeau: Yeah, so the timing of those for new products will be felt more. The beginning of fiscal 2020. what is really important, our priority is right now where we can see the biggest impact on our sales and profits goes back to flower. We have been saying it. Elevating cultivation, is a priority in the business. It is what will drive the biggest transformation of our P&L and our profitability. And we are very I am delighted with the progress that is been done in recent quarters there.

And as we mentioned, we start feeling the benefit of this at the end toward the end of Q3 of this fiscal with full impact at the beginning of 28. what is important as well as we are you know, as we. In the quarter, we reentered the U.K. market. Which is the second largest market in Europe. We have as well done a series of investments in strengthening our access to patients in Germany. We are strengthening our sales team. They are now with capabilities to win with sales. So that is where you will see the bulk. of the growth. Coming from. Thank you.

Operator: Next question from Matt Bottomley with Canaccord Genuity. Please go ahead. Luke, perhaps following on your question, on your answer there, with respect to Germany, how well part 1 is the Tweed brand resonating?

Analyst: 2, how important, yeah, are the genetics that you are bringing to market I am asking that in the context of either helping to better moat your business in Germany and increase your confidence given how noisy and, you know, to some, over perhaps the German market is becoming. Thank you.

Luc Mongeau: I think a good question. The Tweed brand I mean, we are very confident in our ability to win in Germany. You know, in the past, every time we were in stock, we did really well. Poland, same thing with Poland. If you look at recent surveys we have done about brands our brands and our genetics resonate really well we are through the value chain in Germany and Poland. So not only with patients, but as well with doctors, pharmacists and players in the industry.

So for us, that is why we are focused our focus is really increasing the yield of our Kincardine EU-GMP facility because we know when we have the flower we bring it to Germany, Poland, and we are successful. So we have really built, you know, going back to what we talked about the unique ecosystem that Canopy has built. So EU GMP cultivation facility, EU GMP processing facility in Smiths Falls. We have our own ability to bring flour into, into Europe, and we are strengthening our sales team across Europe, our access to patient.

So we are building this end to end ecosystem where not only can we drive integrity of the products because we handle the products all the way, We maintain integrity of margins as well. So imagine this ecosystem with the brands, with the strengths that we are only going to make stronger with the MTL acquisition. And once we are able to significantly increase the amount of tonnage we put through this system, I mean, we will reap the benefits. Thank you.

Operator: The next question comes from Federico Gomez with ATB Cormark Securities. Please go ahead.

Frederico Gomes: Hi. Good morning. I want to ask about your investments in and, I guess, improving yields. When you look at the, I guess, the competitive landscape, where do you think you sit in terms of cost of cultivation and quality and you know, do you think that, you know, with those investments, you know, how soon can you sort of catch up to some of the maybe the leaders in the Canadian rec market? Thank you.

Thomas Carlton Stewart: Yeah. Thanks. Good morning, Frederico. Yeah. I think from a cost-to-grow standpoint, we are definitely not a best in class from a cost-to-grow. I think what we are focused on now with the capital investments that we are making at Kincardine specifically is really using a lot of the know how and the techniques that the MTL team has been successful at in terms of growing their business. And applying it to a much bigger asset to really better utilize the assets that we have.

We do think it will make us much more competitive across the globe, but more importantly, give us a higher amount of good quality flower at the right specs that can service our entire cannabis segment. So that is really, I would say, you know, we are looking-- we are not a greenhouse grower, we will likely not be a lowest cost-to-grow in Canada, but we have ambitions of being some of the highest quality flower in Canada. that is great. Thank you.

Operator: Next question comes from Pablo Ernesto Zuanic with Zuanic and Associates. Please go ahead.

Pablo Zuanic: Thank you, and good morning, everyone. Luke, do you want to make any comments on the proposed changes in the budget, of the government, relating to cannabis? We had seen some good news last night. Thank you.

Luc Mongeau: Yes. Good morning. Those are very encouraging news, and so we welcome these potential changes. It will make it much more commercially easier for Canadian LPs to really drive their business in a much, much simpler and streamlined manner. It will allow greater access for Canadians to good quality flower that is grown and distributed the right way. So we welcome those changes. Thank you.

#3389. Next year’s iPhone Pro redesign gets new update from leaker

Apple reportedly has a big redesign coming to next year’s iPhone Pro models, timed for the iPhone’s 20th anniversary. The latest leak about the design reveals that the dream of a cutout-free display may remain a dream for now.

Yesterday Weibo leaker Digital Chat Station outlined three new iPhone models coming in early 2027: iPhone 18e, iPhone 18, and iPhone Air 2.

His main focus was on the iPhone 18, which is expected to get two Pro-inspired upgrades.

In a follow-up post though, replying to another Weibo user’s question, the leaker addressed a key design question regarding next fall’s iPhone Pro models.

Apple is rumored to be working on a big redesign timed for the iPhone’s 20th anniversary. It will reportedly feature a quad-curved display that wraps around the edges of the device for a visually bezel-free look.

Early rumors indicated the device could also drop the Dynamic Island for a truly all-glass display, with no cutouts.

The Duo2 will also have faceID and will steal the show. Who wants curved glass on all sides of the phone? We all remember how that went for Galaxy Edge phones.

But according to Digital Chat Station, that’s not happening after all.

After being asked if the ‘iPhone 20 Pro Max’ will have a Dynamic Island still, or feature a hole-free display, the leaker confirmed the display will still have holes. Thus, it will retain the Dynamic Island cutout.

It’s unclear if the Dynamic Island will be the same size as that of iPhone 18 Pro, but since the device is expected to have Face ID, that’s highly likely.

Does the inclusion of a display cutout change your interest in the iPhone 20 Pro at all? Let us know in the comments.
