#3369. Why Engineers Should Brave Capitol Hill

Congress needs accurate technical insights

Lucas Laursen is the technology policy editor at IEEE Spectrum.

During this year’s Congressional Visits Day, Nikhil Jathar [second from left] and three other IEEE members met with Nile Whitmore [middle], a legislative assistant for Representative Greg Casar (D-Texas).

When San Antonio–based software engineer Nikhil Jathar first went to Washington, D.C., to advocate for federal support for technology education and research funding, he was in awe of the opportunity. It was spring of 2025, not long after Jathar settled in the United States from India, when he got an invitation to join the annual Congressional Visits Day organized by IEEE-USA.

“My first reaction was, ‘Wow, I get to visit Congress,’ ” says Jathar, CTO of AvanSaber, a business software company he cofounded in 2014. At the time, he did not have a specific lobbying position on behalf of the company. But he was intrigued by the invitation—which goes out to all U.S. IEEE members—and as he read more about congressional visits, his motivation deepened. He realized: “I need to try this. I want to see where it goes.”

What’s Your Ask? Congressional staffers expect clarity from advocates. Be clear on what you plan to ask for when you arrive. Here are some common options:Cosponsor (or oppose) an existing bill or amendment.Preserve, remove, or modify legislative text in a bill under consideration.Add language to an appropriations bill or committee report.Ask a federal agency a specific oversight question.Request a briefing, hearing, Government Accountability Office review, or stakeholder roundtable.Encourage an agency to clarify a technical rule.

Congressional staffers expect clarity from advocates. Be clear on what you plan to ask for when you arrive. Here are some common options:

Congressional staffers say they welcome the knowledge and perspective that engineers like Jathar and other visitors from beyond Washington, D.C., provide. It’s also important for those visitors to be clear on what they are advocating for. One staffer for the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, who agreed to speak anonymously due to the office’s media policy, says, “Ideas for new policies come from multiple places. It could begin at the [legislator] or staff level, an ask from a constituent, or needs from industry. It’s up to us to figure out what would do the most good,” the staffer said. “For instance, if you leave it to the lobbyists, they’re understandably going to do what’s in their clients’ interests.”

For engineers in the United States, speaking with elected representatives is an effective way to shape key policies, but it takes some preparation and the right approach, as Jathar learned over the course of two visits.

Congress’s job is to act on behalf of the people, and it has rules for how people can lobby it. It distinguishes between broader advocacy—conversations between constituents and U.S. representatives—and professional lobbying, which involves paid professionals and is governed by the Lobbying Disclosure Act. Many professional groups like IEEE also organize congressional visits for their members. Those visits can be subject to lobbying rules, so the organizers told Jathar that: “You are representing the organization, not your own views.” He would need to stick to the talking points IEEE-USA had prepared for all its participants, regardless of their specialty, to promote across several congressional offices.

On Jathar’s first visit, those organizational talking points included advocating for funding smart grids, authorizing Department of Energy research, and investing in STEM education. That represents one of the trade-offs of access in Washington. IEEE-USA’s priorities didn’t all overlap directly with Jathar’s work, but they were broad enablers of science and technology and, he says, “STEM education funding is close to my heart.”

Anyone can approach their representatives in Washington with their personal priorities, Jathar notes, but given how pressed for time congressional staff are, they are more likely to prioritize a meeting that represents the views of as many of their constituents as possible. “I could have gone outside the IEEE structure,” Jathar says, but congressional staff “are more likely to listen if you are part of a much bigger organization.”

For Jathar’s first congressional visit, organizers assigned him to call on the offices of several representatives from both political parties based on where he lives: Representatives Greg Casar (D-Texas), Lloyd Doggett (D-Texas), and Barry Moore (R-Ala.). “Meeting a staffer or a senior member from their office is good. They tend to relate to these issues more than a representative, because a representative has 10 different high-level things they have to worry about whereas the staffer can be more focused on the policy details,” Jathar says.

A typical visit like this may last anywhere from 15 minutes to an hour, so Jathar kept his talking points simple and short. “First and foremost you’re gonna get a very small window,” he says, “Make sure you’ve got everything ready to present in bullet points and not a lot of jargon. You can always bring that out later if they ask more questions.” Simple visual aids, in the form of one-page handouts, may be helpful for communicating numeric or technical information, too.

“If you leave it to the lobbyists, they’re understandably going to do what’s in their clients’ interests.”–Staffer for the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology

The House Science Committee staffer agrees: “I prefer meetings where people know what they want and know what we’re doing in Congress.” In addition to having a clear request, the staffer says engineers and other advocates should keep track of where Congress is in its cycle: Is it appropriations season, and when is the next budget being set? How far along is a given piece of legislation in the process, and what is realistic to change at that point?

During Jathar’s 2025 visit to one Capitol Hill office, he learned firsthand the importance of preparation. For one of the three representatives he visited, staff politely pointed out that the legislator they worked for was not on the committee with jurisdiction over the IEEE-USA talking point they were discussing. “They explained that there are only certain things [the legislator] can do on that issue and that there are other people we need to talk to, to achieve more,” Jathar recalls.

Earlier this year, Jathar decided to go back to Capitol Hill with his newfound knowledge, again within the framework of an IEEE-USA visit. This time he was able to provide something else legislative staff want from engineers: authoritative technical knowledge.

“When I introduced myself as a software developer to one staffer, his first question was, ‘Do you think AI will replace coders?’ ” Jathar says. The conversation went back and forth, with the staffer asking Jathar and his other engineering companions questions. Jathar went on to explain that his company developed an open-source business-management software it calls ERPClaw, designed to be used with AI agents such as OpenClaw. That led naturally to discussing the role of open source in AI, which plays a role in one of IEEE-USA’s proposals for democratizing AI. This time Jathar was able to align his organization’s advocacy with his expertise and the staffer’s areas of interest.

It’s too soon to know what legislative impact that advocacy might have, but it’s the sort of informed, relevant proposal that legislative staff seek out. “The people who build trust have more cachet with congressional staff because they’ve asked for something that’s reasonably thought out,” the House Science Committee staffer says. In turn, congressional staffers can advocate better within their offices for policies brought to them by people they trust.

And talking about the issues you care the most about can deepen that trust. The House Science Committee staffer once visited Congress as an advocate before switching to the other side of the table. On that visit, as on Jathar’s, the professional society organizing the visit provided a pitch. “I was making a pitch that was given to me without a lot of personal buy-in,” the staffer says. Instead, “you should feel emotionally connected to any issue you’re advocating for.”

Jathar’s support for the open-source movement is like that. Open source gives smaller companies a foundation they can adapt and build upon, while allowing other developers to extend that work. “We can progress a lot faster,” Jathar says. “I’m not doing it only because it’s good for my business, but because I feel it’s good for any technological advancement.”

Lucas Laursen is the technology policy editor at IEEE Spectrum. He covers how emerging technologies are changing the balance of power between companies, governments, and individuals. The rest of the time, he worries about his own balance on a bicycle, skis, or the side of a mountain.

I found it difficult to get answers from legislative offices, so I'd love to hear what's missing in this story from any legislative staffers either here in the comments or at my email address (on our About page). I also know that things work somewhat differently in each country--are there readers in India or Germany or Chile who might be able to share their experiences working with lawmakers there?

#3367. Five Smartwatch Heart Rate Zone Hacks Every Runner Should Know

If you've spent any time in or around running culture over the last few years, you've undoubtedly encountered someone preaching the gospel of Zone 2 cardio. Legend has it that easy, conversational effort cardio—also known as cardio that takes your heart rate into "Zone 2"—is the secret to unlocking everything from a bigger aerobic engine to faster race times and even a longer life.

To train by heart rate, you aim to keep your heart rate in the "zone" that gives you the desired workout. The catch is that Zone 2 is easy to get wrong, especially since no one can agree on what it actually means.  Your smartwatch can show you your heart rate, but many recreational runners will still drift into a “gray zone” that's too fast to be truly easy, and too slow to give them a real workout. If you're struggling to hit Zone 2 consistently, there are a few smartwatch hacks that can help.

Pace can be a distraction during easy runs, especially considering all the different variables that affect your effort, like hills, humidity, and general fatigue. A 9:30 mile might be Zone 2 on a flat, cool day and Zone 4 on a hot, hilly one.

Dig into your watch's activity settings (on Garmin, it's Activity > Data Screens; on Apple Watch, the Workout app's metrics layout; on Coros, Polar, and Suunto, similar menus) and put live heart rate zone front and center, ideally as a zone number or colored gauge rather than just a raw bpm figure (though this assumes these zones are accurate—more on that below).

Create an alert when your heart rate goes above or below a target range, delivered as a vibration pattern, a beep, or both. Set the alert for the upper boundary of Zone 2, and you've essentially hired a mini coach who taps you on the wrist whenever you get overzealous. Whenever you hear or feel that buzz, you’ll know you need to ease into a slower jog until your heart rate settles.

Instead of free-running and checking your numbers afterward, build structured workouts that carry the targets for you. In Garmin Connect, TrainingPeaks, Apple's Custom Workout feature, Coros Training Hub, or similar platforms, you can create sessions like "10-minute warm-up in Zone 1, 40 minutes in Zone 2, 5-minute cooldown" and sync them straight to your watch.

During the run, your watch displays the current step, the target range, and whether you're above, below, or in the pocket. Many will automatically advance between intervals and alert you when it's time to shift gears.

Heart rate-based intervals, like 4 x 4 minutes in Zone 4 with Zone 1 recovery, where you don't have to do mental math or check the clock.

Progressive long runs that start in Zone 2 and finish in Zone 3.

Hill repeats, where pace is meaningless but effort matters.

Most watches calculate default zones using a generic formula like 220 minus your age, which can be off by 10 to 20 beats for any given individual. If your zones are wrong, your Zone 2 training isn't Zone 2 training.

Here’s how to fix your watch’s heart rate zones:

Find your true max heart rate. The informal way is to just notice what number you see on your watch when you can no longer speak comfortably; the more formal way is this treadmill test. You can also look through your recent hard efforts, like races, hill repeats, or all-out intervals, and see the highest sustained heart rate you've recorded.

Use lactate threshold heart rate instead. Many watches can estimate this automatically after a few hard efforts, and zones built from threshold tend to be more personalized than ones built from max.

Customize the boundaries. Dive into the heart rate zone settings and input your own numbers. Some runners prefer the "MAF" method (180 minus age, with adjustments) for aerobic base building, and most watches let you set that as a custom range.

Recheck every few months. Fitness changes, and so do your zones.

A screen crowded with cadence, vertical oscillation, ground contact time, running power, and lap pace is a recipe for second-guessing.

Create a dedicated Zone 2 data screen with just two or three fields: current heart rate zone, elapsed time, and maybe distance. Turn off auto-scroll so it doesn't flip to a screen full of numbers you don't need. If your watch supports multiple activity profiles, make a separate "Easy Run" profile with this stripped-down layout and keep a different profile for tempo days and races.

A chest strap (or a forearm or upper-arm optical band) is generally more accurate and responsive than the wrist-based sensor on your watch. For heart rate training, where a few beats can mean the difference between Zone 2 and Zone 3, I recommend buying one. This COOSPO heart rate monitor is one of my favorites, and it's only $31.99.

The bottom line: Your smartwatch can make heart rate training far easier, but only if you set it up to support you rather than overwhelm you.

Fee cuts and a new dividend framework amid fresh nonaccruals.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Morgan Stanley Direct Lending Fund (MSDL -3.47%) reported third quarter results and announced a reduction in advisory fees to enhance its value proposition for shareholders. Management reported net investment income of $0.48 per share and declared a new supplemental dividend framework to return excess earnings to investors. The company continued to scale the Capstone Joint Venture and utilized its share repurchase program to provide net asset value accretion. While the quarter was impacted by specific credit restructurings and new nonaccruals, management indicated that the broader portfolio maintains stable fundamentals and remains focused on senior secured lending.

Operator: Please stand by. Good day, and welcome to the Morgan Stanley Direct Lending third quarter 2020 Earnings Call. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. To obtain copies of SEC related filings, please visit our website. With that, I will now turn the call over to Michael Occi.

Michael Occi Jr.: Good morning. And thank you for joining us. I will begin with an overview of the meaningful step we have taken to strengthen MSDL's value proposition for shareholders. Before turning to our third quarter performance. Jeffrey will then cover the market environment and deployment activity, and David will review our financial results in greater detail. We will then open the call for Q&A. We are pleased to announce that the Board has approved a decisive action in our ongoing effort to create value for shareholders. Effective 01/01/2027, we are reducing MSDL's management fee from 100 basis points on assets to 75 basis points on assets, and its incentive fee from 17.5% to 15%.

We believe these reductions will strengthen MSCL's baseline return profile, Combined with our existing incentive fee cap, we believe this makes us a leader on fee structure in the sector. More importantly, this action further strengthens our alignment with shareholders. The fee reduction serves as another proactive step to strengthen MSDL's return profile. And help offset the yield normalization that the industry has experienced over the last several years. We previously established the Capstone joint venture. Increased the size of our share repurchase program, maintained a competitive operating expense profile and optimized our debt stack. The fee reduction is another way to improve shareholder returns while maintaining our disciplined investment mandate.

We have applied this philosophy consistently across our platform, most recently taking a similar action on fees with our non traded BDC offering. The specifics of the improved fee framework were grounded in our objective deliver shareholder value by earning our cost of capital. This move advances that goal, as we believe the per share fee reduction can provide meaningful return accretion. As illustrated in the earnings presentation, on a pro forma basis over the last 12 months, the reduced advisory fees would have increased NII return on NAV by approximately 64 basis points, or approximately $0.03 of quarterly NII per share.

The specific earnings benefit from the lower incentive fee rate will depend on whether the incentive fee cap is in effect, in any given period. This reduction also reinforces our confidence in the durability of the distribution. In addition to declaring the $0.45 regular dividend for the fourth quarter, the Board has declared a quarterly supplemental dividend, which is equivalent to 50% of excess NII per share above the regular dividend. This will be paid during the fourth quarter period resulting in an incremental $0.015 per share for a total distribution yield on NAV of 9.9%. Based on 09/30/2026 NAV per share.

Transitioning now to our third quarter operating results, we generated net investment income of $0.48 per share, compared with $0.45 per share in the prior quarter. Credit indicators were mixed quarter over quarter with the nonaccrual rate increasing modestly and PIK to income declining relative to the second quarter. We did experience mark to market activity, including as a result of 1 realization which led to a decline in NAV in the quarter. Jeffrey will elaborate on this in more detail. Disciplined capital allocation remained a priority in the third quarter. As we navigated the more dynamic market. Continuing our approach from the first half of the year.

We prioritized ramping the JV, and utilizing the buyback and we successfully ended the quarter at what we believe to be near optimal leverage. During the quarter, we continued to scale the Capstone JV including an equity contribution from MSDL of $25 million Because this occurred late in September, this specific step did not meaningfully increase net investment income for the period, However, with this investment, the JV is now approximately 65% utilized and we remain on track to complete the ramp by mid-2027. In our view, there remains a disconnect. Between the direct lending fundamentals and investor sentiment although that gap appears to be gradually narrowing.

To this point, the third quarter saw declining redemption rates at non traded BDCs, including our own. Separating the signal from the noise is admittedly challenging given the 2 distinct realities at play right now in the direct lending market. First, a constructive deployment environment, supported by improved spreads and other lending terms and an upward bias in base rates, and second, pockets of credit softness across the broader market and within MSDL's portfolio. While credit events and dispersion are likely to remain market realities, we believe that the relative value and diversification that this asset class offers for client portfolios remain attractive. Particularly amidst the rate volatility that has challenged public fixed income performance.

We believe this value proposition is enhanced in a wrapper constructed and executed as thoughtfully as MSDL. Our commitment to transparency and alignment with investors is reflected in our actions, including the fee reductions we have outlined today. Leveraging the strength of the Morgan Stanley franchise we believe MSDL remains well positioned to navigate evolving market conditions and deliver long term shareholder value. With that, I will turn the call over to Jeffrey Day.

Jeffrey Day: Thank you, Michael, and good morning. Beginning with the broader direct lending market, we continue to see a favorable environment for disciplined lenders with pricing, documentation, and structural protections remaining meaningfully more attractive than in mid to late 2025. These improvements have proven durable to the third quarter despite continued competition for high quality assets. Our median spread on new deals for the quarter was 38 basis points up from 475 basis points in the prior 2 quarters. Importantly, we are seeing more conservative leverage levels and increased sponsor equity contributions, allowing us to originate loans with more attractive risk adjusted returns and greater structural protections than we were seeing several quarters ago.

From an activity perspective, the market remains somewhat at a crossroads, while overall direct lending volumes remain subdued during the quarter, we have begun to see encouraging signs of renewed M&A interest including within the software sector, where 1 of our existing commitments was taken out as part of a sponsor to sponsor sale process. Private equity sponsors continue to prioritize investment monetization and return of capital to limited partners, which we believe should ultimately support increased transaction activity. At the same time, the Fed's September rate increase and more hawkish outlook introduced an additional headwind for sponsors evaluating new investments and exits.

We believe this dynamic will continue to favor lenders with strong origination relationships, flexible capital and the ability to execute with speed and credibility. Competition remains particularly strong for high quality businesses with durable cash flows, while lenders are demonstrating greater selectivity towards companies facing operational challenges or potential secular disruption. In software specifically, we believe the conversation around AI has become more balanced with increasing recognition that the impact will vary meaningfully by business model. Overall, we remain constructive on the credit fundamentals of our software portfolio while recognizing that the evolving economics of AI reinforce the importance of disciplined underwriting, active portfolio monitoring and investing in market leading businesses with durable competitive positions.

Turning to third quarter activity, MSDL closed 12 investments including 6 new platforms. In addition, the JV balance sheet grew by $132 million which helped further diversify its portfolio and increase earnings. 1 investment to highlight this quarter was Concertis. A global engineering and project advisory platform serving aviation, water, utilities, and technology end markets. initially evaluated the company when RTC Partners acquired it last year but passed given its smaller size. Following a year of strong performance and customer diversification, we are pleased to provide financing for incremental M&A activity. Our underwriting benefited from our team's deep sector experience complemented by differentiated insights from Morgan Stanley's private equity research teams.

The investment was priced as SOFR plus 575 basis points with lender friendly documentation representing an attractive risk adjusted return opportunity for MSDL. Turning to credit, our focus remains on the underlying cash generation and liquidity of our borrowers. While valuation pressure earlier in the year largely reflected broader market concerns around AI disruption and geopolitical uncertainty, recent declines have been driven more by fundamental credit challenges for a limited number of portfolio companies. We believe this softness is not indicative of a deep cycle, but rather we have seen weakness for certain borrowers that reflects idiosyncratic challenges rather than macroeconomic factors such as higher oil prices, weaker consumer demand, or rising base rates.

In particular, we have seen operational and execution challenges at certain highly acquisitive businesses where integration delays cost overruns, and slower than expected synergies have pressured cash flow generation. While these situations warrant close attention, we continue to see stable fundamentals across the broader portfolio without evidence of thematic industry challenges. Against this backdrop and with the potential for higher rates for longer, we remain focused on free cash flow covenant headroom, near term maturities and PIK utilization. We ended the quarter with 5.4% PIK income as a percentage of total income down slightly from the prior quarter and remaining well below the levels observed across our publicly traded BDC peers.

During the quarter, we completed the restructuring of AMCP Pet Holdings, which goes by BrightPet, a manufacturer of premium pet food and treats. Following a deterioration in operating performance driven by company specific operational and execution challenges, ownership of the business was consensually transferred from the sponsor to the lender group. As part of the restructuring, the existing debt was reorganized and the resulting realized loss, while partially offset by the reversal of previously recognized unrealized losses, was the largest contributor to the decline in NAV during the quarter.

While the outcome is disappointing, we believe the challenges at BrightPet are isolated and we are working closely with the management and board to maximize the value of our position over time. In addition to BrightPet, we placed 3 additional investments on nonaccrual during the quarter, representing a $17.2 million at cost. Any Hour and LogRhythm have experienced company specific underperformance for an extended period, while FPG Intermediate HoldCo our afterlife services portfolio company that previously underwent a restructuring, continues to face operational headwinds. Our approach to challenge credits is active and situation specific engaging closely with sponsors and management teams evaluating restructuring alternatives, and maximizing recoveries to preserve shareholder capital.

We remain actively engaged in restructuring discussions for several of our non accrual investments and expect to make further progress towards resolutions over the coming quarters. Importantly, despite these isolated challenges, 93.4% of the portfolio remains in risk rated 1 or 2 assets as of quarter end, underscoring the overall stability of the portfolio. Turning to software. The debate around AI related disruption has become more rational. The discussion is increasingly moving away from broad sector wide assumptions and toward the fundamental of individual companies. Across our own software portfolio, operating performance remains generally healthy supported by continued revenue growth and the detailed company level assessments we have conducted to evaluate potential AI related risks.

Many software businesses are accelerating investments in AI enabled functionality to defend and enhance their competitive positions. Over the near term, we anticipate that this investment along with rising cloud infrastructure and hosting costs, could pressure margin profiles. However, AI driven efficiencies in software development could ultimately help offset some of these incremental expenses. We Through the third quarter, we updated our proprietary AI scorecard which continues to show that only a low single digit percentage of our portfolio is in the category we deem to be at high risk of AI disruption. More broadly, we remain attentive to macroeconomic and geopolitical risks and their potential impact on borrower demand input costs and liquidity.

We continue to stay in close contact with management teams and assess these exposures at individual company level rather than rely on broad sector assumptions. In summary, we continue to see attractive lending opportunities supported by favorable pricing and stronger lender protections even as the operating environment remains challenging for certain borrowers. Our focus remains on disciplined origination, active portfolio management, and preserving shareholder capital while delivering attractive risk adjusted returns. With that, I will turn the call over to David Pessah.

David Pessah: Thank you. Turning to our balance sheet. Our portfolio totaled $3.43 billion at fair value as of quarter end. Our continued focus is at the top of the capital structure with the portfolio being comprised of approximately 96% investments in first lien debt or the JV entity and the remainder in second lien equity and other investments as of September 30. Inclusive of new investment commitments, total investment fundings amounted to approximately $75.1 million during the quarter. Offset by $140.9 million in repayments. We believe the portfolio remains well diversified. With 233 portfolio companies across 37 industries and an average borrower exposure of approximately $14.7 million.

In addition to some of the credit metrics that Jeffrey provided, the weighted average loan to value across our portfolio was approximately 42.4%, and median EBITDA remained relatively unchanged at $91.4 million To provide some additional detail about our JV, the JV has total equity commitments of up to $250 million of which $200 million is committed by MSDL. Total investment income decreased to $86.1 million from $88.8 million The decrease was a function of the impact of positions placed on non accrual and lowered nonrecurring revenue. Total expenses decreased to $45.1 million from $49.8 million in the previous quarter, primarily reflecting lower incentive fees earned which was subject to our incentive fee cap from the restructuring of BrightPet partially offset by higher interest and other financing expenses.

The net change in unrealized depreciation and realized losses for the third quarter was $67.6 million unrealized losses were driven by underperformance in a handful of portfolio companies which includes the aforementioned positions that were placed on nonaccrual. Net realized losses during the period were related to the restructuring of BrightPet. As of September 30, our total assets were $3.59 billion and total net assets were $1.57 billion Our ending NAV per share for the third quarter was $18.76 compared to $19.50 in the prior period. The gross debt to equity ratio closed the quarter at 1.25x, modestly above the 1.21x multiple from the previous quarter.

Additionally, in the third quarter, we proactively refinanced the upcoming February 2027 maturity with a 5-year $350 million unsecured note issuance. While the transaction creates some incremental near term interest expense, it enable us to secure funding ahead of the recent widening in credit spreads and avoid potentially higher borrowing costs had we waited. Overall, we remain confident in the strength and positioning of our debt portfolio through the remainder of 2026 and into 2027. During the period, we repurchased approximately $12.8 million of our shares at prices below NAV, which was $0.04 of accretion to NAV per share. We have approximately $71 million of capacity remaining on the $100 million share repurchase program we refreshed earlier this year.

Regarding distributions, we declared a $0.45 regular distribution for the third quarter. Our Board of Directors declared a $0.45 per share regular distribution for the fourth quarter payable to shareholders of record as of 12/31/2026. and $0.015 per share supplemental distribution payable to shareholders of record as of 11/30/2026. Our spillover income was approximately $0.85 per share. With that, operator, please open the line for questions.

Operator: Thank you. If you would like to signal with questions, please press star 1 on your touchtone phone. Please make sure your mute function is turned off. To allow your signal to reach our equipment. Again, that is star 1 if you would like to signal with questions. And the first question will come from Finian O'Shea with Wells Fargo Securities.

Finian O'Shea: Hi, everyone. Good morning. So you start with a bit big changes on the fee structure Can you talk about sort of why now? Was this a long time coming and sort of what were the drivers behind why these new levels?

Michael Occi Jr.: Hi, Finian. As I alluded to, it really comes down to a reduction of fees, proactive step, to enhance shareholder economics, improve the earnings power, in isolation. We are constantly looking for ways to improve returns. We believe the new structure aligns our economics with shareholders. It provides meaningful uplift to the earnings power. In terms of the why now, As I alluded to, we have seen a maturity in this sector in these product suites, including the non tradeds. You know, mathematically, bridge to double digits if you look at the LTM math we provided. Optically, these happen to be the net levels associated with the post IPO waivers. So we have been there before.

They were not completely random. But that is kind of a little bit on the why now. I would just reinforce the point that shareholder alignment has always been critical. We have decided to take and harness this moment really across the platform. To even more powerfully align ourselves with shareholders. And it allows us to do that, improve returns without violating what is core to us from an investment strategy perspective and that is critical. At the end of the day, that is the mission is to deliver best in class risk adjusted returns through that credit box. But it is really important to us to get everything else right.

All the big stuff, all the small stuff, from a structure perspective, and this is us doing that.

Finian O'Shea: I appreciate that. And second question, you flagged a software exit sounded like a good outcome. Can you, now that we have kind of seen a few more of those with you and across the space, Can you give some color on sort of what you learned on the characteristics that a sort of a movable software name needs and then maybe provide some dimension on amongst the sort of the haves and have nots. Of software credits to I guess, help us determine how many of these will move and how many will be longer term sort of workouts.

Jeffrey Day: Yeah. Hey, Finian. it is Jeffrey. I think, it obviously, we were happy to see that there is and it remains a market for these software assets And obviously, seeing sponsor to sponsor trades, I think, is a positive thing to see. I think, from our perspective, you know, obviously, there is been a whole lot of press on AI and the potential impacts that exist. I think there is a lot of. As we have talked in the past, there is a lot of software businesses out there, particularly those that we have focused on lending to that have not experienced that impact and disruption from AI.

These are businesses that you know, own and house data, and so they have had that in-remote from software. I think, you know, we continue to see, you know, strong, you know, revenue and EBITDA growth across our software portfolio. I think strong, you know, gross to net retention is a key tenant to the success of software businesses. And so I think as we look across our portfolio, we continue to see those continued drivers that continue to create value, in the companies that we have lent to.

Finian O'Shea: Great. Thanks. that is all for me.

Operator: And the next question comes from Heli Sheth with Raymond James.

Heli Sheth: Good morning. Thanks for the question. What are you seeing in terms of the spreads, which assets are repaying at versus where you are currently deploying capital. And where do these spreads go from here?

Michael Occi Jr.: Yeah, Heli. Thanks for the question. I would just acknowledge upfront, and you can see it in the deck, We did see a downtick in repays in the third quarter. This had been tracking pretty reliably. It call it 5%, if not more. By quarter relative to the total portfolio. Probably a little bit muted, given volatility in the BSL market, probably a bit of a moment in time slowdown in M&A activity. And some of it has to do with private to private. Refinancings. Slowing down a little bit. Given how much had been done in 2024, 2025. But over the LTM period, it is still north of 20%.

It would not make too much about the specific outcome in the third quarter. What came off versus what went on is a little bit noisy just given the makeup of what we did from an origination perspective. When you consider the fact that the JV was a piece of that. But by and large, we have seen a widening in spread for new deployment relative to the legacy book and specifically where we were back in the third quarter of 2025. We think that is healthy. And if we are being honest, probably a little bit surprised by the staying power of that. In this, you know, deep into 2026.

Attribute maybe that to some of that to the volatility in the public markets. Got it.

Heli Sheth: Thanks for the color. And on that, what should we expect going forward in terms of repayment and originations not just for the remainder of the year, but also into 2027. Especially because 2026 has just been pretty stagnant activity wise. So what near term catalyst do you think could drive activity?

Michael Occi Jr.: Yeah. So a couple of things, if you look a layer deeper into the makeup of the true repayments in the quarter, you see $140 million, roughly 45 of that was dropped down into JV associated with, what we alluded to earlier. So the true $90 million of repayments was lower than in prior quarters, but pretty diversified in mix. So you had a strategic takeout, You had, 1 sale to a financial buyer, and then something that was a refinancing. So you are still seeing good mix. Going forward, I would expect to see some level of ongoing portfolio turnover, although it is tough to predict timing and magnitude.

With precision, To your point, just on the trajectory of asset balances, we think about originations on the other side. We are in optimization mode. Based on where valuations have been from a stock price, leverage is more or less dictated the capital that we have to consume, right, in any given period. As we talked about, we continue to prioritize the buyback that was $13 million You couple that with the valuation move in the quarter, and that effectively dictated that we wanted to shrink the book $65 or so million net to keep within the leverage target. And so the JV was 1 component of that was a net negative even though there is a $25 million contribution.

And so with the 90 or so of true repayments, away from that, we had the ability to go and deploy $50 million or so. So we are going to continue to be in the mode of optimizing those levers. To maximize returns. I think we are-- it is constructive to see that the deployment environment and the terms that Jeffrey alluded to continue to be really constructive. This fund, even if it is range-bound from a total size perspective, continues to benefit from being part of a bigger platform from an allocation point of view. And the diversification benefits even in quarters like these benefit are significant given that dynamic.

Heli Sheth: Got it. I appreciate the detail.

Operator: And we will take a question from Paul Johnson with KBW.

Paul Johnson: Hey, good morning. Thanks for taking my question. Applaud the fee change. it is fairly meaningful. As you have in your slide here, 64 basis points in incremental ROE. Certainly very, very significant, in this environment. In terms of the, you know, the fee change, again, very positive, but we also expect those shareholders probably need to also see, I guess, the confidence alongside that, that credit can improve from here.

So I guess I would just ask, you know, where do you think you are, in that process, as we continue to see kind of normalization broadly across the space, you know, how close do you think we are here in terms of kind of hitting a peak of non-accruals and restructurings and such?

Michael Occi Jr.: Yeah. Yeah. Paul, thanks for the question. And the acknowledgment on the on the steps that we have taken on the profitability profile on credit. And Jeffrey covered some of this. But I would characterize the outcome in the third quarter and to a certain extent, the year to date period as being just a function of a small pocket of the portfolio where we had seen identifiable weakness taking a leg or so lower. At the same time, if you look at the portfolio at large, we continue to see pretty good, resilient operating performance. A couple other points I would make just to make that come to life. First, as David alluded to, it is concentrated.

And so if you look at the 5, biggest movers, it accounted for more than 70% of the unrealized mark to market in the quarter. The second point I would make is in terms of what is driving it, it is generally not macro, generally not industry themes. it is more management, you know, sponsor execution missteps. And while that is still unfortunate and some even more unpredictable, it is better in our view than something that is more levered to, let's say, consumer weakness or higher prices at large, which can metastasize, is our belief more quickly if you see a big market shock.

So you know, while the trends are probably symptomatic of a portfolio that is seasoned to a certain extent. The asset base broadly continues to demonstrate pretty good health. And, I wish I could tell you with precision, what happens over the next quarter or 2. But we are sticking to our knitting. The basics of the investment strategy continue to be on track. The first-- Track of the first lien orientation the noncyclical orientation. We are actively working through the small group of problem children that have underperformed vis-a-vis restructurings. 1's already happened In the course of the 4 q to date period. We are maximizing recoveries.

And we believe at large, the portfolio continues to be very well positioned from a marketplace perspective.

Paul Johnson: Appreciate all that color, and apologize I dialed in late. So I missed David's comments, but once again, thanks for the answer. Appreciate that. that is all for me.

Operator: And the next question comes from Melissa Wedel with UBS.

Melissa Wedel: Good morning. Thanks for taking my questions. Quick follow-up on the 1 you just mentioned. The restructuring or recovery that has occurred so far in 4Q to-date. Is there any color you can add there? Anything we should be thinking about in terms of resolution that was different from fair value mark at 3Q?

Michael Occi Jr.: Yep. Melissa, hi. The, not much color I can provide. The name of the of the business restructure is not yet public. So we look forward to updating you on that. The only other thing I would say is with respect to the 39 marks, which is a function of our rigorous valuation system taking into account as part of the policy. All the best information that we have at the time, we think is an appropriate reflection of fair value.

Melissa Wedel: Okay. Appreciate that. Also mentioned on a couple of the new companies that were added to the non-accrual status during the quarter. The ones that have been having some weakness leading up to that addition to non-accrual status. So what I am trying to reconcile that comment with what you have mentioned earlier about some of the challenged products in the portfolio have been ones where it is an acquisitive and integration has taken longer than expected. Or are those companies on non accrual status right now?

And if so, do you view those differently in terms of the potential recovery or return to accrual status than Perhaps somebody who is got a more challenged capital structure or top line headwinds?

Rebecca Shaoul: Yeah. Hey, Melissa. it is Rebecca. I would say it is it is a bit of a mix in terms of what we see with the nonaccrual assets as it relates to the drivers. There are certain investments that do have that characteristic that is driven underperformance. But as Jeffrey and Michael alluded to, we are seeing very company specific issues that have driven the underperformance in the non-accrual bucket. And it is really-- it is companies that span different industries and end markets and have experienced different challenges that have led to some of the financial deterioration. So in certain cases, has been 1 of the issues in this category.

But it is company specific and some of the challenges that M&A or execution issues have driven do range in terms of severity of the impact to the borrower. As to whether it moved into this non accrual category or not.

Operator: The next question will come from Kenneth Lee with RBC Capital Markets.

Kenneth Lee: Hey, good morning. Thanks for taking my question. Appreciate the new supplemental dividend framework there. Curious whether you have any updated thoughts in terms of dividend coverage. I think previously you had said that the current base dividend was appropriate over the medium term there. Thanks.

Michael Occi Jr.: Yes. Hi, Kenneth. Thanks for the question. We continue to feel good about the regular Thanks for calling out the supplemental. Maybe it is cleanest to just to break down a little bit what we saw from an NII perspective. In comparison to the second quarter and the $0.45. We call it a clean NII in the low to mid forties for this quarter. You had relative to Q2, about $0.06 a help from the look back relative to the benefit you saw in the prior quarter. Other income was a penny light. Income from the JV was flat. To the point that you did not see the benefit of the chunky drop down near the end of the quarter.

Debt expense was a little bit of a drag, but that is more or less here to stay. Just as you think about the. That line item relative to the second quarter. On the go forward, which is more responsive to, to your question, there is going to be in our view, incremental upside from the JV at full ramp relative to where we were, you know, at 65% or below that earlier in the quarter. it is probably another 4-ish cents when you are at that 100% period. So it is gonna happen gradually. it is not gonna be a straight line as David alluded to.

In addition to that, the Fed's obviously a variable The September hike yet to see a benefit, in terms of the impact Not gonna be massive, but you will see a lot of that impact in the fourth quarter. And then, of course, the fee reduction, we have quantified the baseline potential upside from that will kick in obviously, beginning with the first quarter credits as a variable, a little bit tougher to gauge. So you boil that altogether, and the core earnings power, we think it puts us in a comfortable position as it relates to having confidence on the $0.45.

The supplemental just on top of that, we look at as an effective means to return some excess earnings to shareholders in a formulaic way, as some of these things come online. Right? Of course, there is no guarantees. On the magnitude, but we think it is a nice structure to augment what we are doing with the regular.

Kenneth Lee: Great. Very helpful color there. And then just 1 follow-up, if I may. Wonder if you could just add, at a higher level, remind us again of MSDL's, you know, workout and restructuring capabilities and perhaps potential access to the broader, MSP private credit platform for additional resources there? Thanks.

Jeffrey Day: Sure. Hey, Kenneth. it is Jeffrey. So we have a really robust, you know, infrastructure here not only on our team but we leverage the broader Morgan Stanley ecosystem as well. So specifically, as it relates to our team, we do have a dedicated workout team. We have got several individuals on our team who are complementary to our deal teams in terms of working through underperforming credits. We pull in additional resources as needed, including, you know, Rebecca, and David Kulikos who is our head of underwriting, who has significant workout experience.

But we are able to leverage additional resources as well We sit within what is the broader, you know, private credit and equity solutions business within Morgan Stanley. So we are able to leverage some of the operating partners that exist on our private equity franchise. As needed, and then the broader restructuring capabilities of Morgan Stanley more holistically, we can pull in those resources as needed. So we feel like we have got a really robust infrastructure, to help work through underperforming credits.

Kenneth Lee: Great. Very helpful there. Thanks again.

Operator: Thank you. At this time, I would like to turn the call back to Michael Occi for closing remarks.

Michael Occi Jr.: On behalf of our team, thanks for your time today. And your continued support of Morgan Stanley Direct Lending Fund. Today's fee reductions put our commitment to shareholder alignment in action. And advance our objective of delivering long term value for investors. We remain confident in our portfolio's resilience and our ability to execute a differentiated investment strategy supported by the scale, sourcing capabilities, and institutional infrastructure that Morgan Stanley brings to our private credit platform. We look forward to sharing our fourth quarter results on our earnings call in February. Thank you.

Operator: And that does conclude today's conference. We do thank you for your participation. Have an excellent day.

#3365. Livestream: Watch Labrinth create a song from scratch tonight using Apple’s new MacBook Pro

To promote the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, Apple is hosting a livestream in which singer-songwriter Labrinth will create a song from scratch overnight at the company’s Tower Theatre store in Downtown Los Angeles. Watch the livestream below.

Last week, Apple announced the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display at a special event in Los Angeles, where it invited members of the press and content creators to get an early look at the redesigned laptop.

Now, Apple is continuing its Los Angeles-centered promotional campaign with another event, this time involving singer-songwriter Labrinth.

Starting at 8 p.m. PT / 11 p.m. ET tonight, Labrinth will spend the night at Apple’s Tower Theatre store in Downtown LA, creating an entire song from scratch using the new MacBook Pro and Logic Pro.

The entire process will be livestreamed on his YouTube channel, allowing viewers to follow along in real time and ask questions as he works. Apple says the finished song will be released next week.

Tonight’s livestream comes ahead of the new MacBook Pro’s launch this Friday, November 6.

During last week’s demos, Apple showcased the laptop’s music production capabilities, including the ability to play virtual instruments directly on its touchscreen using Logic Pro.

Tune in below starting at 8 p.m. PT / 11 p.m. ET to watch Labrinth create his new song live from Apple’s Tower Theatre store.

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, a program that helps engineers through hands-on training.

This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!

If you’re an engineer, you may feel like your skills aren’t commanding the premium they once did. Many engineers have faced layoffs or restructuring. But even for those of us who still have jobs, something corrosive is happening. You may have heard some version of this:

“ChatGPT answered that in five seconds. Why can’t you?”

Or, “I made this app in a weekend. Why is our team taking so long?”

I worked on a team where leadership said things like this directly to engineers. This was in 2024 and 2025, when the AI craze was in full swing and Claude and ChatGPT adoption was rising.

Generative AI (and the marketing behind it) gives people the illusion that the work is simpler than it is. A working demo hides complexity, and once someone has a website that works, they may decide they no longer need engineers, or start to distrust the ones they do have.

Some CEOs want to believe they can replace an engineering team with a few sexy prompts. Many companies also want them to believe this.

That website works great in the demo—under specific conditions and without users with thumbs for fingers. Then it has to plug into a system with millions of lines of old code, satisfy legal requirements, meet accessibility standards, and be delivered in a complex deployment process.

Thinking that writing code was the only bottleneck for deploying new software is like the Titanic seeing the tip of the iceberg and assuming there was nothing underneath it.

Engineers have a unique position in the AI space, because you have the capacity to understand how these models work much better than the average person. Use this to your advantage.

Learn how AI models work. If you can’t already explain that LLMs are probabilistic, what tokens are, or why training data matters, spend a weekend fixing that. You don’t need to become a full-blown AI researcher. A few fundamentals will put you ahead of most people making the AI decisions.

Teach upward. Turn that knowledge into teaching moments for the people who lead you. Explain the limits of these tools, and why a demo and a production system are different animals. It keeps people from truly believing that a notebook full of prompts can replace an engineering team.

Consider the criticism of today’s processes. Some of what we do has been treated as ceremony for too long. Be willing to say, “you know what, maybe you’re right, this process is too slow for the speed we can work at now.” Conceding that earns you the credibility to defend the steps that matter.

I still believe that speed at the cost of everything else is harmful—but that’s a topic for another time.

Find your voice. Engineers at the forefront of AI adoption need to push back and explain why we do things the way we do. Nobody else in the room is going to do it for us.

Your goal, in my opinion, is to save your organization from buying into the hype so much that they chase the wrong thing. Our job, before and after AI, is building safe and useful products for human beings, and engineers are still best suited for that.

The need to educate engineering students about ethics and social responsibility is widely recognized, but today’s curricula often miss the mark. Three professors propose a new approach: adding ethics training directly to core technical coursework.

Looking for a career in quantum computing hardware? An IBM spin-off called Anderon could receive up to $1 billion in funding from the U.S. CHIPS and Science Act for its quantum foundry, established earlier this year. Could Anderon do for quantum hardware what TSMC did for conventional chips?

When Gurmeet Saran joined Anthropic’s technical staff in 2025, he entered a role focused on a key question: How do you know whether you can trust a chatbot like Claude? Learn more about Saran’s path and his work at the AI company.

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, an online education platform that helps people break into AI and modern software roles through project-based learning and one-on-one mentorship with senior developers. Parsity helps career changers transition into software by focusing on practical skills, real-world systems, and the kind of experience companies actually look for.Outside Parsity, Brian works a senior software engineer in the SF Bay Area.Brian is also a father of three, and when he’s not working with students or building programs, you might catch him running around Lake Merritt in Oakland, California.

#3362. Resident Evil director Zach Cregger explains why the iPhone is vital to his work

There have been a number of high-profile movies technically shot on iPhone, but in most cases they are using the same professional cinematography kit they would use with other cameras, including lenses costing tens of thousands of dollars.

Resident Evil director Zach Cregger uses his own iPhone in a rather different way, taking an approach that could be useful to amateur and professional filmmakers alike …

There’s an ongoing debate about how meaningful it is to claim that a high-profile movie, ad, or keynote video was shot on iPhone. Naysayers argue that the quality is all down to the professional lenses, lighting rigs, and editing employed, while those on the other side of the fence point out that everything was captured by the iPhone sensor.

Cregger mostly sidesteps all of that, describing his own use of an iPhone for shot planning, creating photo boards that accurately represent the image that will be captured by each of the Pro lenses he intends to use.

We grew up with video games informing our visual sense just as much as movies and television did, and I feel like I’m able to make a movie that involves the gameplay. [Here] I have a wide angle lens, our protagonist is in the center of the frame as he’s moving, we’re following locked right behind him when he looks right and we swing, right. His attention is dictating where the camera goes, and I think that the effect of that is is a much more immersive horror experience where you’re feeling informed.

I’m a hyper prepper. I’ve got the iPhone that is, like, always on me. I’ll go to the location with my cinematographer and I’ll use Cadrage, an app that approximates different lenses, and I will basically plan out the sequence. I will know exactly what shot is going to cut to what shot, and I will print out these images and everyone will know we’re using this lens for these shots. This is what’s going to be in the frame, and there’s no guesswork.

He does, however, add that an iPhone is all that you need to make a movie, even if his own budgets give him access to rather more expensive kit.

Anybody can make a movie with what’s in your pocket right now.

At the other end of the scale, I use my iPhone in a similar way to him when planning my own amateur videos. I take still photos to create a photo board so that I have a visual reference for each of my planned shots. The videos themselves may be shot on my Blackmagic rig, my iPhone, or some mix of the two.

You can watch Cregger talk through his process for Apple TV here.

Resident Evil director Zach Cregger counts iPhone among his go-to filmmaking tools.Go inside his unique approach to crafting immersive horror experiences, and watch his latest movie now on the Apple TV app. https://t.co/oOpQL0mJde pic.twitter.com/RHWwlPjFID

#3361. These Early Black Friday Ring Camera Deals Start at $24.99

If you’re browsing home security options, Ring has one of the best early Black Friday deals that should be on your radar. Right now, you can add an indoor camera and another one at your front door for less than $65. The Ring Indoor Cam 2K is 58% off at $24.99 (originally $59.99), while the Ring Battery Doorbell 2K is 60% off at $39.99 (originally $99.99)—both at their lowest-ever price.

Both offer features like 2K video and two-way talk, but the indoor cam is the simpler purchase if you mainly want to check on a pet or kids and see what’s happening near an entrance. It plugs into an outlet, so there’s no battery to recharge, and its low-light color video helps preserve detail when lights are off or dimmed. However, since it’s a fixed-view camera, keep in mind that you’ll need to position it carefully.

The Battery Doorbell is the better pick if alerting you to visitors, deliveries, and potential intruders is your priority. It has a 140-degree horizontal and vertical field of view that provides head-to-toe framing, plus up to 6x zoom for better detail. You can install it without wiring, though you’ll need to recharge its built-in battery. It also requires a 2.4GHz wifi network.

The main catch with both devices is the ongoing subscription cost: Live viewing, two-way talk, and basic real-time notifications all work without a subscription, but reviewing saved footage requires a paid plan, starting at $4.99 per month or $49.99 annually for one device; coverage for multiple devices at one location starts at $9.99 monthly or $99.99 annually.

At these prices, the Ring Indoor Cam 2K is perfect for occasional live check-ins, while the Ring Battery Doorbell 2K is better suited to monitoring your front entrance. Buying both makes sense if you already have a Ring plan that covers extra devices.

#3359. From Chip Lab to Center Stage

This integrated circuit designer explains wearables to consumers

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute.

IEEE Member Preethi Ashwath is one of the few women who work in analog integrated circuit design, where about 11 percent are female.

Many engineers are more comfortable working behind the scenes developing technology than speaking to consumers about products. But Preethi Ashwath has learned to take center stage, talking about the “hearable” and wearable devices she has had a hand in developing as an analog integrated circuit designer in the consumer electronics division at Analog Devices of Wilmington, Mass.

The IEEE member is one of the few women who work in the specialized field, where about 11 percent are female, according to career platform Zippia.

Preethi Ashwath Employer Analog Devices, in BostonTitle Integrated circuit designerMember grade MemberAlma maters SJB Institute of Technology in Bengaluru, India; University of California, Irvine

SJB Institute of Technology in Bengaluru, India; University of California, Irvine

Ashwath stepped out from behind the scenes last year to meet with attendees at the Consumer Electronics Show (CES) in Las Vegas. She demonstrated Analog’s new earbuds, which track people’s heart and lung health through vibrations in their ear canals.

After she demonstrated her ability to explain the technology to consumers in simple terms, Analog selected her to represent the company at other events. She says she has “come to see speaking as part of contributing to the field, rather than something separate from technical work.”

She also gives technical talks on various aspects of electrostatic discharge (ESD) and other topics, as well as participates in panel discussions, she says, because they “reach engineers well beyond my immediate team.”

Ashwath is an active volunteer with the IEEE Circuits and Systems Society.

“Whether through designing semiconductor products, publishing technical articles, reviewing conference papers, or speaking at industry events, I try to contribute to the growth of the engineering community and the advancement of the field,” she says.

Ashwath, who grew up in Bengaluru, India, learned about electronics engineering from her high school physics tutor.

That introduction led her to take electronics as one of her core courses in her final years there. At the time, Ashwath’s older sister was pursuing an engineering degree.

“Between my interest in electronics and seeing her already on that path, it became clear to me that engineering was the way to go,” Ashwath says.

After earning a bachelor’s degree in electronics and communications engineering at the SJB Institute of Technology, in Bengaluru, she wanted to pursue a career in very-large-scale integration. But that changed once she moved to the United States and began her master’s program in electrical engineering at the University of California, Irvine.

She discovered her passion for circuits and devices during an internship at Intel in Santa Clara, Calif. She learned about circuit design, package design, and reliability verification tools such as Ansys Totem.

“Seeing every layer of the chip development process gave me a more complete picture of what goes into building a semiconductor product,” she says. “Through that experience, I realized I felt most connected to design.

“It was the hard work and creativity that drew me in. You start with a specification, build a circuit, simulate it, then wait for the chip to come back from fabrication. When your design works, it’s a real feeling of satisfaction. It teaches you patience and perseverance.”

After attaining her master’s degree, she was hired by Intel as an analog design engineer. She gained experience in mixed-signal circuit design before joining Analog. In her current role, she works on consumer hearables such as earbuds and wearables including fitness trackers and health monitors.

Her main focus is designing ESD pad rings, the borders of specialized circuits built around a microchip’s outermost edge to protect it from the discharge, which can damage circuit paths or introduce latent defects that lead to failures later in the chip’s life cycle.

“On a chip with multiple voltage domains, you have to plan how the protection structures are placed and connected across the whole pad ring—and get it right,” Ashwath says. “A mistake there could cause a chip to fail in the field in ways that are very hard to debug afterward.

“It’s detailed work that requires understanding both the device physics and how the whole chip fits together.”

Part of the job is designing and creating an integrated circuit’s building blocks, including ESD protection structures and other mixed-signal blocks. Ashwath conducts rigorous checks to verify they work as intended before being integrated into a chip.

She collaborates with ESD advisors, layout designers, and the digital team that designs the chip’s digital logic.

“I work with them to make sure my analog circuits and their digital blocks work together correctly,” she says. “No two days look exactly the same.”

In 2024 she was recognized with the company’s Impact Award for her “exceptional work on a critical project with significant cross-functional business impact.”

Ashwath was selected to represent Analog at events after a senior leader encouraged her to ask for high-visibility opportunities, she says.

“Most of my time is spent on designing circuits and simulations,” she says. “At CES, I stood in front of customers, engineers, and members of the press, explaining our technology and answering questions on the spot.”

The earbuds she demonstrated monitor minute vibrations from a user’s heart and lungs, according to the Analog website. The vibrations can detect arrhythmia, a leaky heart valve, or fluid in the lungs.

“Hearables are evolving from playing back audio to becoming health-monitoring platforms,” she says. “The ear turns out to be a good location for picking up physiological signals, so these devices can capture vital signs while someone is simply wearing them normally.

“The hard part is achieving high signal quality. The signals you’re trying to detect are very small and buried in the noise from the person’s movements and the surrounding environment.

“That’s where analog front-end design becomes critical. Extracting a meaningful signal from a noisy real-world environment is fundamentally an analog problem.”

Being face-to-face with customers at the conference was new to her.

“What struck me most was seeing how people react to the technology,” she says. “When you’re designing a block, you’re focused on specifications and margins. At CES, after explaining what the product does, I had a better understanding of why it matters to them.

“That connection between the circuit work and the final product is something you don’t always see from the design bench.”

Since the CES, Ashwath has presented other technologies she’s worked on. At the annual National Association of Music Merchants show in Anaheim, Calif., she demonstrated the A2B Automotive Audio Bus to the audio industry. The bus uses a low-cost unshielded twisted-pair cable to carry multichannel digital audio, control data, synchronized clock signals, and power in fewer than 50 microseconds, according to Analog.

“IEEE connects you with academia, which you don’t get much exposure to once you’re in industry. That connection between industry and academic work is valuable in both directions.”

At the company’s Global Technology Conference—an internal event held in Boston that draws engineers from the company’s more than 50 sites around the world—Ashwath led a demonstration of its solutions for augmented reality smart glasses.

“Each of these events has a different audience,” she says. “Learning to explain my technical work to different people has become a skill I’ve acquired.”

The most rewarding part of her job, she says, is seeing the end result of her work.

“You spend months on a design, and there’s a long wait between finishing it and finding out whether your instincts were right,” she says. “When the measurements match what you simulated, that’s the most satisfying moment in this job.

“The other part is knowing my work ends up in a real product. The circuits I design go into devices people actually use every day.”

Like many engineers, Ashwath joined IEEE to access research published in the IEEE Xplore Digital Library. It keeps her current in a field that keeps moving, she says.

During her first year of membership, in 2021, she discovered other perks including networking and educational opportunities.

“IEEE connects you to a community outside your own company,” she says. “Attending lectures and technical talks exposes you to approaches and problems you wouldn’t encounter in your own work.”

She eventually began seeking out volunteer opportunities, specifically with IEEE conferences and journals, because they are “how you stay current with what’s happening in circuits and systems beyond your own day-to-day work,” she says.

“As an analog designer,” she says, “being connected to that broader community matters. The field moves, and you need a way to keep learning from it.”

She serves as a peer reviewer of papers for several IEEE conferences including the IEEE International Symposium on Circuits and Systems and the IEEE International Midwest Symposium on Circuits and Systems. ISCAS is the flagship conference of the IEEE Circuits and Systems Society. MWSCAS is the oldest U.S. conference on the technologies.

“Someone has to assess whether submitted work is technically sound and worth presenting,” she says, “and that only happens if practicing engineers are willing to put in the time.”

The combination of learning from the community and contributing to it is what makes her membership worthwhile, she says.

“Analog design is a field where you’re always learning. Just when you feel you understand one architecture, there’s another one to learn,” she says. “Being an active learner isn’t optional in this field; it’s the requirement, and being part of the IEEE community helps with that.

“IEEE also connects you with academia, which you don’t get much exposure to once you’re in industry.

“Reviewing papers means reading what researchers are working on, which is often quite different from how the same problems get approached in a product environment. That connection between industry and academic work is valuable in both directions.”

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute, covering the work and accomplishments of IEEE members and IEEE and technology-related events. She has a master's degree in health communications from Rutgers University, in New Brunswick, N.J.

#3358. Apple Won't Make a Small Phone so This Company Is Stepping In

Big smartphones have long been the norm. It seems many, if not most, of us prefer our smartphones to be akin to tiny tablets. Even Apple's smallest iPhone isn't that small, with a 6.1-inch display. (Compare that to the 5.4-inch iPhone mini it used to sell.) But just because a lot of us like it that way doesn't mean all of us do.

Despite what companies like Apple would lead you to believe, there are plenty of people out there who want their smartphones to be smaller. For some, the iPhone mini was perfect, featuring a design that most could use comfortably with one hand. While the sales might not have been steady enough for Apple to continue producing the mini line, anecdotally, I know quite a few people who would happily keep using iPhones this small, if only Apple would make more of them. Perhaps you know people like this too; maybe you're one of them.

While the rumor mill does not suggest that Apple plans to make a new iPhone mini, that doesn't mean the dream of the tiny smartphone is dead. Enter "Enough Phone," a new device with a humble goal: to create a "small, modern smartphone that's enough."

Enough Phone really does seem small. The company says its upcoming device is 133mm by 64mm, and less than 12mm thick. That's the equivalent of 5.24 inches by 2.52 inches, and less than 0.47 inches thick. It's remarkably similar to the iPhone 13 mini, at 5.18 by 2.53 inches, and 0.3 inches thick. While the Enough Phone might be a tad larger overall, and perhaps noticeably thicker, it's still reminiscent of that "mini" footprint.

The Enough Phone's 5.3-inch display isn't particularly modern, however. While we don't know the display type, we do know that it has a resolution of 1520 x 720, which may look less sharp to anyone coming from the 2340 x 1080 resolution of the iPhone 13 mini. I'd wager that most people interested in a device like this aren't looking for an ultra-sharp OLED display anyway, but it's worth noting here.

As for the Enough Phone's other specs, the company says it plans to pack in a 2.4GHz MediaTek Dimensity 7500 chip with 8GB of RAM, 128GB of built-in storage, though you can expand that with a microSD card (something you don't see on many smartphones these days). The current plan is to ship with a single 50MP Sony IMX766 rear camera, and a 32MP selfie cam, which would be amongst the highest-resolution front-facing cameras on any smartphone. It supports 5G, Wi-Fi 6, and eSIM, with the option to use a physical SIM as well.

Enough is also aiming to make its smartphone more repairable than the competition. While smartphone OEMs have made slight improvements to repairability in recent years, few phones are made to be opened up by the user, and their components replaced. While Enough Phone isn't fully modular, it is designed with easy-to-open screws, and comes with a fully replaceable 3,500 mAh battery. Combined with promised software support through 2032, Enough says this device "should last you into the next decade."

Now, all of these specs are targets, as the phone is currently in the prototype stage. Enough says that final details may change "slightly" during testing. I would at least hope that the dimensions, particularly the screen size, remain the same by launch. What will likely stay the same, however, are the ringtones: Enough says they hired composer Brian Squillance of LAANDS to produce the jingles for its phone, which is a neat touch.

Unfortunately for Apple fans, however, Enough Phone isn't an iPhone. That said, it doesn't have to be an Android phone, either. While you can buy the phone with Android 17 installed, you can also choose to run OdysseyOS, a minimalist "de-Googled" operating system made by SLEKE. Enough says OdysseyOS is meant for "intentional phone use," which might appeal to anyone looking for a phone that's "dumb" as well as small.

Of course, neither operating system is iOS. Unfortunately for Apple users, the only true iPhone options here are to continue using an old iPhone mini, which Apple does still support, or to opt for an iPhone 17e, the smallest iPhone the company currently makes. It's pretty easy to find a used and refurbished iPhone 13 mini for reasonable price; but while they can still run the latest version of iOS, you won't be able to take advantage of all of Apple's newest features. Plus, while there's no telling how long Apple plans to support the 13 line for, it won't support it forever—by iOS 28 or iOS 29, your phone might lose support entirely.

If the promise of a modern mini smartphone entices you, you can back the Enough Phone on Kickstarter today. While the company's $399 "Super Early Bird" reward is already sold out, as of this article, the "Early Bird" reward is still up. That reward costs $449, and includes a glass screen protector pre-installed, a protective case, a USB-C cable, a USB-C to 3.5mm headphone adapter, a hex screwdriver, and green "Founders' Edition" backplate screws. Enough says that the retail price for its phone will be $599 after the campaign, so you can save $150 by backing the phone today—if you're serious about small phones. The Enough Phone is slated for a May 2027 launch.

#3357. Nintendo Switch games running natively on Apple TV using Claude Code port

A Redditor has just released an open-source project allowing Switch and Switch 2 games to run natively on Apple TV.

So far, both Super Mario Odyssey and Animal Crossing: New Horizons are running, with work ongoing on The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom …

We’ve seen people using Claude Code to do some pretty wild things, like reverse engineering Adobe’s pro apps in order to create open-source versions of them. The latest example is a Redditor who’s created an open-source project called TVport to recompile Nintendo games from the Switch and Switch 2 to Apple TV.

Redditor FloatingFalafel shared the work on GitHub. They’ve so far ported three games to Apple TV, with one of them still a work in progress.

I have been working on a fork of nxnative that recompiles your OG Switch and Switch 2 dumps for AppleTV. Currently, this only works on a game-by-game basis. Most games run essentially the same on the switch, but some load textures into memory differently and need to be diagnosed and fixed before the game will run properly. My hope is to find outliers during this beta so more fixes can be added into the program, making it a seamless experience […]

Super Mario Odyssey – Runs at 60FPS, very slight stutters on occasion, and some audio issues around waterfalls specifically.

Animal Crossing: Horizon – Runs at 30FPS, zero issues so far on my plays.

Zelda: TOTK – Still being worked on, runs at 30FPS, gets thermal throttled. I have a work around for the thermal throttle. I have a render scale selection set at 75% and I am working on adding MetalFX upscaling.

They note you’ll need the 4th-gen Apple TV with its 8GB RAM in order to support some games, though these ones run on the 3rd-gen box.

Another Redditor is working on porting Nintendo 64 games to Apple TV using an app called Nativecade. How long any of these types of projects will survive is anyone’s guess.

Director Vasilis Katsoupis filmed the movie in chronological order over seven weeks, helping capture the physical and psychological toll of the character's ordeal. It's a great choice if you enjoy claustrophobic thrillers.
