Nemo (Willem Dafoe) is an experienced art thief who breaks into a luxurious New York penthouse to steal several valuable paintings. However, when the apartment's advanced security system malfunctions, he finds himself locked inside with no way to contact the outside world. Initially expecting his accomplices to come to his rescue, Nemo soon realizes he's been abandoned. With limited food and water, he must find increasingly inventive ways to navigate the apartment, which is filled with expensive artwork and high-tech features. As the days turn into weeks, Nemo's attempts to escape become more desperate.

"Carolina Caroline" is an indie crime thriller with a neo-noir romantic twist, bringing director Adam Carter Rehmeier and actor Kyle Gallner back together after their cult favorite "Dinner in America." Set against the dusty backroads and forgotten towns of the American South, the movie has a distinctive look, with plenty of retro vibes. Caroline Daniels (Samara Weaving) is a young woman working at a gas station in rural Texas who dreams of leaving her small-town life behind. When she meets Oliver (Kyle Gallner), a charming drifter and experienced con artist, she becomes fascinated by his tricks and soon joins him on the road. The pair travel across the American South, pulling off increasingly daring scams and bank robberies while developing a passionate relationship. Along the way, Caroline hopes to track down her estranged mother in South Carolina. However, the couple soon find themselves in some dangerous situations.

#3355. Everything You Need to Know About Amazon's 2026 Black Friday and Cyber Monday Sales

Gone are the days when holiday sales had a firm beginning and end. These days, if you're not scouring the internet weeks before the actual date of the event, you will miss out on deals. Black Friday is no exception. Amazon released some vague official plans for their sale, but there's plenty that's discounted already, many reaching or matching their lowest price ever—we know, because we use tools to verify and track their deals.

While Amazon has released some press releases announcing they will be partaking in the sale (as they do every year), they haven't officially said what dates the sale will take place. Once they do, we'll update you here.

Yes, you will need to be a Prime Member to shop the exclusive sales during Black Friday and Cyber Monday. Prime membership starts at $14.99 per month. While only you can decide if buying a yearly Prime membership is worth it for you, remember you can always sign up and then cancel your Prime membership once the sale is over: Amazon offers a free 30-day trial, so you can shop during both Black Friday and Cyber Monday before canceling without being charged. Here's how to sign up for a Prime account and all of the benefits that come with it.

As stated already, just because the sale hasn't officially started, it doesn't mean you can't find great deals. Here are some of the best early Black Friday deals:

The WH-1000XM5 were at the top of their class until they were supplanted by the XM6. They're currently discounted to $198 (originally $399.99).

The Bose SoundLink Plus hasn’t been on the market for long, but it’s already earned strong reviews—CNET labeled it “the Goldilocks of Bose Bluetooth speakers,” and it’s down to $179 (originally $269).

The all-in-one Eufy E25 robot vacuum and mop has a self-cleaning roller mop, and it is 40% off at $599.98 (originally $999.99). The roller is rinsed with clean water as it mops, then cleaned at the dock, so you don't need to spend as much time cleaning it yourself.

Amazon is selling the latest MacBook Airs at a $200 discount. That brings the 13-inch MacBook Air to $1,099.99 (down from $1,299) and the 15-inch MacBook Air to $1,299 (originally $1,499), reaching their lowest prices since the June price hikes.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 only launched in September, and it’s already seeing an early Black Friday discount of $100, bringing it down to $699.99 (originally $799).

The other major retailers doing sales are Best Buy, Target, and Walmart. Currently, Best Buy is offering one of the largest Cyber Week sales, with new deals available every Friday. Target has some week-long deals and a Deal of the Day. Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Cyber Monday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, Nov. 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers that can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our live blog.

If this will be your first Black Friday shopping at Amazon, there are some basic things you need to know about Amazon sales:

You can share your Prime membership with family members even if they don't live with you.

You can set price alerts for products you want and your Alexa devices can notify you when they go on sale.

There are usually some "Invite-Only" deals that you can sign up for.

There are tools you can use to see if the deal you're looking at is worthwhile or not.

But if you only take one bit of advice for shopping on Amazon, let it be this one: Don't buy anything you weren't going to buy anyway. A good way to make sure you do this is by making a list of the products you do want, and only having eyes for those.

Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, use price trackers or refer to guides like our live blog that use price trackers for you, and don’t stress over finding the perfect timing.

#3354. Fidelity (FNF) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Investments and a sharp October order drop tested title margins.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Fidelity National Financial, Inc. (FNF +2.21%) reported quarterly results supported by record commercial title performance and growth in its F&G annuities segment. Management reported that the title segment generated an industry-leading 17.1% margin despite a low-transaction environment in residential real estate driven by elevated mortgage rates. The company is managing through the current cycle by focusing on operational discipline and long-term investments in technology and recruitment. Management stated that the F&G segment has surpassed $75 billion in assets under management before reinsurance, contributing 22% of the company's adjusted net earnings for the first nine months of the year. The company continues to prioritize capital returns, having returned $561 million to shareholders year to date through dividends and share repurchases.

Operator: Good morning. Welcome to FNF's Third Quarter 26 Earnings Conference Call. During today's presentation, all callers will be placed in a listen-only mode. Following management's prepared remarks, the conference will be open for questions with instructions to follow at that time. I would now like to turn the call over to Lisa Foxworthy-Parker, Senior Vice President, Investor and External Relations. Please go ahead.

Lisa Foxworthy-Parker: Thanks, operator, and welcome, everyone. I am joined today by Mike Nolan, CEO and Tony Park, CFO. We look forward to addressing your questions following our prepared remarks. F and G's management team, including Conor Murphy, CEO and President and Mike Bailey, CFO, will also be available for Q and A. Today's earnings call may include forward-looking statements and projections under the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act which do not guarantee future events or performance. We do not undertake any duty to revise or update such statements to reflect new information subsequent events, or changes in strategy.

Please refer to our most recent quarterly and annual reports and other SEC filings for details on important factors that could cause actual results to differ materially from those expressed or implied. This morning's discussion also includes non GAAP measures which management believes are relevant in assessing the financial performance of the business. Non GAAP measures have been reconciled to GAAP as required and in accordance with SEC rules within our earnings materials available on the company's investor website. Please note that today's call is being recorded and will be available for webcast replay. And with that, I will hand the call over to Mike Nolan.

Michael Joseph Nolan: Thank you, Lisa, and good morning. We delivered strong third quarter results across both our title business and F and G segment, demonstrating the power of our dual earnings engines and our ability to execute in dynamic market conditions. I would like to start by thanking our employees for their hard work and dedication. There is no doubt we are navigating a challenging real estate cycle. Yet our team continues to generate industry leading performance that is well ahead of the competition. Together, we are managing through this period with a disciplined operating strategy which generates a steady level of free cash flow.

This allows us to continue to invest in recruiting talent, attractive acquisitions technology and innovation, as we manage the business for the long term while performing in the immediate term. Turning to our title segment, we delivered adjusted pre tax title earnings of $422 million for the third quarter, up 3% over the third quarter of 2025. This generated an industry leading adjusted pretax title margin of 17.1% for the third quarter as compared to 17.8% in both the sequential and prior year quarters.

As we discussed on our second quarter call, we expected some modest sequential compression due to recent strategic investments in recruiting and attractive tuck in acquisitions in recent months, where expenses tend to come ahead of the associated revenue contribution. The compression compared to the third quarter of 25 was also expected, due to favorable onetime items in the prior year period and continued investment in technology. Overall, our third quarter results reflect strong performance across the business and disciplined expense management. Looking at our title results more closely, starting with purchase, U. S. Existing home sales continue to reflect a low transactional environment due to mortgage rates and housing market dynamics.

Mortgage rates remain high, but have fallen from the recent peak following the Federal Reserve rate hike in September. This is the opposite of the trend we saw in 2025,, and has amplified the normal seasonal decline. Over the course of the year, purchase orders opened have held up well through August, with each month comparing favorably to the prior year, before falling behind by 2% for the month of September. Importantly, we continue to steadily outperform relative to our peers. For the quarter, our daily purchase orders opened were up 3% over the third quarter of 2025, down 9% from the second quarter of 2026 and down 6% for the month of October versus the prior year.

Our residential refinance volumes continue to be responsive to 30 year mortgage rates, although accounting for only 6% of our direct revenue in the third quarter. Notably, we have demonstrated our ability to generate strong adjusted pretax title margins without a substantial refinance market over the past 5 years. Refinance orders opened were 1.4 thousand per day in the third quarter, as compared to 1.6 thousand in both the prior year and sequential quarters. Given mortgage rates in October, we saw refinance orders opened decreased to 1.2 thousand per day reflecting how refinance volumes can quickly change with moves in rates.

Our refinance orders opened per day were down 11% from the third quarter of 2025, down 7% from the second quarter of 2026, and down 35% for the month of October versus the prior year. Our commercial business is on pace for a record year. Direct commercial revenue was $1.2 billion in the first 9 months, up 22% over $1 billion in the first 9 months of 2025. National and local market daily orders opened trended down 1% and up 6%, respectively, in the third quarter as compared to the prior year quarter.

Total commercial orders opened were 876 per day, up 2% over the third quarter of 2025 down 5% from the second quarter of 2026 and down 6% for the month of October versus the prior year. We closed 24 transactions generating over $1 million each in premiums in the third quarter across multiple asset classes. In both our direct and agency businesses. This is reflected in our higher trending commercial fee per file. We view the current momentum in commercial as sustainable over the near term. Our commercial strength continues to be broad based, across both geographies and asset classes.

The composition of our commercial pipeline remains healthy and includes a mix of industrial, data centers, multifamily, affordable housing, retail and energy transactions. At this time, we expect office to gradually recover with top tier properties leading the rebound. 1 question that I often receive is around data centers. We have seen data center transactions in our pipeline over the past 4 years. And in some cases have already seen refinances of transactions that close between 2022 and 2024 which is an underappreciated demand driver. Similar to energy, data centers tend to be higher premium transactions although comprising a small portion of the overall order count.

This shows up in our national fee per file which benefits from the larger energy and data center deals. To bring it all together, total orders opened averaged 5.8 thousand per day in the third quarter, with July at 5.9 thousand August at 5.8 thousand and September at 5.6 thousand. For the month of October, total orders opened were 4.7 thousand per day down 17% from the prior year. Looking to the fourth quarter, we remain optimistic about our commercial momentum although we recognize the impact on residential purchase and refinance volumes of elevated mortgage rates and the typical fourth quarter seasonality.

All else equal, we would expect our adjusted pretax title margin to move toward the lower end of our 15%-20% normal range in the fourth quarter. Over time, as mortgage rates eventually improve, we believe residential purchase and refinance activity will accelerate and trend toward historical levels. This recovery represents additional earnings power given the operational leverage that we have built into our model. This operational leverage is also supported by the investments we continue to make in technology and AI. FNF provides essential services that extend well beyond the title insurance policy we also manage the settlement process from start to finish. We are the rails on which real estate transactions run.

For years, we have invested with the vision of building a differentiated technology platform with 1 overarching objective, to make every real estate transaction faster safer, and simpler. That objective is showing up in what we are delivering today. Since we rolled out our partnership with Clear last year, we have run nearly 100 thousand enhanced identity verifications across our operations to counter impersonation and wire fraud in property sales. Since we launched property monitoring earlier this year, we have provided visibility and alerts as a complementary service to over 250 thousand homeowners after closing. We continue to receive positive feedback from our customers on this value add service.

We are accelerating our property monitoring rollout and we expect it to become the largest footprint in the industry. We are also driving deeper digital engagement with nearly 88% adoption of inHere across eligible residential sale transactions. That is the foundation. AI is the next layer. We are already deploying AI driven agents into production workflows, to improve speed and execution across the Title I settlement process This is not a pilot. it is operational. AI is still early, but the direction is clear. A better experience for our customers and higher productivity for us.

Combined with our broader technology investments, these capabilities strengthen our competitive position and our ability to consistently deliver industry leading adjusted pretax title margins over time. Turning now to our F and G segment. F and G's assets under management before reinsurance have surpassed the $75 billion milestone at September 30. Gross AUM of $76.2 billion was up 7% over the prior year quarter. F and G continues to expand its retail and institutional franchises and delivered its best core retail sales quarter in history. Opportunistic sales intentionally lower due to returns below threshold, as F and G continues to allocate capital to the highest return opportunities.

On a stand alone basis, FNG reported GAAP equity excluding AOCI of $6.7 billion at quarter end. And has grown its book value per share excluding AOCI to $51.37, up 87% since the 2020 acquisition. We believe that the components of F and G's business the new business platform, profitable in force block and capital light fee based strategies each represent a distinct and measurable source of long term value that are not yet fully reflected in F and G's current market valuation. At recent levels, the FG stock has an especially attractive dividend yield of around 5%. Which is above average for the publicly traded life and annuity sector.

We remain pleased with F and G's operating performance and foresee plenty of opportunities to grow AUM and increase the value of the business over time. With that, let me now turn the call over to Tony to review FNF's third quarter financial performance and provide additional insights.

Anthony John Park: Thank you, Mike. Starting with our consolidated results, we generated $3.6 billion in total revenue in the third quarter. Excluding net recognized gains and losses, our total revenue was $3.5 billion as compared with $3.9 billion in the third quarter of 2025. We reported third quarter net earnings of $633 million including net recognized gains of $29 million versus net earnings of $358 million including $176 million of net recognized gains in the third quarter of 2025. Adjusted net earnings were $352 million or $1.32 per diluted share compared with $439 million or $1.63 per share in the third quarter of 2025.

The title segment contributed $315 million The F and G segment contributed $72 million and the Corporate segment had an adjusted net loss of $7 million before eliminating $28 million of dividend income from F and G in the consolidated financial statements. Turning to third quarter financial highlights specific to the Title segment. Our Title segment generated $2.5 billion in total revenue in the third quarter. Excluding net recognized loss of $19 million compared with $2.3 billion in the third quarter of 2025. Direct premiums increased 11% over the prior year Agency premiums increased 3%. And escrow, title related, and other fees increased 10%. Personnel costs increased 10%, and other operating expenses increased 13%.

All in, the title business generated adjusted pretax title earnings of $422 million up 3% over $410 million in the third quarter of 2025. And a 17.1% adjusted pretax title margin in the quarter versus 17.8% in the prior year quarter. Our title and corporate investment portfolio totaled $5 billion at September 30, Interest and investment income in the Title and Corporate segments was $98 million down 10% from the prior year quarter and excluding income from F and G dividends to the holding company. The prior year period included a benefit from a legal settlement of $7 million.

Looking ahead, we expect quarterly interest and investment income to trend up from $98 million in the third quarter to around $105 million in the fourth quarter and then increase around $5 million in each subsequent quarter through 2027. Assuming an additional 75 basis points of Fed rate hikes over the next 9 months. In addition, we expect $28 million per quarter of common and preferred dividend income from F and G to the corporate segment in the next 2 quarters. F and G's dividend income will decrease to a approximately $25 million per quarter thereafter. Following conversion, of the mandatory convertible preferred stock during the first quarter.

Our title claims paid of $72 million were $3 million lower than our provision of $75 million for the third quarter. The carried reserve for title claim losses is $10 million or 1% above the actuary's central estimate. We continue to provide for title claims at 4.5% of total title premiums. Next, turning to financial highlights specific to the F and G segment. Since F and G hosted its earnings call earlier this morning, and provided a thorough update, I will provide a few key highlights. F and G's top line AUM before reinsurance increased to $76.2 billion at September 30. Up 7% over the prior year.

This includes retained assets under management of $56.2 billion F and G reported gross sales of $3 billion for the third quarter. Gross sales were comprised of $2.3 billion of core sales including record core retail sales of $2.1 billion and nearly $700 million of opportunistic sales. This mix reflects pricing discipline and capital allocation to highest return opportunities. F and G's net sales were $1.4 billion in the third quarter. This reflects flow reinsurance in line with capital targets for multiyear guaranteed annuities and fixed indexed annuities. F and G's retained investment portfolio performed very well once again this quarter. The portfolio is high quality, with 97% of fixed maturities being investment grade.

It is well matched to the liability profile and diversified across asset types. Credit related impairments have remained low and stable. Importantly, F and G has a clean governance model with Blackstone with no inherent conflict of interest. Adjusted net earnings for the F and G segment were $72 million for the third quarter, reflecting our approximate 72% ownership stake compared with $139 million in the third quarter of 2025, which reflected our approximate 82% ownership stake and included the F and G Life Free subsidiary which was sold on 03/01/2026. F and G's core spread remains consistent as the business maintained disciplined pricing and rate setting. F and G continues to provide an important complement to our title business.

In the first 9 months, the F and G segment contributed 22% of F&F's adjusted net earnings. Down from 32% for the first 9 months of 2025. Turning to capital and liquidity. FNF continues to maintain a strong balance sheet and balanced capital allocation strategy. As Mike mentioned, we have consistently generated a steady level of free cash flow. Allowing us to continue to invest in our business and build for the long term. We also continue to return excess cash to shareholders. During the third quarter, FNF returned approximately $143 million of capital to shareholders.

This brought capital return to shareholders during the first 9 months of the year to approximately $561 million Of note, we only completed $5 million of share repurchases during the third quarter given that we were in a closed trading window for much of the quarter. Due to the timing of material nonpublic information and our standard corporate governance policies. From a capital allocation perspective, we ended 2025 with $659 million in cash and short term liquid investments at the holding company.

During the first 9 months, our cash position and cash generation funded $417 million of common dividends paid $61 million of holding company interest expense $144 million in opportunistic share repurchases, and approximately $60 million of investments in a handful of tuck in, and other title related acquisitions. The majority of which were in the third quarter. All while keeping pace with wage inflation and funding the continued higher spend in risk and technology required in today's landscape. We ended the third quarter with $545 million in cash and short term liquid investments at the holding company. Which is about 83% of the amount held at year-end 2025. This concludes our prepared remarks.

And let me now turn the call back to our operator for questions.

#3353. MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display review: A lot more than touch

Apple unveiled the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display last week, and it brings some of the biggest changes to the Mac in years. There’s a tandem OLED screen, a significantly lighter design, and the long-awaited addition of touch. Oh, and the Apple logo glows again.

Here’s what it’s like actually using the new MacBook Pro.

In 2016, Apple unveiled an all-new MacBook Pro design that prioritized thinness and portability above almost everything else, kickstarting what proved to be a rocky period for Apple laptops. The thinner, lighter MacBook Pro was marred by the butterfly keyboard, poor thermals, and an overall focus on form over function.

In 2021, Apple righted the ship. It unveiled a completely redesigned MacBook Pro that reversed many of those controversial decisions, bringing back ports, replacing the Touch Bar with a physical function row, and dramatically improving performance with Apple Silicon.

There was a trade-off, though: the MacBook Pro got bigger and noticeably heavier. The smaller model grew from 13 inches and 3.1 pounds to 14 inches and 3.5 pounds, while the 16-inch model went from 4.3 pounds to 4.7 pounds.

At the time, we were all willing to make that compromise. Now, with the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, Apple is once again making its pro laptops lighter — but without sacrificing what made the 2021 redesign so great.

The 14-inch model has dropped from 3.5 pounds to just 3.0 pounds, while the 16-inch model has gone from 4.7 pounds to 4.0 pounds. In fact, both new MacBook Pro models weigh essentially the same as their 2016 counterparts, despite having larger displays, significantly more powerful hardware, and none of the compromises that defined that generation.

Both models are also slightly thinner than before, with the 14-inch model measuring 0.59 inches thick (down from 0.61 inches) and the 16-inch measuring 0.63 inches (down from 0.66 inches).

How did Apple pull this off? The biggest change is the switch from mini-LED to OLED. Because OLED doesn’t require a separate backlight, Apple could make the display assembly significantly thinner and lighter. The company is also using custom on-cell touch technology to integrate touch sensing into the display panel, instead of adding multiple separate layers.

But while the new display technology played a major role, the weight reduction also came from countless other smaller engineering optimizations throughout the machine.

You notice the lighter weight of the new MacBook Pro immediately when you pick it up. My review unit is the 16-inch MacBook Pro, and I’m genuinely surprised at how nice it feels. It’s not light, but it feels less like a tank.

I’ve always used the smaller of the two MacBook Pro models for portability, most recently a 14-inch M4 Pro. The weight of the new 16-inch MacBook Pro has me reconsidering that preference, though. It feels remarkably nice for a laptop with such a large display, and I’ve really enjoyed having the extra screen space without feeling like I’m sacrificing too much portability.

The new MacBook Pro also features slimmer bezels around the display. Apple has eliminated the thicker bottom bezel, and for the first time, all four corners of the display are rounded. It’s a relatively small change, but I think it gives the MacBook Pro a cleaner, more symmetrical look.

And finally: the glowing Apple logo is back. Unlike older MacBooks, which used light from the display’s backlight to illuminate the logo, the new OLED MacBook Pro has no backlight to draw from, requiring a different approach.

The logo’s brightness is still tied to the display brightness, just like it was a decade ago. The higher your display brightness, the brighter the Apple logo on the back. It also factors in your environment’s ambient brightness.

When the MacBook Pro is closed, the logo looks like polished metal, just like it has since the 2016 redesign. Open it up, and it glows. It’s unnecessary, but I’m so thrilled it’s back.

The display is what Apple is most proud of on this new MacBook Pro. After all, the full marketing name is apparently “MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display.” It doesn’t exactly roll off the tongue, but I think it shows what Apple sees as the big differentiator compared to other MacBook Pro models it still sells.

And rightfully so. The PROLED XDR Display is stunning. It’s a major upgrade over the mini-LED display that Apple debuted in the MacBook Pro back in 2021 (which was no slouch, to be clear). The OLED panel’s color saturation, contrast, and deep blacks are miles better than any other laptop I’ve seen, including Windows PCs with high-end OLED displays.

The viewing angles are also noticeably better, with colors and brightness staying remarkably consistent even when you look at the display from the side.

One downside of the MacBook Pro with mini-LED is blooming. Because the mini-LED display used local dimming zones, there was a subtle halo around bright objects against dark backgrounds. With the OLED display on these new MacBook Pros, every pixel is independently illuminated, so that blooming effect is gone.

If you’re worried about burn-in, Apple says the new MacBook Pros have a revamped display engine that continuously monitors pixel usage, temperature, and other factors. It compensates individual pixels in real time to mitigate burn-in and maintain brightness. We’ll have to wait and see whether this holds true over time, but anecdotally I haven’t noticed any burn-in on my OLED iPad Pro after more than two years.

The improvements on the new MacBook Pro’s display go well beyond simply being OLED. Brightness is another area Apple emphasizes.

In direct sunlight by a window or on the patio, the display gets more than bright enough to remain easily readable. I rarely find myself needing to crank the brightness all the way up.

Those brightness improvements dovetail nicely with another area of emphasis on the new MacBook Pro: reflectivity. The new MacBook Pro’s glossy display has just 1% reflectance, which Apple says is due to two things. First, the OLED panel itself is designed to minimize reflections. It also has a custom antireflective coating that reduces reflections from the cover glass.

My review unit has a standard glossy display, and my previous MacBook Pro was a 14-inch model with nano-texture, so I’ve been paying especially close attention to the differences in reflectivity.

As I write this review, I’m sitting next to a large window that gets a lot of direct light. I’m very impressed with how well this glossy 16-inch MacBook Pro display handles reflections. It’s not, of course, as antireflective as my 14-inch MacBook Pro with nano-texture. But it’s much closer than I expected, and significantly better than my glossy MacBook Air.

I haven’t had a chance to try the nano-texture on the new MacBook Pro with PROLED, but Apple says the nano-texture is now “precisely etched into the cover glass,” so it should be even better than before.

All told, the PROLED XDR Display is impressive by every metric, both on paper and in the real world. Whether it’s the core improvements of an OLED panel, improved reflectivity, or higher brightness, you’ll notice the better display from the moment you turn the MacBook Pro on.

There’s something uncanny about using the new touchscreen MacBook Pro for the first time. This is still unmistakably macOS, with the same interface and software controls that we’ve known for years. Except now, you can reach out and touch the screen … and it actually responds.

Apple famously resisted adding touch to the Mac until now. Steve Jobs called the idea of a touchscreen Mac “ergonomically terrible” in 2010.

When Apple announced these touchscreen MacBooks, that clip of Jobs went viral. As usual, Jobs’ comments have more nuance than last week’s social media reaction suggests.

“Touch surfaces don’t want to be vertical,” Jobs said at the time. “It gives great demo, but after a short period of time you start to fatigue, and after an extended period of time, your arm wants to fall off.”

A lot has changed since those comments from Jobs, but I don’t think adding touch to the MacBook Pro proves him wrong. The ergonomics of using a touchscreen as the primary input method on a laptop-style device are, in fact, terrible. Your arm does get tired.

The good news, however, is that Apple is very intentionally not trying to make touch the primary interaction method on these new MacBook Pros. It’s clear from both using this touchscreen MacBook Pro and Apple’s own messaging that touch is intended to be a secondary input method. It’s there when you need it or want it, but you can also ignore it completely and never feel like you’re missing out.

So, with that out of the way: what’s it like using a touchscreen MacBook Pro?

Apple has made a variety of small tweaks throughout macOS to accommodate touch input. For example, when macOS detects touch input, items in contextual menus are spaced further apart.

When you long-press on something like an app icon in the Dock, it enlarges and shows you a more spaced-out list of contextual menu items. If you long-press an item in Finder, it lifts up under your finger, and you can drag it or drop it anywhere else.

The classic traffic light window controls also expand after you tap them. The first tap expands the controls without actually activating any of them. Then, tap a second time on the specific control you’re trying to activate. It’s a bit awkward having to tap the same spot twice in a row like that.

These tweaks are all about making macOS dynamically adapt to the fact that your finger is less precise than a pointer. Rather than redesigning macOS around touch, Apple has made the existing interface accommodate it when needed.

You also get all the typical touch gestures. You can pinch to zoom, swipe with four fingers to switch between Spaces or Mission Control, and swipe up to reveal the dock. You can pull to refresh in Safari, double-tap a window to fill the screen, and flick a window to the side to tile it.

Apple has also added automatic video stabilization that compensates for screen movement when you tap the display during a video call. This helps keep your camera feed steady, even when the screen itself wobbles slightly. It seems to work as advertised in my testing.

So far, I’ve found the touchscreen on MacBook Pro to be a “nice-to-have” addition, but not a reinvention of how I use the Mac. I catch myself idly reaching up to scroll a webpage instead of using the trackpad, tapping on the occasional Dock icon, and using pinch-to-zoom in the Photos app.

Touch input is also legitimately useful in places like iPhone Mirroring and the Xcode simulator. I can imagine people who regularly use rendering apps like Blender will find the touchscreen more useful than I do, since my primary job is manipulating text.

One reason I think touch might be less useful, or less important, on a Mac than on a Windows PC is that Apple’s trackpads are simply too good. There’s little reason for me to bother reaching up and using four fingers to swipe between Spaces when I can do it on the beautiful, big, glass trackpad. On a Windows PC with a crappy plastic trackpad? I bet multi-touch interaction is much more appealing on the touchscreen.

There have been a few instances where I just forget this MacBook Pro has a touchscreen until I reach up to flick a piece of lint or dog hair off the screen, and accidentally tap on something.

But I think that’s exactly how it should be. Using the touchscreen is a conscious choice, not a requirement. You can buy this computer and literally never touch the screen, or turn it off entirely via Accessibility in System Settings. For some Mac users, this is probably the most important thing. Apple hasn’t compromised the traditional macOS experience to accommodate touch.

The one thing that hasn’t changed with the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is performance. Much like the standard MacBook Pro models unveiled earlier this year, the new PROLED models are available with M5 Pro and M5 Max chips.

Apple says that the new MacBook Pro has a redesigned thermal system optimized for the new design, while also maintaining the same performance of M5 Pro and M5 Max we’ve come to expect.

My review unit is the 16-inch M5 Pro configuration with an 18-core CPU, 20-core GPU, and 48GB of unified memory. In GeekBench testing, the new MacBook Pro performs virtually the same as the models introduced earlier this year.

In my day-to-day use, I haven’t noticed any differences in performance or thermal behavior compared to my previous MacBook Pro. Admittedly, my workflow of writing, researching, editing photos, and dozens of Safari tabs doesn’t come close to pushing the M5 Pro to its limits. But the new MacBook Pro handles all of that effortlessly, without noticeable heat or fan noise. In fact, I haven’t heard the fans kick in once.

That’s not a definitive test of Apple’s claims about sustained performance, but it’s reassuring that the thinner and lighter design hasn’t introduced any noticeable compromises in my everyday use or in benchmarks.

This makes for an interesting predicament for MacBook Pro shoppers. Rumors say that Apple believes the M7 generation will offer such a dramatic improvement in performance, particularly around AI, that it’s skipping the higher-end M6 chips altogether.

The first M7 chips are expected sometime next year, likely late in the year for the high-end MacBook Pro. This means that if you buy an M5-equipped MacBook Pro right now, you’re buying a computer with a chip that will effectively be two generations behind in less than a year.

The M5 Pro and M5 Max chips are plenty fast, and these MacBook Pros also come with OLED, touch, and other changes mentioned throughout this review. Still, there’s something a little strange about Apple pairing its biggest MacBook Pro redesign in five years with chips that debuted eight months ago, particularly with the next major leap in Apple silicon reportedly on the horizon.

The Dynamic Island comes to the Mac for the first time with the new MacBook Pro. It never made sense to me that Apple added the notch to the MacBook Pro with so little software accommodation. The Dynamic Island finally addresses that, bringing a familiar iPhone experience to the Mac.

Live Activities now show up in the Dynamic Island, along with Now Playing info from apps like Music and Podcasts. For example, clicking (or tapping) the Dynamic Island while Music is playing brings up the mini player for easy access to controls. From the mini player, you can click again to open the full Music app. Live Activities from your iPhone also show up in the Dynamic Island on MacBook Pro, rather than in your menu bar like on other Macs. Spotlight on Mac bounces out of the Dynamic Island.

I’ve very much enjoyed having the Dynamic Island on the Mac. It’s one of my favorite iPhone features, especially for Live Activities. The implementation on the Mac is a great continuation of that experience.

Apple says that the new MacBook Pro has a redesigned six-speaker system that delivers 50% deeper bass. The speakers do indeed sound fantastic. Apple also specifically calls out improved speaker tuning when using the MacBook Pro with its lid closed and connected to an external display. In my testing, the difference is noticeable. The speakers sound less muffled and significantly louder.

Apple says battery life is unchanged on the new MacBook Pro models compared to the non-OLED variants.

I haven’t done any scientific battery testing, but anecdotally, my 16-inch M5 Pro model seems on track to match Apple’s claim of up to 17 hours of wireless web browsing.

The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is a fascinating product. It’s both a major evolution of the MacBook Pro and a better version of the same laptop we’ve come to love since its Apple Silicon reinvigoration in 2021.

The addition of touch is getting all the attention, but I think the lighter design is actually the more significant change in day-to-day use. I never expected a 16-inch MacBook Pro to have me reconsidering my longstanding preference for the 14-inch model.

Touch hasn’t fundamentally changed how I use the Mac, but it’s a welcome addition that feels overdue. People reasonably expect to touch their laptop screen and have it respond. Some people will undoubtedly find it more useful than I have, and Apple has done an excellent job integrating it into macOS without compromising the traditional experience.

With or without touch, the PROLED XDR display is a spectacular upgrade, with improvements in brightness, contrast, and reflectivity that you’ll notice every time you open the lid.

These new OLED MacBook Pro models command a $400 premium over the mini-LED M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pro models Apple is still selling. Those machines are also heavier, lack touchscreens, and miss some of the bells and whistles of the pricier models. Presumably, these two product lines will eventually converge, but right now the MacBook Pro lineup is a little awkward. The 14-inch PROLED model starts at $2,899, while the 16-inch starts at $3,399.

But that awkward positioning doesn’t take away from the product. This is still the same MacBook Pro we’ve come to love over the last five years. Apple has taken an already excellent laptop and made meaningful improvements to nearly every aspect of the experience. And it just so happens to have a touchscreen now, too.

#3352. Poetry for Engineers: Of Code and Shortleaf Pine

Read Ralph Earle’s poem from the November 2026 issue

After retiring from IBM as a senior software engineer in 2017, Ralph Earle has published two poetry collections.

I step into the warm moist airamong the columns of the pines,their net of twigs and rootscomplex as any lines of code.

The trees purify and anchor.Their branches balance my restlessness.

Their calling is to be present,mine to develop apps. Our tasksverge toward a common logic:living filaments of root, of interface.

Ralph Earle joined the IBM Software Lab in Raleigh, N.C., in 1990 as a technical editor and retired as a senior software engineer in 2017. While at IBM, he coauthored Enterprise Computing with Objects: From Client/Server Environments to the Internet for Addison-Wesley’s Bloch-Jacobson-Rumbaugh Object Technology Series, and he published articles in technical journals, including IEEE Computer Magazine, IBM Systems Journal, Distributed Computing, Management Directions, and Object Magazine.

In retirement, Earle has flourished in a second career as a poet. His poetry collections are Everything You Love Is New (Redhawk Publications, 2024) and The Way the Rain Works (Sable Books, 2015). He has been nominated for the Pushcart Prize three times and comanages a monthly poetry series at a Chapel Hill, N.C., bookstore. His poems have appeared in many print and online outlets, including The Sun, Carolina Quarterly, and Sufi Journal.

Love of the complexity behind the interfaces.

#3351. Amazon Fire TV Stick HD Review: Small, speedy, and easy on the wallet

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Amazon Fire TV Stick HD is a simple, affordable way to make a 1080p TV smarter. The new Vega OS feels quick, its slimmer design can run straight off your TV's USB port, and setup is a breeze. It's limited to 1080p and can't sideload apps like Fire OS, so if you own a 4K TV, you should spend a bit more on the new Amazon Fire Stick 4K.

Responsive, easy-to-use interface with new Vega OS

Slim design that runs off your TV's USB port

No third-party app sideloading like Fire OS

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Streaming sticks don't need to be fancy to hit their mark, and the Amazon Fire TV Stick HD is a great reminder of that. If you've got an older TV that's still going strong but has sluggish smart features (or perhaps none at all), a $35 streaming stick is an easy fix.

The 2026 Fire TV Stick HD runs Vega OS, Amazon's Linux-based software, which replaces the Android-based Fire OS that powered previous models. Amazon says the changes make it more than 30 percent faster, and it also brings a slimmer body, USB power, Wi-Fi 6 support, and free Alexa+.

It's not all pros across the board. The resolution caps out at 1080p, you can't sideload third-party apps anymore, and there's no support for Dolby Vision. But if you're shopping for a bedroom, guest room, or an older TV set that you don't primarily use, the Fire TV Stick HD is one of the cheaper streaming devices you should take a closer look at.

The Amazon Fire TV Stick HD launched on April 29, 2026, for $34.99, which is the same price as the 2024 model it replaced. It's Amazon's cheapest streaming stick, and it sits below the Fire TV Stick 4K and the Fire TV Stick 4K Max. Amazon ran a limited-time deal that brought the stick down to $21.99 shortly after launch, so we'll likely see temporary price cuts around the holiday shopping season.

Keep in mind that the stick's new "Direct Power" feature means that it gets power right from your TV's USB port. If your TV doesn't have a USB port, you'll need to pick up an adapter separately.

The Fire TV Stick HD is about as minimal as a streaming device gets, and Amazon says it's the slimmest Fire TV device the company has made. That makes it really easy to tuck behind a TV or toss in a bag for a trip, and it won't crowd the other ports and cables on your set.

The only other connection is a USB-C port for power, and thanks to "Direct Power," you can plug it straight into your TV's USB port with the included cable. That means you'll have one less wall adapter to hide, and your setup will look a lot cleaner as a result.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

The included Alexa Voice Remote covers all the basics, including voice search, menu navigation, TV power, and volume controls. It doesn't have fancy extras like a remote finder or backlit buttons, but it gets the job done. (If you want Amazon's redesigned Fire TV remote, which I liked a lot more, you'll have to get the Fire TV Stick 4K.)

Setup is about as easy as it gets. Just plug the stick into your TV's HDMI port, connect the USB-C cable to your TV's USB port, and follow the on-screen prompts. You'll then have to connect to Wi-Fi and sign in with your Amazon account, and you're off to the races.

Since Vega OS only lets you install apps from the Amazon app store, you should make sure that the ones you use most are actually available. Netflix, YouTube, Disney+, Prime Video, Hulu, and other popular streaming services all run natively, but niche apps may be missing due to the lack of third-party app sideloading, which the older Fire OS allowed you to do.

The Fire TV Stick HD has a quad-core 1.7GHz processor and 8GB of storage. It can stream up to 1080p resolution with HDR10, HDR10+, and HLG, and it supports Dolby Atmos through HDMI pass-through if you have a compatible sound setup. There's no Dolby Vision here, and it won't output 4K, so it's really only meant for 1080p TV sets.

Vega OS keeps menus and home screen rows moving smoothly, and apps open quickly. I didn't have any issues switching between my most used apps on the fly. Amazon's "30 percent faster" figure is its own claim, so I wouldn't treat it as fact, but it definitely felt faster than my past Fire OS experiences.

I also like that the Fire TV Stick HD isn't limited to video. You can pair a Bluetooth game controller and play cloud games through Amazon Luna or Xbox Game Pass, which is a fun bonus, and you can even connect a pair of headphones for late-night viewing. It comes with Alexa+ free of charge, which can come in handy when you're trying to hunt down something new to watch.

The downsides are pretty familiar to past Fire TV Sticks. A big chunk of the Fire TV home screen is taken up by recommendations and sponsored content, and you'll definitely notice it (especially if you're used to Roku's cleaner layout like I am).

Sideloading third-party apps is also gone, which will bug those who liked using older Fire TV Sticks for apps that aren't available in Amazon's app store. Neither is a dealbreaker for the average viewer, but they're worth knowing about before diving in.

The Amazon Fire TV Stick HD is a fast, simple, and affordable streaming stick that's a perfect match for older HD TVs and secondary rooms. Vega OS feels speedy, the slim design and USB power keep things neat, and setup takes just a few minutes. You won't get 4K streaming resolution, Dolby Vision, or third-party app sideloading, but for $34.99 (or less on sale), it's hard to complain.

If you're looking for an alternative pick, the base model Roku Streaming Stick ($39) also tops out at 1080p, but has a cleaner interface.

In Amazon’s ecosystem, the new Fire TV Stick 4K costs $25 more, but you get 4K resolution output and a redesigned (and much better) remote. And if you're a tinkerer who wants to sideload apps, the Fire TV Stick 4K Max is the only Amazon stick that still runs Android-based Fire OS.

If you've got an older 1080p TV and want a cheap way to get streaming apps on it, the Fire TV Stick HD is a solid choice that won't break the bank.

#3348. Build a Hidden Lock With a Magnetic Imager

Stephen Cass is the special projects editor at IEEE Spectrum.

Only a programmable secret gesture with a magnet can open this lockbox. (Or a hammer. It’s a proof of concept.)

Like many a nerd, I have a certain fascination with locks. This originates in reading the memoir Surely You’re Joking, Mr. Feynman as a teenager, in which Richard Feynman recounts picking locks and cracking combinations while at his day job working on the Manhattan Project at Los Alamos. I currently have a couple of locksport pick sets and training locks that I purchased at hacker conferences over the years (although I’m still terrible at it), and I delight in the YouTube exploits of folks like the LockPickingLawyer.

All of which left me wondering if I could try building an interesting lock. One dodge that lockmakers have long used to challenge would-be plunderers is to conceal the existence of the lock itself. A modern variant of this is the magnetic lock, where a magnet is held or slid against an innocuous portion of a door or box, releasing a catch. The problem with this is that, once you guess the location of the lock, any strong magnet will open it.

So I started thinking about embedding an RFID reader under the surface and resigning myself to keeping track of yet another access card. But then I stumbled across something much more interesting: SparkFun’s US $100 magnetic imaging tile. I realized I could use this to build a magnetic lock that opens with a programmable secret gesture.

I used a few discrete components to drive the servo motor and put the lock into program mode [top], controlled by a Teensy 4.1 microcontroller [middle]. An array of Hall-effect sensors detect magnetic fields [bottom].James Provost

The magnetic imaging tile is a small-run SparkFun board based on the work of Peter Jansen. It features an 8-by-8 grid of Hall-effect sensors, and uses an SPI interface to talk to the microcontroller of your choice. These sensors can detect both the magnitude and polarity of a magnetic field, and the board can report its measurements hundreds to thousands of times per second, depending on how much processing power your microcontroller has available. This is easily fast enough to capture the motion of a magnet being moved by hand across the board’s sensor area—my secret gesture.

An interesting thing about using magnetic fields is that if I was in extreme paranoia mode, I could shield the entire lock behind copper sheeting, something I couldn’t do with an RFID reader. The copper sheet would act as a Faraday cage, blocking any RFID signal, along with any other electromagnetic fields an attacker with an EMF meter might use to locate the lock.

I chose a Teensy 4.1 as my microcontroller. I like the Teensy because it offers loads of input/output, a 600-megahertz processor, a megabyte of RAM, and a built-in SD card, all in a slim package with an equally slim $32 price tag.

Wiring the Teensy to the magnetic-imaging tile was trivial, only complicated by the fact that one side of the board has a silk-screen error that misidentifies the SPI connections (SparkFun says this will be fixed in future runs of the board).

In extreme paranoia mode, I could shield the entire lock behind copper sheeting.

To create the gesture-recognition software, I once again turned to vibe coding. If you read my Hands On piece in the April 2026 issue of IEEE Spectrum on creating a teletext suite for ham radio, you’ll know I’ve been grappling with how vibe coding should be used in DIY projects, if at all. So this time, instead of letting Claude write all the software, I confined it to writing just two support libraries, which you can find in our online repository at https://github.com/IEEESpectrumHandsOn.

One library is in charge of recording a lock gesture and saving it to the Teensy’s nonvolatile storage. The other library monitors the tile and reports whether or not a newly detected gesture passes a selectable threshold to be considered a match.

I wrote the top-level code myself to keep it as DIY as possible. This code handles things like a button that puts the system in gesture-recording mode after a brief delay, the indicator LED for recording mode, and the code that operates the physical locking mechanism.

Hall-effect sensors rely on a current passing through a p-type slab of silicon. A magnetic field passing through the silicon deflects charge carriers toward the edges of the slab, creating a voltage proportional to the field [left]. By looking at the intensities of the voltages across an 8-by-8 grid of sensors, the microcontroller can reconstruct a gesture [right]. James Provost

Of course, I needed something to lock to demonstrate my proof of concept. I bought a wooden craft box and removed the existing lid latch. I glued a notched beam inside the lid and built a mechanism that uses a servo motor to rotate another beam in and out of this notch. I will be the first to admit this mechanism goes beyond “simple” and into “simplistic,” but it’s sufficiently robust for my demo. The box has ample room for the magnetic imaging tile to be mounted against one wall, along with the Teensy and other supporting electronics. These include a battery pack, the recording button, and a small additional board with two NPN transistors. These convert the Teensy’s 3.3-volt control signals to a 5-V signal needed to drive the servo.

Once it was all put together, I soon discovered that the small size of the magnetic tile’s sensing area—just 3 centimeters square—made it easy to fit the tile inside the box but hard to do the unlock gesture on the outside so that it is read correctly. Marking the outline of the sensor area on the outside defeated the point of having a hidden lock, so instead I once again turned to mining my Irish heritage. I created a Celtic knotwork pattern that runs in a band across the front of the lockbox (I used an online knotwork generator and then projected and traced the pattern onto the box). Using the pattern as a camouflaged reference grid I can make a repeatable gesture within the confines of the sensor area. (To make the gestures I’m using a magnetic stylus borrowed from a ferrite core-memory kit we featured in 2022.)

There’s obvious room for improvement in any more serious installation. The biggest drawback currently is that if the box is locked when the battery runs out, you can’t open it again without breaking something. This could be solved by adding a hidden inductive charging coil. Nonetheless, the demo lockbox works well—now I just have to think what I should store in it!

Stephen Cass is the special projects editor at IEEE Spectrum. He currently helms Spectrum's Hands On column, and is also responsible for interactive projects such as the Top Programming Languages app. He has a bachelor's degree in experimental physics from Trinity College Dublin.

#3345. IEEE Xplore Digital Library Adds AI Assistant

The search tool offers summaries and verifiable source links

Claire Olini is the senior manager for IEEE Corporate and Strategic Product Launch and Engagement.

Michael Spada is director of IEEE Product Launch and Engagement Strategy.

IEEE recently released the IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite, built on the full text of millions of peer-reviewed publications in the IEEE Xplore Digital Library. The library offers full-text access to IEEE standards, journals, magazines, conference proceedings, and more.

Researchers who use the AI suite to search the digital library receive answers grounded in verified scientific results, ensuring a high level of accuracy and trust.

Powered by a proprietary AI system optimized for STEM literature, the suite introduces powerful, intelligent features within the digital library. The suite enables users to seamlessly search and discover articles to accelerate their comprehension of complex technical papers.

The system surfaces deep insights, replacing the typical keyword queries with natural, conversational research workflows.

As AI tools become more common in conducting research, IEEE collaborated to build the suite around a simple principle: Answers should be trustworthy, not just fast, says W. Clem Karl, vice president, IEEE Publication Services and Products.

“AI can be a highly effective and beneficial tool that can help researchers accelerate discovery, enhance decision-making, and surface new connections,” Karl says. “However, many AI engines present a great risk of hallucinating answers or introducing bias into otherwise credible research. With this in mind, IEEE has taken a responsible approach in our AI strategy by developing concrete safeguards to ensure our solution is rigorously grounded in scientific evidence that users can trust.

“As stewards of the scholarly record, we held the new AI engine to the same standards as the peer-reviewed research we publish: A researcher shouldn’t have to trust an answer; they should be able to verify the work behind it.”

The IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite was developed in close collaboration with global scientific and library communities.

The development process began with research into user needs and the challenges associated with existing AI research assistants. More than 3,000 testers—including engineers, scientists, and library information professionals—provided feedback to refine the AI engine and support research workflows.

To mitigate the risk of AI hallucinations, the search-retrieval process is limited to querying the millions of IEEE peer-reviewed full-text documents, alongside an expertly curated dataset of STEM metadata. If the AI tool is unable to find relevant scientific content within the defined dataset, it is designed to inform the user rather than generate fabricated answers.

“IEEE is committed to providing the technical community with a highly precise and reliable research experience,” says Steven Heffner, IEEE’s chief publication officer and managing director of IEEE Publications. “The IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite offers something unique in that it is the only AI research assistant that leverages both the full-text and metadata of IEEE’s peer-reviewed content, rather than abstracts alone.

“The difference is significant: Our internal testing showed a threefold increase in result quality and accuracy across every key metric. These results underscore how critical full-text grounding is for technical research.”

For more information about features and coverage, or to request a demo for your organization, visit the IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite website.

Claire Olini is the senior manager for IEEE Corporate and Strategic Product Launch and Engagement.

Michael Spada is director of IEEE Product Launch and Engagement Strategy.

#3343. iPhone Duo durability tested on unfolding livestream, now over 260,000 folds

CNET built a ‘Fold-a-Phone’ machine that’s been constantly folding and unfolding iPhone Duo for over a week to test durability, while livestreaming daily. Here’s how it’s going.

How durable is the iPhone Duo’s hinge and folding display? Several early reviews tried to answer that question, including in some cases by building machines that constantly folded and unfolded the device.

But perhaps the best test yet is still ongoing.

CNET built a custom ‘Fold-a-Phone’ machine that has been folding and unfolding the iPhone Duo 24 hours per day, 7 days a week for over a week now.

The issue with this is that it is kind of pointless, it is like the IP rating tests - very precise in lab conditions, but of limited value in the real world. As has been shown with all the recent foldables, in labs using machines they can do hundreds of thousands of folds. But in the real world, with varying conditions, dust, being put in and out of pockets, and with humans opening/closing, who do not repeat identically every time, these things will break more often. This isn't Apple related, it is just the reality of all foldables.

It’s livestreaming the process here on YouTube every weekday from 1-5 p.m. ET.

When the livestream wrapped up yesterday, iPhone Duo had hit just over 260,000 folds.

So far, the hinge and crease seem to be holding up extremely well. But CNET says it will continue testing daily until at least November 20 to see if anything might change over time.

#3342. After the Midterm Rally, the Dow Is on Track to Beat the Nasdaq for the First Time Since 2022. Here's What History Says Could Come Next.

The Dow tends to outperform the Nasdaq during growth stock-driven sell-offs.

In the first market session following the midterm elections, the Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI -0.46%) gained 3% -- well ahead of the S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.31%) and Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC +1.09%). As of market close on Nov. 4, the Dow is up 11% year-to-date (YTD) -- ahead of the Nasdaq Composite's 10.7% gain. Which is a stark contrast from where the indexes were just one month ago, when the Nasdaq was outperforming the Dow by more than ten percentage points.

Here's why the Dow is outpacing the Nasdaq and where the indexes could be headed from here.

Democrats retaking the House and Senate could lead to stricter artificial intelligence (AI) regulation that could slow the AI data center build-out. But the Nasdaq was already in a steep drawdown leading up to midterms. Higher interest rates make borrowing capital to fund AI spending more expensive. A sell-off in the semiconductor industry, paired with brutal drawdowns in major stocks like Alphabet (GOOG +0.78%) (GOOGL +0.78%), was weighing on the index.

Investors have grown increasingly concerned with capital expenditures (capex) going toward AI -- especially from companies like Alphabet, Amazon (AMZN -0.35%), and Meta Platforms that have turned free cash flow (FCF) negative. A lot of that capex is funneling toward technology infrastructure, networking equipment, custom AI chips, and other long-term data center costs.

For the AI build-out to be sustainable, spending has to show a return on investment for the cloud giants and frontier models such as OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude. Anthropic could go public as soon as mid-November. Anthropic will face far more scrutiny under the public markets' microscope than it did as a private company. And if investors view its compute spending as excessive, that could add further doubt to the broader AI investment thesis -- which affects the Nasdaq Composite much more than the S&P 500 or the Dow.

Given its higher weighting in value stocks and blue-chip dividend stocks, the Dow tends to hold up better than the Nasdaq during times of uncertainty or tech-driven sell-offs. However, investors should be aware that comparing today's Dow to past versions of the index can be misleading.

The Dow has just 30 components compared to thousands in the Nasdaq Composite. Since 2020, the Dow has added Salesforce, Honeywell Technologies, Amgen, Amazon, Nvidia, Sherwin-Williams, and Alphabet – replacing ExxonMobil, RTX, Pfizer, Walgreens Boots Alliance, Intel, Dow, and Verizon Communications. So the Dow isn't as value- or industrial-driven as it used to be. It's still less tech-heavy than the Nasdaq, but it's also more of a growth index too.

The Dow is also price-weighted, meaning that the companies with the highest stock prices, rather than those with the highest market cap, carry the most weight. In the Nasdaq, Apple, Nvidia, and Microsoft are the most heavily weighted components because they have the largest market caps. Those three stocks are also in the Dow, but all are weighted less than Goldman Sachs because of its high stock price and lack of stock splits since going public in 1999. This weighting structure further complicates the Dow's moves.

The last time the Dow outperformed the Nasdaq was in 2022, when the Nasdaq plunged 33.1%, and the Dow fell 8.8%.

Including that brutal decline, you would have still been better off buying the Nasdaq on Jan. 1, 2022 than the Dow, as the Nasdaq is up 68% since then compared to 56% for the Dow -- even when factoring in dividends.

History says that the six months following midterm elections tend to be a seasonally excellent period for the stock market. And over the long term, trading in and out of stocks and sectors based on political outcomes is a grave mistake.

A far better approach is to build your portfolio around fundamentally sound companies with a runway for future earnings growth. Despite being more volatile than the Dow, the Nasdaq has produced superior gains over the last three-, five-, 10-, and 20-year periods because the earnings growth rates of major Nasdaq companies have been impeccable.

While AI capex is definitely a strain on FCF for hyperscalers, it's a mistake to overlook the operational efficiency of top Nasdaq stocks. According to data from Yardeni Research, analyst estimates for the S&P 500 annual operating margin are in the mid- to high-teens. Meanwhile, Apple is converting 33 cents of every dollar in trailing 12-month revenue into operating income. Alphabet, Microsoft, Broadcom, and Nvidia are even better. Amazon achieved a 13.9% operating margin in its latest quarter -- an all-time high for the company. But its operating margin is dragged down by its retail business. In Amazon's latest quarter, Amazon Web Services had an operating margin of 38.7%.

Safe sectors like consumer staples and healthcare can rally during periods of uncertainty due to their recession-resistant nature. These sectors can be excellent for risk-averse investors, those focused on capital preservation over appreciation, or income investors looking to supplement income in retirement. But tech-focused companies will likely continue to outperform the Dow over the long term because they have more opportunities to invest in high-potential ideas that offset the ideas that don't work out. A consumer staple like Coca-Cola developing or acquiring another beverage brand has a far different risk and potential reward profile than paradigm-shifting technologies that fundamentally change businesses and everyday life.

Investors should continue to scrutinize AI capex spending. But the cash burn won't continue forever. If AI investments begin showing returns for hyperscalers and, downstream, for software companies, it will create a ripple effect through the Nasdaq and, in turn, justify more spending on compute and AI infrastructure.

With midterms in the rearview, now is a good time for investors to conduct a portfolio review to ensure they have high conviction in the Nasdaq stocks they do own. Volatility is simply the price of admission for the tech-heavy Nasdaq. But over the long term, high-quality growth stocks will likely continue rewarding patient investors far more than safe stocks.

#3341. iOS 27.3 gives Apple One’s high-end tier a compelling upgrade

iOS 27.3 is coming next month and is packed with new features, including some that make Apple One Premier more compelling than ever.

Apple One launched in 2019 with Individual, Family, and Premier plans. And in the seven years since, the service bundle has stayed remarkably consistent.

Every plan has always included Apple Music, Apple TV, Apple Arcade, and iCloud+. And the high-end Premier option adds Apple News+ and Fitness+ alongside more iCloud storage.

Apple News+ has gotten a lot better over the years. Following the New York Times playbook, Apple has added daily puzzle games, food-focused content like recipes, and audio stories, all while continuing to improve the basic news experience.

Apple Fitness+ keeps improving too, but there’s an upgrade in iOS 27.3 that makes it far more compelling in my view: Gym Strength.

Built-in video demonstrations accompany your personalized plan, making strength training accessible even for newcomers. And you can track your progress in the app, with key Apple Watch integration too.

I’ve used Fitness+ plenty and enjoyed it, but a comprehensive strength plan like this was a big gap in the service previously. With iOS 27.3 though, Fitness+ takes a big leap forward and makes Apple One Premier more compelling than ever.

Also relevant: with the new HomeView product and other Apple Home accessories almost here, Apple One Premier’s support for Apple Intelligence video summaries and clips with HomeKit Secure Video becomes more valuable. All of this together amounts to a stronger-than-ever Premier plan.

Apple One starts at $21.95/month and includes services like Apple TV, Apple Music, iCloud+, and more.
