The queues are overstated. The public is concerned. When they talk about 75% of people don't want a data center developed in their community, I don't even know what the question really means because the community might mean next door. But if they're developed by our power plant like the one that we're developing next to our Comanche Peak plant, there was a town hall held this week with Amazon and members of our site, and it was very well received. That's a data center going next to an industrial facility, obviously, our nuclear power plant. The public, I don't think has a strong reaction against data centers being next to power plants.

The other thing the public struggles with is it's different to have one data center somewhere in the area. But if you think 10 are coming to your area, which is what happens with these overstated queues, you get a reaction. So I think we're all on the same page with respect to raising the bar, fitting the queues and getting to the real projects that are going to move it forward. And Governor-elect Hinojosa on new circuits and some of her early commentary wants to see Texas grow. She just wants to see the benefits of that growth be evenly distributed as do we.

So I actually view where we sit today is just clarity of some sort, not having it tied us directly to an election season is going to be beneficial to taking some of the noise. I think it's been overdone, as you mentioned, James, in the last couple of days. That doesn't change our outlook. In fact, if anything, you heard Kris talk about the buyback and leaning in there, it can create opportunities for Vistra. Our customer conversations, and I'll give Stacey a chance to comment on a later question because I'm sure we're going to get it. Customer conversations have been consistent throughout.

And I actually think this is going to provide some opportunities to bring some of these to completion. So overall, we're positive on the trajectory of where we can go as it relates to our business opportunities.

Operator: Next up will be Michael Sullivan with Wolfe.

Michael Sullivan: I want to appreciate the kind of updated free cash flow per share outlook and understand there's a bunch of assumptions. But maybe can you just help us with thinking about kind of the core power price outlook there, like just given you're hedged near term, ERCOT is in pretty steep contango. So just thinking about the puts and the takes of what power prices are doing to that outlook as you step from '27 to '30.

James Burke: Yes. And Michael, I was trying to -- maybe I wasn't as clear as I needed to be. We are not making any assumptions about power price recoveries. It reflects the curves as you see them as noted in our hedge profiles and just kind of stepping that forward based off public available information. Now we think the near term on this is really going to be a function of how does Texas get back into gear in terms of hooking up load. We know there is load that's approved to energize, but it has not been allowed to energize. There's been the audits. As you know, there's been some permit holds at TCEQ.

We think by the long term, the '29, '30 period, we think we still end up in a similar place for ERCOT. So I think it's more about this near term where we see a little bit more of this pricing pressure. There's a chance for ERCOT to even go better than where the curves are even out, even though it is contango to go better than that from a pricing standpoint if we kind of get our mojo back, and I think we can. And so -- but we're not making any special assumptions as it relates to get to that $24.

Michael Sullivan: Okay. Great. That's very helpful. And then I just wanted to ask the latest on the contracting environment for you all, given what we've seen from some peers, like on the nuclear front, we've seen Constellation continue to leverage uprates. You have a couple of those still available yourself. And then just today, some news on gas finally from someone. So just how you're thinking about puts and takes there.

James Burke: Sure, sure. Michael, I'm going to let Stacey jump in because I'm going to send it to the person who's doing the bulk of these negotiations on a daily basis. And thanks for your question on that.

Stacey Dore: Yes. Michael, thanks for the question. We -- we've said this for a while, but we just continue to see interest in Vistra's assets and Vistra's capabilities, and we're involved in multiple conversations around our existing assets, around new build. We continue to just see a large appetite for these kinds of projects. And I think you've continued to see the hyperscalers, as an example, talk about increasing their CapEx spend. So there certainly is no slowdown on that front. As typical, we're not going to comment on the timing of new deals, but we're confident in our ability to execute additional nuclear PPAs. We still have not contracted Beaver Valley.

We still have not contracted the second part of Comanche Peak. There's an upgrade potential at Comanche Peak as well. So we have a lot of megawatts still to contract on nuclear. We're in a number of conversations about our existing gas plants as well as new gas build, and we feel confident on our ability to execute there. And in fact, in this quarter, we announced a PPA for our existing Odessa gas plant in Texas. So I think we've demonstrated an ability to execute on existing gas plants, and we believe there's more to come on that front as well.

The load interconnection process does continue to be a timing constraint on particularly the gas asset projects because for those types of PPAs, the customer does typically want a grid connection. And so that's why we continue to advocate for thinning the queues and raising the bar on the load interconnection queue so that we can begin to get approval for load interconnections that would support additional gas plant deals as well. So we just feel really good about our opportunity set. It's busier than ever.

And it allows -- the fact that we have so many opportunities in our pipeline allows us to also be selective about the counterparties that we work with, about the projects that we work on. And so we really prioritize the opportunities that we have the best chance of execution on as well as the ones that meet, of course, our return targets and our economic objectives. So we feel really good about it. We're excited about the months and years to come to serve these customers.

James Burke: Yes. And Michael, I'm just going to add real quick as a supportive point to what Stacey is saying is that over the course of the year, there's also been a lot of concern about how will the PJM rules evolve and is that going to limit our ability to do contracting with existing or even colocation. We've seen through time, these things never play out at the level that the initial concern is. So there's usually an immediate reaction and then we work our way through it. I think that's happening right now in PJM.

And so I do think that the opportunity set with existing assets, even though it does still take time to get through the study process, but FERC is trying to accelerate that as well. So I do think it's been choppy. It's probably choppier than anybody would like. But when you see that settle, the dust settle, the opportunity set continues to be clear, and that's why we're bullish about being able to bring some of these across the finish line.

Operator: Your next question will come from the line of Rinny Singh with Bank of America.

Rinny Singh: I guess to just add on to the previous question. As you think about these customer negotiations, and you mentioned that grid interconnection is a key constraint. How do you think about the economics for them and then the willingness to be flexible or add additionality? What's, I guess, the bars that -- and the conversations you're having on that front?

Stacey Dore: Yes. Thanks, Rinny, for the question. So these customers are the hyperscalers as well as the model companies and other data center and developers. They're all somewhat unique in their priorities and their wishes for the types of projects that they want to work on. So it's really hard to just group it all into one bucket. But I would say -- they all -- one consistent theme is they all really do want to be on the grid as quickly as they can. But I think the grid interconnection process across our markets, which has been slower than anyone wants it to be, does -- has resulted in customers expressing a lot of interest in bridge solutions.

And so you will see and you have seen projects that will start with a behind-the-meter solution until there can be a grid connection. And so that obviously is an expensive -- a more expensive solution for these customers than just starting with the grid connection. And so they certainly are showing a willingness to pay for that. From Vistra's perspective, any project that we do really just needs to -- needs to meet our return thresholds, which we've expressed as mid-teens returns and/or higher. And that's what we go after, and that's what we've been able to achieve and better. So that's how we think about the economic opportunity there.

In terms of flexibility, the customers have really come a long way in being willing and able to consider being flexible. We were very pleased to see that FERC struck down PJM's IRAS proposal, which was going to require customers to bring brand-new generation capacity, megawatt for megawatt for any new load that they brought. And we consistently said over time that, that's not the right way to approach the flexibility question. These customers are willing to be flexible. But as FERC recognized, discriminating against existing resources on the grid by requiring a strict BYOG policy is not really the right way to encourage resource adequacy and reliability on the grid today.

And so we think the elimination of the IRS proposal really has given customers the additional clarity that they need to move forward with projects where -- they have a variety of options. They can bring some additionality with new generation. They can choose instead to just bring backup generation and connect to an existing plant so that they can be available during emergencies for the grid, which is what Amazon is doing at Comanche Peak. They can also choose to just curtail their load. And so they -- those choices should be theirs to make.

And the markets, in our view, should support the customer choice as to how to make sure that they can be flexible and support the grid during times of need.

Rinny Singh: Very helpful. And then I guess, can I just ask on the Texas legislature. Jim, I think you mentioned that all these governors and they just kind of want these deals to be done right in a respectable way and benefiting the community. So as we get to the Texas legislative process, what do you think is kind of going to be addressed? And what do you expect, I guess, to see to, I guess, get to this more realistic view of what can actually come on the grid?

James Burke: Yes, Rinny, thank you. I think, well, before we even get to the leg session, there's a process underway, which we expect will continue, which is the audit process that Governor Abbott started, and there's been some additional RFIs issued to large loads to complete the questions and complete the information being sought. Whether that leads to some of these projects dropping out of the queue or not, I don't know. But the intent, I think, of that audit and ultimately, the review that's being done is to make sure that complete applications are being used to then establish this Batch Zero.

Obviously, the permit hold that's been in place, we expect when it was initially put in place that it might be lifted as part of the sort of mid-December timing for completing the audit work. Again, back to the comments we've made on this call and previous calls, we would be comfortable if the bar continue to be raised on projects so that doing projects the right way is rewarded and that those projects get higher allocations and they get moved to earlier in the interconnection process. So even before we get into the session, I think the business as usual could potentially thin some of this by this mid-December time frame.

I think the 765 kV projects are going to continue to move forward. I think that's important because that's part of the backbone of being able to energize some of the Batch Zero, not all of them, but some of the Batch Zero projects. I think if the 765s keep moving forward, and I think the third East-West line has a chance to be approved here by the end of the year by the PUC. That now establishes the foundation for the load being able to be hooked up and served with existing generation on the system as some new generation continues to be built out.

You're then going to want that load to come on to the system and share in the cost of the 765. And that's also part of the focus of the Public Utility Commission is to create a tariff that large loads would be committing to that would have some minimum take requirements and a duration requirement so that costs don't get pushed on to residential customers. So there's actually a lot already underway with the PUC and ERCOT that I think is going to set the stage heading into the legislative session that I think will give some comfort to lawmakers and the governor elect that the PUC and ERCOT are thinking about some of these issues.

And then what the legislature ends up deciding to do is hard to say. We don't have a crystal ball. Obviously, with sort of a split House and Senate, it's unclear what legislative environment we're going to actually be in. But what I like about this issue is there's not really that much of an argument happening between Republicans and Democrats on this issue. This issue has general concern for both parties to get it right. And so whether they let PUC and ERCOT more manage that or they decide to be a little bit more hands-on during the legislative session, I think it's too early to call.

But the direction of travel is to raise the bar and do high-quality projects. And we're supportive of that. And I think the legislature is going to look for ways to add to what the PUC and ERCOT are doing if they don't think it's sufficient. But we're supportive. We're supportive and we've been supportive of raising the bar.

Operator: Your next question will come from David Arcaro with Morgan Stanley.

David Arcaro: Maybe a little bit following on that line of questions. I was curious to the extent there is any effort to move forward with something like a moratorium on data centers next year in Texas. I was wondering how you're thinking about whether there could be any risk to the Comanche Peak contract and construction that's going on there? And maybe more broadly, whether that could impact some of your efforts in the Batch Zero process if there's potential risk of delay or push out there.

James Burke: Yes. David, I'll tell you, if Texas decides to just go down a moratorium, it would be problematic, I think, for lots of customers, not just our Comanche Peak project. I don't know what form that would actually take. So that would take some potential legislative activity, I think, to have something that would create that type of a significant limiter. As we noted, construction has started with Comanche Peak, and we expect high-quality projects to move forward. So I think it's more about raising the bar than I think the conceptual moratorium. I mean you heard the Governor-elect say she wants Texas to grow.

The moratorium, I think where this language has come in, obviously, even audits were kind of viewed as a moratorium. Any time you've got to study something and clear a bar, it does take some time to do that. But I have not heard, I have not heard the Governor-elect, and I haven't heard the legislature say they do not want Texas to have any of this load. So clearly, if someone changed their mind and the whole legislature decided to go along with it, that would be difficult, right, for us as a power company, but certainly difficult for people that are bringing hundreds of billions of dollars of capital to the state of Texas.

And I just think that is where the conversations just kind of continue to sort of fester a little bit out of concern. That is not the conversations we're having with leaders, and it's not the conversations we're having with members that are returning for this upcoming session. So I just don't entertain that, David, because I really just think that's a bridge too far from where the dialogue is at this point.

David Arcaro: Got it. Yes. That's helpful. That makes sense. And then maybe shifting over to PJM. I was wondering if you might be able to give your latest maybe progress and thinking around the RBP and some of your bilateral efforts there. What's -- what are the prospects for those? Have those changed as the timing has shifted kind of into next year?

James Burke: Sure. I'm going to let Stacey comment on that, David. I think the -- I'll just say that at the highest level, we've been supportive of the emphasis on bilaterals and markets moving towards contracting for capacity and energy and not being as dependent on a single clearing price of a centralized auction. And I think the pushout of the RBP a little bit from a timing standpoint can help facilitate some of those bilateral conversations. But even if it's not to new projects, just what we've already done with Meta, what we're doing with other conversations is contracting even with existing. I just think that starts to put the onus on the load-serving entities like Vistra.

And I think that's a responsibility that we accept in serving customers from residential to large commercial industrial and data centers. So all of that from a theme standpoint, we're supportive of. And Stacey, I'll let you comment about how we're thinking about the bilateral process.

Stacey Dore: Yes. thanks for the question. We continue -- we do continue to have a lot of bilateral discussions in PJM. As I mentioned earlier, I think the FERC striking down the IRAS proposal actually was helpful in that it kind of removed one layer of uncertainty for customers about how they might want to contract and kind of what the rules of the road might be around that. And so I think that was helpful.

Pushing out the RBP to next year is also helpful because it just gives more time for those bilateral discussions to really result in agreements and also more time, frankly, for anyone who's thinking about building new generation in PJM to understand what the network upgrade costs might be and the generation interconnection costs might be, which was a concern we had expressed about the timing -- the previous timing of the RBP being in September is that there just wasn't a lot of certainty about what those costs are. So it's hard to build into your contracting process when you don't know what those costs are. So I think all of that is positive.

I do think that customers still have a big incentive to do bilateral contracts in relation to the RBP because, as you know, if you have a bilateral contract, you can present it to PJM as a means of reducing the ultimate procurement target for the RBP and therefore, reducing a customer's cost allocation responsibility as well for the RBP. So I think we'll -- we're optimistic that we'll see a number of bilateral contracts in the market that are presented to reduce the ultimate RBP target.

And frankly, the smaller the target is the better because it means that the bilateral contracts have really satisfied the forecasted need as opposed to using this kind of bifurcated RBP process, which, as a matter of principle, we typically wouldn't support, but we think it's going to end up being small enough that it mitigates that risk. So we continue to have active conversations about uprates and other opportunities across our fleet as a means to reduce that RBP ultimate target. So we feel good about that.

Operator: Next question will come from Paul Zimbardo with Jefferies.

Paul Zimbardo: Apologies if I missed it earlier. The timing change on Helix investment potential, if you could discuss that a little bit. And I know you've mentioned a few times the mid-teens target returns. And I know IRRs are not the same as free cash flow yield, but just using your $24 in the stock price, you get to a number higher than mid-teens on buying back your stock. So just curious if kind of your return thresholds have changed with the stock price.

Kristopher Moldovan: Yes. On the second one, I think -- we view the $1 billion a year, obviously, that's something that we view as a commitment that we've made. Obviously, it's not set in stone, but I would say it's pretty close. We continue to weigh all projects against our share buybacks. And so as our stock price has come under -- has been challenged the last couple of days, I mean, that moves the needle. But we also have a lot of projects, as we said in the prepared remarks, that are with existing assets that have little cost for us and have extremely high returns.

Some of the deals that we've struck have almost 0 or basically 0 cost, and we get premium on those transactions. So we're going to continue to look at opportunities. We're going to still try to stay relatively balanced, but we do compare all opportunities against share buybacks.

James Burke: And Paul, what I would add is these customer conversations, they can be 6 months, 12 months in duration. Our stock might move $30 in 2 days. We're not going to work with long-term customer relationships and negotiate around $1 or $2 a megawatt hour trying to just react to the stock buyback opportunity in the moment. This is a franchise, and we have a reputation, and we're going to build a book of business that will also be a contracted book of business, which I think also lowers the discount rate ultimately. So it's a little different in horizon to be thinking about it relative to our free cash flow yield and a buyback at a point in time.

Having said that, you can bet that's the conversation we have as a management team and with our Board, and that's why the Board was comfortable authorizing a larger share repurchase to take us through that 2028 period because it's not lost on us that as we think about what are we going to do to build that next incremental value, the hurdles do rise when you have this kind of an alternative for the cash. So it's -- there's a tension there. The last thing I'll say is on Helix, that's really about a draw schedule. So Helix is not about us just pushing cash to them to sit.

It's what are the projects that Helix is driving where they're going to have a capital call. We're working with Helix on a number of projects. So we're just assuming that from a timing standpoint, it's going to fall more into next year than this year. But that's not surprising just given all the things we've been talking about how the political environment has slowed down some of the activities in any of the markets really. And we see that picking back up, and that's why we moved the capital assumption.

Paul Zimbardo: Okay. No, that's very helpful. And I know it's a tougher one to answer, just given the volatility. I appreciate that. And then the last one, just to check in. I know you kind of -- I don't want to put words in your mouth, it sounds like you acknowledge maybe softer power pricing dynamic in Texas in the near-term years. Does that influence kind of the hedging profile that you pursue, whether kind of more hedges in -- I know you have a lot in '27, but maybe a '28, '29.

James Burke: It does, Paul. In fact, with the 78% hedged for '28, we are much less hedged in ERCOT than the 78%. So we do not look at the curves for 2028 and feel a need to be moving a lot of power at this point in time. And I do think as we see what the pace of play is for hooking up load in 2027 and seeing what the pent-up demand is because the utilities are reporting on their calls the pent-up demand that they see. Some of it is actually not AI related. It's manufacturing, it's government, it's oil and gas.

If we start to see that pick up pace, then I think you might see some response in 2028, and we're certainly more open in 2028 in ERCOT than we are in the other markets.

Operator: Our next question will come from Jeremy Tonet with JPMorgan.

Vrathan Reddy: This is Vrathan Reddy on for Jeremy. I think it's been hit on a couple of times, but I just wanted to ask, PJM versus ERCOT, is there any change you're seeing in terms of the customer interest, one versus the other? And if that's -- I guess, just broadly how that's evolved post election?

James Burke: Well, I'm going to let Stacey take that one. It's a lot to digest just postelection. But maybe leading into the election and post election, Stacey, can you provide some context on the relative attractiveness.

Stacey Dore: Yes. Look, Texas continues to be attractive to these customers. Any given day, of course, they're looking at the political environment. They're looking at some of the guardrail proposals and they're trying to decide what the risk profile is across these different markets. But frankly, almost every market and every state that we're operating in as well as states we're not operating in where they may be pursuing projects has been looking at these similar types of guardrails. So across the country, states and local bodies are looking at things like water usage and land usage and tax incentives. So I really think -- I know the election was a surprise to some in Texas, in particular.

But I really think if you take a step back, there's not a higher risk profile in Texas versus other places that are considering these same types of guardrails. And in fact, we believe Texas continues to be one of the easiest places to get things built and will continue to be so in the long run. So leading up to the election, we did not see a change in customer behavior of Texas versus PJM. We just got questions about both, and we continue to get questions about both. Ohio, as an example, had a change of administration as well, and they're in PJM. So again, I don't see Texas as standing out as peculiar in this regard.

And I think customers across the country are just looking at their opportunities, looking at, number one, speed to power; number two, where can they be welcomed into the communities; and number three, how much political support are they going to get. And so I think that continues to be the case and everybody is trying to assess their alternatives. But for Vistra, the good news is we operate across almost 20 states in all of the competitive markets, and we have opportunities in all of those markets to serve these customers. So we really try to follow their lead and also help them navigate some of these political and regulatory hurdles that we've all been dealing with.

I think the fact that we had the election and it's now over and the results are clear, as Jim referenced earlier, is actually a help to us, and it will be a help to us in getting a lot of our projects across the finish line because we can now kind of understand a little bit more about what the rules of the road are. But to have -- we'll continue to have regulation that comes into play. And the kinds of customers that we deal with, and this is kind of with reference to my earlier comment about us being able to be a bit choosy about the customers we work with.

The customers that we work with, they're going to clear this higher bar that policymakers are putting into place. And that's one reason we advocate to raise the bar because our projects like the one we have with Amazon, the one we have with Meta, the PPAs that we have with Meta, our projects clear those -- all of those bars by far. And so we're not concerned about the regulation. We just want certainty and clarity to continue to come and then our projects will be able to move forward.

Operator: This concludes our Q&A session. I will now turn the call back to Jim Burke for closing remarks.

James Burke: Yes. Thank you, everybody, for joining. I especially want to thank our Vistra team for their continued execution and service to our customers and communities. Once again, we want to welcome the Cogentrix team. And for our investors, we know this is a very dynamic time, and our team is very focused on delivering. We do appreciate your interest in Vistra, and we hope to see you in person soon. Have a great rest of your day and a nice weekend.

Operator: The call has concluded. Thank you for joining. You may now disconnect.

#3299. Apple expected to bid for F1 streaming rights in more countries, says Formula 1 CEO

On the latest earnings call for F1’s parent company Liberty Media, the CEO of Formula 1 Stefano Domenicali said that both parties are happy with the US deal, and he expects that Apple will bid for rights in more countries as the opportunities become available.

F1 has previously expressed that they are not currently looking for one media partner to take global broadcast rights for the sport; they want a portfolio of deals, picking the best partners for each geographic market.

We have already seen this play out in the United Kingdom, with broadcaster Sky renewing its deal for F1 rights through 2034, seemingly locking Apple out of that region. So, despite the apparent demand, Apple will not be able to just walk in and take over the future of the sport’s worldwide distribution.

However, it seems the league is open to striking more deals with Apple in certain markets.

On the earnings call, in response to a question from an investor about Apple’s interest, Domenicali said “this is part of our discussion, if there are opportunities that can be in other markets, they will do it … they’re going to do it as soon as these opportunities will be open for them”.

Liberty Media CEO Derek Chang said they continue to think about what new innovation they can bring to the product side, and noted that “Apple as a potential bidder in other markets is helpful” for their business.

As a reminder, all Formula 1 races are available to watch live and on-demand with an Apple TV subscription, in the United States. The company recently launched a Dolby Atmos audio track for its F1 streams, as well as expanded support for Multiview on more platforms, including iPhone Duo.

Just last month, Amazon's personal AI shopping agent got a major upgrade that gave users over 100 new ways to utilize it. Being able to create lists, ask questions about various Amazon subscriptions & benefits, manage those same subscriptions, update the instructions for incoming deliveries, get answers to one’s billing & payment questions and more are all now possible through Alexa for Shopping.

Now, Alexa for Shopping has gotten yet another major upgrade. And this time, it gives users the ability to have a direct chat with it right from their text messages without even having to open the Amazon app or site. Here’s how that new nifty shopping feature works and who can currently access it.

Texting with Alexa for Shopping is the latest feature that has come to Amazon’s AI shopping agent and is currently rolling out to a select number of US customers through invitations.

And over the coming weeks, even more Amazon customers will have that option expanded to them in the same manner. Amazon shoppers should keep an eye out for a text message inviting them to try out the new Alexa for Shopping feature—other users can check out this landing page and sign up to get updates on when more invites for that latest update begin rolling out.

Amazon has listed a wide range of best-use cases for users who’ll begin texting Alexa for Shopping. Those examples include texting Alexa to begin producing your weekly shopping list, looking up a birthday gift you need by a certain day, sharing a photo of a piece of clothing & asking the AI agent to find similar options and making sure it resupplies your pet food supply after letting it know you’ve run out.

Attendees in Region 4 learn about AI, cybersecurity, and more

Siva Rama Krishna Varma Bayyavarapu is an IEEE senior member and secretary of the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter.

To help engineers keep up with emerging technologies such as AI, cloud computing, and sustainable infrastructure, and learn how they can be applied in practice, the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter recently launched its Tech Talk Series.

The live webinar series connects IEEE members, undergrad and graduate students, and engineering professionals from IEEE Region 4 with industry practitioners. The monthly sessions have covered AI governance and security, agentic systems, and related topics. The sessions featured speakers from Apple, software company Tavant, and cybersecurity concern Zscaler.

Upcoming sessions and registration details are available on the IEEE Region 4 virtual events calendar.

Rather than presenting on emerging technologies only at a conceptual level, speakers discussed the design decisions behind specific tools and systems, how the systems are structured, and implementation challenges. They also shared lessons learned from using the tools in their daily work.

Sessions also include technical walkthroughs and practical examples.

The live format allows attendees to discuss and compare their approaches when evaluating and implementing new technologies with those used by other organizations.

The organizers chose to make the series virtual so that chapter members and other attendees could participate in technical discussions with engineers from major technology companies and eliminate the need to travel.

For young professionals, the sessions connect what they’ve learned in a classroom with the realities of the workplace.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Attendees learn how practitioners approach projects such as system architecture, reliability, security, governance, and product delivery. For experienced professionals, the talks offer a forum to examine new ways of designing, securing, and operating software systems, and compare technical approaches. They can ask questions relevant to systems being evaluated or deployed within their organization.

The most recent webinar, Feeding and Fencing AI Agents: Engineering Governed Agentic Systems on Real-Time Data, featured Gajendra Babu Thokala, a senior engineering leader at Apple in Seattle.

The IEEE senior member explained how teams can move beyond adding isolated AI features to applications and instead build governed AI-agent systems that use real-time business data to complete multistep business workflows.

Another recent session, Building AI Native Products: A Playbook for Agentic Systems, explored how products built around AI agents differ from traditional software. It also covered how agentic systems can help users complete multistep tasks and workflows. IEEE Senior Member Sandeep Shivam, a product and technology leader at Tavant in Dallas, led the webinar.

Those two sessions illustrate the series’ purpose: helping participants understand what a technology can do and what is required to use it responsibly.

Future sessions are being planned on areas including enterprise AI, software reliability, and responsible AI usage. In addition to speakers from technology companies, the chapter also plans to invite speakers from startups, universities, and research organizations.

Upcoming sessions are expected to cover cloud platforms, enterprise integrations, and the responsible development of AI systems.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

#3296. TSMC is weighing a move into AI memory chips at Nvidia’s request

The world's largest chipmaker is drafting plans for 3D DRAM as an AI-driven memory shortage drags on.

The TSMC logo on one of the company’s factories in the Central Taiwan Science Park, Taichung.

TSMC is considering making advanced memory chips and has begun drafting plans for 3D DRAM at Nvidia’s request, The Information reports. It would put TSMC up against Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron as AI demand keeps memory scarce.

TSMC is considering making advanced memory chips, Bloomberg reported on Friday, citing The Information. The move would give the world’s largest chipmaker an even bigger share of the AI hardware supply chain.

TSMC recently began drafting plans to make 3D DRAM, which stacks memory cells vertically to pack in more capacity, at the request of Nvidia, its biggest customer. It could build new factories or buy an existing plant and convert it, Reuters reported, citing The Information.

The work is led by Hsu Kuo-chin, a TSMC vice president who oversees advanced packaging, according to the report. TSMC and Nvidia did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Memory is in short supply as AI data centres soak it up, sending prices soaring. Micron expects the shortage to last into 2028, and Apple raised Mac and iPad prices in June, citing memory costs. Some customers want their own supply: Elon Musk is planning a $55B chip plant to cut his reliance on Micron.

TSMC is already moving closer to memory. In October, Nvidia reportedly asked Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron to build the base layer of its custom HBM memory on TSMC’s 3nm process. Making DRAM itself would put TSMC up against all three, including SK Hynix, which plans to spend $720B on new plants.

#3295. Report: iPad shipments drop 27.5% as global tablet market plunges in Q3

Despite global iPad shipments dropping 27.5% year-over-year in the third calendar quarter, Apple maintained its lead in the tablet market, according to a new report released today. Here are the details.

According to a new report published by Omdia (via MacMagazine), Apple shipped 11,5 million iPads during Q3 2026, accounting for 36% of all shipments.

Compared to Q3 2025, that was a 27.5% drop in shipments, and a 2.2 percentage-point decline in market share.

For context, the global tablet market saw a 23% year-over-year drop, with total shipments going from 41.8 million to 32.2 million units. Omdia noted this was the lowest level in nearly three years.

As for Apple’s competitors, Samsung remained in second place with 16.9% market share, followed by Lenovo with 12.7%, Xiaomi with 7.3%, and Huawei with 5.7%.

Bring xcode,terminal and ability to download apps from anywhere on iPad Pro!

When it comes to shipment growth, Lenovo was the only company among the top five to post a positive result, up 11.9% year over year. Huawei saw the steepest decline at 43%, followed by Apple at 27.5%, Samsung at 21.7%, and Xiaomi at 10.6%.

Commenting on the results, Omdia Research Manager Himani Mukka said supply constraints are “limiting vendors’ ability to deliver meaningful specification upgrades, leaving fewer compelling differences between new models and their predecessors.”

“As a result,” she added, “consumers are increasingly expected to delay purchases until more substantial improvements become available.”

#3294. Amazon's CEO Andy Jassy Just Announced Huge News for Amazon Investors

AWS could be a $1 trillion division in a decade.

Andy Jassy is the CEO of Amazon (AMZN -0.35%), succeeding founder Jeff Bezos a few years ago. Jassy used to lead Amazon Web Services (AWS), and his appointment as CEO a few years ago clearly indicated that this was the direction Amazon's business was heading. Bezos was correct in this assessment, as AWS has become a huge part of Amazon's business.

However, it's about to get even bigger. Andy Jassy made a bold prediction during Amazon's third-quarter earnings call that investors need to digest, as it could have big implications for the stock.

CEO Andy Jassy Amazon: Image source: Amazon.com Inc.

During Amazon's Q3 earnings call, Jassy noted that AWS could grow by more than 40% in both 2027 and 2028, driven by significant investments in the platform. Over the next five to 10 years, that could grow to become a $1 trillion business. For reference, AWS, Amazon's cloud computing unit, grew at 39% in Q3, and its trailing-12-month sales totaled $161 billion.

That's huge news for investors, but what does it mean for the stock?

The biggest thing investors must realize is just how much better of a business AWS is than commerce. Commerce businesses in general operate on razor-thin margins, and while Amazon is one of the best at maximizing its margins, it's still much lower than what AWS puts up. During Q3, AWS' operating margin reached 39% on operating income of $17.8 billion. Its North American commerce segment delivered $8.7 billion in operating income on a 7.7% margin.

That's a huge mismatch, and it shows why Amazon is investing in AWS so heavily: It has a superior operating profile. As Amazon leans more heavily into AWS, it will be great news for the stock. Let's assume AWS hits a $1 trillion run rate a decade from now. If Amazon can maintain a 39% margin, that's $390 billion in operating income. Over the past 12 months, Amazon has produced $106 billion in operating income.

AMZN Operating Income (TTM) data by YCharts.

That means its operating income could more than quadruple over the next decade, which would result in huge returns for shareholders. AWS headed to $1 trillion in annual revenue would be huge news for investors, and if Jassy is right, could indicate that Amazon is a top stock to buy in the market now.

#3293. Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras

With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery

Advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated. The techniques reveal fine details in the sun’s corona, which is white in this image. The tiny pink shapes seen along portions of the edge of the blacked-out solar disk are prominences, which are extensions of relatively cool plasma that can jut out hundreds of thousands of kilometers into space.

The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza, it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing.

A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse.

In the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out.

“It will.” Miloslav Druckmüller glances calmly at his group of doctoral candidates, now making final checks of the equipment in preparation for totality. Here in Spain, on this 12th day of August, Druckmüller is getting ready for his 19th solar eclipse. He knows from long experience that weather can turn quickly when the moon’s shadow suddenly pushes the temperature down. Plus, there’s no sense in riling up the grad students any more than they already are.

Miloslav Druckmüller led the design and construction of a unique optical instrument that incorporates eight astrocameras. Each is equipped with a spectral filter for sensing and recording specific emission spectra from the solar corona. Each of those spectra, in turn, is associated with a particular ionic species of iron atoms. Because the temperature needed to ionize iron varies depending on the ionic species, analyzing the locations and relative abundance of these ionic species offers valuable insights into the distribution of heat in the corona.Václav Široký

During totality, the moon blocks the overwhelming glare of the solar disk, revealing delicate structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. Using custom-built telescope systems and image-processing techniques that Druckmüller has spent decades developing, the researchers aim to gain insights into the processes in this enigmatic region that is otherwise hard to study. In addition to imaging the visible coronal light, the team will try to track the dispersal of superhot ions of iron into interplanetary space, which could give rare insights into the pattern of heat emanating from the corona.

And they’ll have 107 seconds to do all that.

Druckmüller is a professor of mathematics and image processing at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic and a leading figure in the Solar Wind Sherpas, an international team that studies the sun’s corona during total eclipses. In the solar eclipse world, he is nothing short of a legend, albeit a reluctant one.

An image from Miloslav Druckmüller’s first solar-eclipse expedition, to Hungary, vividly shows Baily’s Beads. These elongated white lights along a piece of the left edge of the blacked-out solar disk are caused by beams of sunlight shining through gaps in the irregular lunar surface during the eclipse. The pink shapes are solar prominences, which are jets of plasma extending out into space and held in place by the sun’s intense magnetic field.

He photographed his first solar eclipse in 1999, in what he thought would be a one-off lark. During that eclipse, the moon’s deep shadow missed Druckmüller’s native Czechia by just a few tens of kilometers, so he chased it to Hungary with a 30-year-old Soviet MTO 1,000-millimeter lens. All he remembers from that day is the rush of adrenaline he felt while trying to find the sun in the sky with the lens’s minuscule field of view and keep it in focus for the two minutes of the eclipse.

He insists that he has never enjoyed any of the eclipses he has photographed. “In fact, I have never properly seen any of those eclipses. You are just watching the screens, making sure that it’s all doing what it’s supposed to do. There are so many things that can go wrong and you can’t redo it.”

A composite sequence of photographs shows the 12 August 2026 solar eclipse as seen from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain.

Despite Druckmüller’s outward tranquility on this Spanish hillside, the stakes are high. Just 45 minutes ago, his group heard from their colleagues in Iceland, where viewing conditions had promised to be better than in Spain. But a vast low-pressure system had clouded the entire sky, leaving all three Iceland teams without a view.

On the Pico Trigaza mountain in Spain, two postgraduate researchers used a laser to get a rough, initial alignment for the tracking mount of an optical instrument. The alignment was necessary to precisely compensate for the Earth’s motion.

The corona has been a mystery for centuries. Though dimmer—by a factor of a million—than the sun’s visible surface, the corona is nevertheless extremely hot: about a million degrees Celsius compared to 5,500 degrees on the surface. Because the sun’s nuclear fusion engine churns at the star’s heart, it might seem that temperatures should fall farther from the core.

To observe the faint corona in visible light, researchers must block the sun’s ferocious glare. Specialized telescopes called coronagraphs do this with an opaque disk called an occulter. But because light bends around the occulter’s edges in an effect called diffraction, it must block an area much larger than that of the solar disk to prevent light from spilling over and ruining the images. But doing so means obstructing the inner part of the corona, which harbors the most important processes that underpin the puzzling phenomena of the sun’s upper atmosphere.

That’s why total eclipses matter so much to solar physicists. By sheer chance, the moon is exactly the right size and at just the right distance to completely cover the sun during a total solar eclipse. Because the moon is so far away from Earth, the view is not marred by diffraction, and the corona reveals itself nearly all the way down to the sun’s surface.

As astrocameras recorded spectral data about the sun’s corona, a laptop computer [on table, at left] displayed the phase of the eclipse.

Space probes can image the solar surface in other wavelengths, but those views have limitations, too. Spacecraft such as NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory do see the innermost parts of the corona in extreme ultraviolet light, explains Shadia Habbal, a solar physicist at the University of Hawaii and leader of the Solar Wind Sherpas project. “But it cuts off very quickly, so you don’t see its extension into space as well as we can see it in the visible emission lines” during an eclipse. “That’s the biggest advantage,” she says, of solar eclipse photography.

The European Proba-3 mission, launched in 2024, simulates total solar eclipses by flying two spacecraft in a formation 150 meters apart with one acting as an occulter and the other as the telescope. The instruments aboard that satellite, however, have limitations compared to the equipment used by the Solar Wind Sherpas team.

When Druckmüller developed the film from his 1999 eclipse expedition, the photographs didn’t do justice to the event’s eerie beauty. He spent countless evenings applying his expertise in numerical image processing in an attempt to re-create in his photographs the sights he witnessed in that Hungarian corn field.

It took two years, but eventually he succeeded. Where before there were dull views of the blackened lunar disk surrounded by the blunt wisps of the corona, Druckmüller revealed the subtlest details of the magnetic field lines stretching from the sun far into space. As his photographs circulated among solar physicists, invitations to eclipse expeditions began to arrive.

Solar researchers Miloslav Druckmüller and Shadia Habbal have been collaborating for two decades and 15 eclipses.

Habbal learned about the images from a Ph.D. student who had seen them at a conference presentation that didn’t credit Druckmüller. When Habbal’s team later published the images in a paper, they misattributed them to another researcher. Druckmüller found out through an astrophysicist friend. “I wrote her a rather disappointed email and she responded within 10 minutes,” Druckmüller recalls. “She really didn’t have a clue.”

The error was corrected, and within weeks, Habbal and Druckmüller began a collaboration that grew into a friendship. “Milos’s processing brings out details that nobody has seen before, and they tell you a lot about very tiny features in the corona that you don’t see otherwise,” says Habbal.

Capturing the corona’s delicate structures means finding a way to show its brightest and faintest features in the same image. “During the solar eclipse, the contrast between the darkest and brightest parts of the corona is enormous, possibly one to a million,” Druckmüller explains. “But a computer monitor only allows you to display a contrast ratio of one to about 800.” (Some modern monitors, particularly OLED ones, can deliver higher contrast ratios.)

The human eye can adjust to this enormous range of brightness, allowing an observer to see both the bright corona and the faint stars and planets that briefly emerge in the darkened sky. To bring those details together in a photograph, Druckmüller uses custom image-processing algorithms to combine exposures that capture different parts of that range.

Researchers Martin Šebek and Peter Urgoš make fine adjustments to the focus and alignment of the astrocameras on a key optical instrument before the 12 August solar eclipse.

To create a single image, Druckmüller’s teams need to take 200 individual frames during the eclipse at exposure times ranging from 0.001 second to two seconds. The data must then be calibrated against a vast number of reference images to filter out noise and imperfections. Flat fields, which depict a uniform light background, help correct for defects caused by telescope optics, dust spots, and variations in pixel sensitivity. Dark frames, taken with light blocked from the sensor, help correct for artifacts created by the camera’s image sensor itself. “It takes the computer more than two days to process one image,” Druckmüller says. Including the calibration data, a single finished image requires about 3,000 input frames.

Since 2008, teams directed by Habbal and Druckmüller have traveled to every total solar eclipse, spreading out across multiple locations to hedge against bad weather. About half of the teams return with usable data. For the others, it’s just a short and stressful voyage. For the 12 August eclipse, three groups deployed to Iceland and two to Spain.

The teams seek sites close to the center of the band of totality, where the moon blocks the sun for longest. In Spain, the 12 August band of totality cut across the north of the country; the center line of the shadow passed within 11 kilometers of Pico Trigaza, promising Druckmüller and his colleagues a precious 107 seconds of totality.

But duration is only part of the calculation. Totality on Pico Trigaza will commence 51 minutes before sunset, with the sun just 8 degrees above the horizon. That low, the rays must pass through a much thicker layer of the atmosphere than when the sun is higher in the sky, increasing the light distortion that complicates photography. At the researchers’ camp on Pico Trigaza, 1,600 meters above sea level, the thinner air should help a bit.

An abandoned hut on the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain was spruced up so that it could serve as a home base for the research team recording the 12 August solar eclipse.

“Iceland would have been a much better place for us than Spain because the sun was higher up, some 25 degrees above the horizon,” Druckmüller says wistfully. But Iceland’s notoriously unpredictable weather made Spain an essential backup.

If you pack a van with thousands of dollars’ worth of cameras and optical gear and then set out on a 2,351-kilometer journey, you shouldn’t be surprised if you finish the trip with a few striking photographs [top]. The sleeping arrangements for the grad students at the Pico Trigaza hut [bottom] were spartan, but the views were first-rate.Top: Martin Šebek; Bottom: Václav Široký

On the mountain, locals have spruced up a rustic, long-unused hut for the researchers, running power cables from a nearby telecommunication outpost and bringing in a water tank. Five Ph.D. students drove more than 2,000 kilometers from Brno and have spent nearly a week preparing the equipment. Druckmüller and his wife joined them two days before the eclipse. They cook on a small propane grill and sleep in sleeping bags on yoga mats. “We have plenty of space here to set up our telescopes, beautiful views, and a roof over our heads,” Druckmüller says with a grin. “It’s perfect.”

But even the best equipment and a carefully chosen site count for nothing if the clouds roll in. “So much work goes into the preparations and then, if you end up with nothing, you just feel terrible sadness,” says Jana Hoderová, an assistant professor of mathematics at Brno University of Technology and one of Druckmüller’s key collaborators.

As the moon continues to slide in front of the solar disk, the pesky cumulus cloud that kept everybody on edge begins to dissolve. It’s 10 minutes to totality. The relief is palpable.

The countdown on the computers that control the cameras has begun. The screens are now showing only a tiny orange sliver, and the evening is becoming perceptibly less bright.

Twenty astrophotography cameras, most of them drawing power from a car battery that was also buffering the cameras from any grid instabilities, are pointed at the sun. Alongside equipment capturing the corona’s visible light, the team has built an assembly of eight cameras to detect light emitted by various iron ions that arise in the corona.

Among the optical gear assembled at Pico Trigaza to capture the 12 August solar eclipse was a unique instrument designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona [at left]. Václav Široký

Those instruments looking for iron ions have been put together with resourcefulness and thrift. A colleague of Druckmüller’s laser-cut the aluminum plates holding the carefully aligned lenses in exchange “for two bottles of whisky.” The brackets and attachments were 3D-printed at Brno University of Technology. The lenses, produced for the defunct camera maker Contax, were bought at steep discounts on eBay. By far the most expensive elements are interference filters that isolate the wavelengths emitted by the iron ions.

Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still.

“That’s something nobody else in the world can do,” Druckmüller says with visible satisfaction. The unique technology, codeveloped with Habbal’s Hawaii team, has already enabled researchers to map the distribution of temperatures across the entire corona and to discover previously unseen structures, dubbed “smoke rings,” in the coronal plasma. The photographs also revealed the boundary region where the solar plasma becomes so thin that its ions stop colliding.

The optical assembly designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona is outfitted with astrocameras, each of which captures spectra from a different ionic species. To do that, each astrocamera is equipped with a spectral filter whose bandwidth is so narrow—one nanometer—that the filter appears as a mirror.Martin Fornůsek

“Iron is the most abundant of the heavy elements that we see in the solar corona,” says Habbal. “And because the corona is so hot, the iron atoms lose electrons and get ionized. The larger the loss, the higher the temperature.”

For example, a temperature of around 1.6 million °C is necessary to produce an iron ion that has lost 12 electrons. But only 1.4 million °C is needed to strip an iron atom of 11 electrons. Once it’s in a particular electrical state, the ion retains its specific ionization, even as it travels outward with the solar wind. Each of those ions, whether +11 or +12, emits a different wavelength of light, allowing the researchers to map not just temperatures within the corona, but also how those iron ions spread into interplanetary space and distribute heat. Habbal and her colleagues had long been trying to image those iron ions during solar eclipses. But it wasn’t until Druckmüller entered the picture that they were able to develop the gear and the mathematical techniques to do it.

With just a minute to go to totality, the researchers begin removing protective filters from the lenses. It’s 50 minutes to sunset, and the waning sun has just begun to light up the clouds above the horizon with the first tinge of orange. Then, suddenly, the evening begins a rapid and premature descent into darkness. Along the edge of the fantastically thin solar crescent, the brilliant orange points known as Baily’s Beads flash and disappear—the last fragments of photospheric light visible through deep lunar valleys. As totality begins, observers remove their glasses. The hot air cools. The graduate students remain quietly and intently focused on their gear.

Druckmüller looks up from his camera toward the darkened plains. Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still. The sky is ablaze with fiery colors all along the horizon where the deep lunar shadow drops off. Venus burns brilliantly in the southwest, a sharp white pinpoint in the darkened sky. The sound of camera shutters suddenly fills the air. Then, as quickly as it fell, the darkness begins to recede, bid farewell with another handful of golden Baily’s Beads.

The crowd erupts in cheers. The Ph.D. students throw themselves at each other and hug like they mean it.

“The students did most of the work this time, so I actually allowed myself to really look at it,” Druckmüller says. “It was beautiful. Pico Trigaza may not have been the best for science photography, but from the aesthetic point of view, it was extraordinary.”

The 2026 solar-eclipse team at Pico Trigaza in Spain included [from left] Magdalena Šrotířová, Peter Urgoš, Martin Fornůsek, Miloslav Druckmüller, Václav Široký, and Martin Šebek.Václav Široký

But for Druckmüller, this is just the beginning. While other eclipse chasers will race to release their images, he will take his time. He expects to publish the first visible-light images of the corona in about two weeks. Processing the iron-ion images, and uncovering whatever insights they may hold, will take months—maybe even a whole year.

“Probably until the next eclipse in 2027” in North Africa, Druckmüller says.

Who knows? Maybe he’ll even enjoy that one, too.

Tereza Pultarova is a London-based journalist specializing in aerospace and defense technologies. She is a native of the Czech Republic.

Those are some pretty impressive photos! It also seems like the iron ion filtering is pretty unique. I love seeing cases where people build something they want to see in the world with minimal outside support. Seems like it would be a solid return on more public money to seek out and support scrappy projects like this one.

#3292. WhatsApp’s AI-powered photo expansion tool starts rolling out on iOS

Select WhatsApp users on TestFlight and in the main app are now seeing the option to expand an image in the app’s photo editor. Here are the details.

iPhone users with access to Apple Intelligence have a native AI-powered photo expansion tool called Extend, which lets users pinch or drag to expand an image beyond its original borders.

This feature, which is also present on AI chatbots such as ChatGPT and image-editing platforms like Photoshop, is now also making its way into WhatsApp.

According to WABetaInfo, the platform is rolling out a Meta AI-powered image expansion tool, though it is currently limited to select users, primarily those in WhatsApp’s beta program via TestFlight.

When users select a photo in their chats, WhatsApp opens the drawing editor. Here, they can choose to apply some AI effect to improve it. Among these, users can find a new option to expand their photos. Once users select this option, Meta AI takes a few seconds to analyze the photo and generate the expanded version. Once the process is complete, WhatsApp shows the expanded photo in the drawing editor, and users can choose to send it. Note that this feature is also compatible with status updates.

The site notes that if the user isn’t happy with the result, they can tap an undo button to revert to the original and then try using the tool again to generate a different result.

As is usually the case with beta features on WhatsApp, there is no telling when it might become widely available.

That said, given that it has also rolled out to users in the Android beta and some users on the public iOS version already have access, a broader rollout might not be too far off.

#3291. MVB Financial: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

AI-driven cost cuts are offsetting credit headwinds, a rare operational strength that could sustain profitability through cycles.

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Oct. 29, 2026, MVB Financial (MVBF +1.33%) reported expanding core profit margins despite taking an elevated loan loss provision. Fintech deposit growth and strict cost discipline position the bank to offset credit noise over time.

Core net interest margin, the spread earned on loans above funding costs, expanded sequentially to 4.02%. Rapid growth in lower-cost payment partner deposits helped drive the margin improvement across MVB Financial.

A single land loan caused nearly three-quarters of the quarterly increase in nonperforming loans, defined as loans where borrowers are behind on payments. Management established specific reserves for the credit and confirmed the broader loan portfolio shows no widespread deterioration.

Noninterest expense, or operating overhead costs, fell 10% year over year to $29.8 million. Management automated workflows by launching internal digital tools and training engineers on artificial intelligence software.

Specialized loan demand remains active, and fintech partner onboarding continues to accelerate. Management leverages its national digital footprint to maintain steady balance sheet growth.

Priorities for 2027 focus on margin optimization and onboarding higher-yield financial technology clients.

#3290. Apollo-backed Brightspeed seeks up to $3B from creditors for fibre

The rural broadband provider has about $10B of debt and has warned it may not survive as a going concern.

Fibre optic cables connected to telecommunications equipment in a network rack.

Brightspeed, a US fibre broadband provider owned by Apollo, is in talks with creditors to raise $2B to $3B of new money, Bloomberg reports. It has about $10B of debt, has warned about its survival, and may file for bankruptcy as soon as December.

Brightspeed, an Apollo-backed US fibre broadband provider, is in talks to raise $2B to $3B of new money from its creditors. That is according to Bloomberg, which cited people familiar with the matter on Friday. The amount, and whether the deal will go through a bankruptcy court, are still being worked out.

Brightspeed and Apollo declined to comment. The Wall Street Journal reported last week that the company could file for bankruptcy as soon as December, Light Reading reported.

Brightspeed has about $10B of debt and warned in September that it may not be able to continue as a going concern. Nearly all its debt trades at distressed levels: one $2.5B loan was quoted at about 17 cents on the dollar on Friday.

Brightspeed was formed in 2022, when Apollo bought Lumen’s local phone and broadband business in 20 states for $7.5B. It is spending heavily to bring fibre to mostly rural and suburban areas there. It passed 3 million fibre-ready locations in April, and fibre sales are up 16% from a year earlier.

It has been through this before. In 2024, Brightspeed cut $1.1B of debt and raised $3.7B of new capital in a deal with its lenders. This month, it named Shawn O’Donnell, a former senior managing director at FTI Consulting, as chief executive.

Apollo is better known in tech circles for its lending to AI, including a $36B debt deal it is arranging with Blackstone to buy chips for Anthropic. Lumen, meanwhile, has turned to AI customers, and this week agreed to sell AI networks with Microsoft.

#3288. Use Your Year-End Review to Reach for a Promotion

Maintaining a document of your successes throughout the year gives you a starting point

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, a program that helps engineers through hands-on training.

This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!

When I landed my first job as a software engineer, I had a simple plan: Work hard and somebody would notice. Eventually a manager would tap me on the shoulder and hand me a promotion (probably with a nice little speech).

That plan stalled my career for about five years.

I switched jobs twice, kept my head down, read a stack of programming books, and sometimes pulled 12-hour days. I was never promoted. At my third job, out of frustration, I started interviewing at other companies and almost immediately got an offer for a senior engineer role.

So I went back to my job and quit. My team was blindsided. I liked my manager and the people I worked with, and they came back with a counteroffer. Then someone from HR asked me, “Why didn’t you just ask us?”

I took the counteroffer and stayed. Three jobs in, I finally got promoted, and all it took was asking (in the most dramatic way possible).

Today, I would take a different approach.

Year-end review discussions are a great time to push for a promotion. But at most companies, raises and promotions are largely settled before the formal review conversation happens. If the year-end review is the first time your manager hears you want a promotion, you’re usually too late.

Now is a great time to start the conversation.

Engineers tend to believe good work speaks for itself. It rarely does. Your manager is juggling a team, a roadmap, and their own boss. They see a fraction of what you do, and the work they don’t see might as well not exist when raises get decided.

Perception is reality, so you have to shape it. That means learning to brag a little.

A “brag document” is a running list of what you accomplished, when, and why it mattered. Add to it every two weeks or once a month, and write each entry so your manager’s manager would understand it.

Engineers tend to write things like “migrated the billing service.” A better entry reads “migrated the billing service, which cut failed payments by 30 percent and unblocked the Q3 pricing launch.” If there’s no number, name who benefited and how.

Include the work people forget to count, too: handling incidents, mentoring new hires, interviewing candidates, and writing the docs everyone else relies on. If you helped your team adopt AI tools this year, write that down. (It counts as leadership, whether or not anyone called it that.)

The document does two jobs. It gives you ammunition when you make your case, and it gives your manager something to ctrl + c then ctrl + v when they argue for you in meetings you’ll never attend.

Bragging builds the case. Asking forces action.

If your goal is a promotion or a raise, you might ask: “What would it take for me to get to [the next level] in the next year?”

A good manager will give you an outline that can turn into a plan. Push for specifics until you have deliverables you can work toward, then send a short recap email so the plan exists somewhere besides your manager’s memory. (Managers change jobs too.)

Sometimes the answer will still be “not this year,” and the reason may have nothing to do with you.

Budgets get frozen, promotion slots get capped, and decisions get made above your manager’s head where even a manager who wants to help can’t.

Don’t read too much into that. But be honest with yourself, too. Most of the time, a no means there’s something you aren’t doing yet. Find out what it is instead of guessing for five years like I did.

Asking costs you one slightly awkward conversation. Sitting back and waiting to be noticed can cost you years.

Don’t try this at home: To better understand the risk AI slop poses to scientific publishing today, IEEE Spectrum contributor Benjamin Skuse put IEEE’s research integrity checks to the test by submitting two entirely AI-generated papers. “Science has a spam problem. And the spam filter is getting clogged up…”

Policy change doesn’t just come down to paid lobbyists—lawmakers want to hear from working experts, too. One engineer shares what he learned from his first two visits to Capitol Hill.

Could community colleges help fill the coming talent shortage in the U.S. semiconductor industry? Alternatives to four-year university degrees are a promising option for the technicians who will be needed to run new fabs.

#3287. Apple explains how to turn off the new MacBook Pro’s glowing logo

While the illuminated Apple logo on the new MacBook Pro drew one of the biggest cheers during last week’s announcement, Apple knows that not everyone will want to keep it on. Here’s the company’s official guide to turning it off.

The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display marks the return of the illuminated Apple logo on its lid after a decade.

As Chance Miller explained in his review of the new MacBook Pro, “unlike older MacBooks, which used light from the display’s backlight to illuminate the logo, the new OLED MacBook Pro has no backlight to draw from, requiring a different approach.”

He added that, as with the old Macs, the logo’s brightness is tied to the screen brightness, though it also accounts for overall ambient brightness. He also noted that “when the MacBook Pro is closed, the logo looks like polished metal, just like it has since the 2016 redesign.”

The review echoed some of the findings developer Gui Rambo shared on X a few days ago:

The glowing Apple logo on the new MacBook Pro is controllable by software. It has 25kHz PWM and per-device calibration. CoreBrightness controls the relationship between screen and logo brightness. The brightness of the logo is adjusted differently depending on the enclosure color pic.twitter.com/baqBEkzJUo

Now, Apple has published an official support document that also explains how the illuminated logo works and how to turn it off completely.

The Apple logo behind the built-in display is illuminated whenever the Mac is awake. It automatically dims or brightens based on the brightness level of the built-in screen and the lighting conditions detected by the computer’s ambient light sensor. For all screen-brightness levels, the Apple logo will be dimmer in a dim room and brighter in a bright room.

For users who’d rather keep the logo turned off at all times, Apple explains that they can run the following command in Terminal, provided they have the administrator password:

sudo defaults write com.apple.CoreBrightness LEBacklightMode -int 0

Since it's actually two, opposite, single line command states;

Why can't it simply be an on/off button, in Settings?

To revert the command and have the logo be illuminated again, users will need to run the following command:

sudo defaults delete com.apple.CoreBrightness LEBacklightMode

Apple notes that reinstalling macOS will also turn the logo illumination back on.
